Discussion Name:
What is the best religion to believe?

1. Question:
What religion [1] should people follow?

  1.1. Thesis:
  Judaism [2]

    1.1.1. Pro:
    Following Judaism is beneficial to society.

      1.1.1.1. Pro:
      The Jewish practice of tikkun olam promotes social responsibility [3] and seeks to improve the world.

        1.1.1.1.1. Con:
        Tikkun olam has overwhelmingly become associated with liberal politics [4], ignoring other perspectives that can contribute to social good.

        1.1.1.1.2. Pro:
        A great deal of charity and altruism [5] are motivated by tikkun olam.

      1.1.1.2. Pro:
      Judaism teaches a beneficial moral code.

        1.1.1.2.1. Con:
        Judaism is too legalistic, and some Jews still follow outdated laws [6] from the Torah.

          1.1.1.2.1.1. Pro:
          Haredi Jewish men largely devote themselves to studying the Torah rather than working, which contributes to high levels of poverty [7] within Haredi communities.

          1.1.1.2.1.2. Con:
          The majority of Jews throughout the world don't follow [8] the 613 commandments [9] in the Torah, but rather the legal codes of the Rabbis written centuries later, which allow a great deal of room for debate and interpretation.

        1.1.1.2.2. Con:
        Judaism is not a moral code, but an expression of Shema [10], which commands that one love God.

        1.1.1.2.3. Pro:
        Judaism insists that its adherents consider moral questions, to the point that they are called upon to argue with God. This prevents them from being sloppy or lazy in considerations of scripture.

        1.1.1.2.4. Pro:
        Jews consider the Golden Rule to be the essence [11] of all Halakhah [12].

      1.1.1.3. Con:
      Judaic law is imbued with misogyny [13].

        1.1.1.3.1. Pro:
        The Torah teaches that menstruating women are unclean [14] and should be ostracised [15].

          1.1.1.3.1.1. Con:
          Similar standards are applied to men. For instance, when a man has an 'emission of semen [16]', he is also unclean.

          1.1.1.3.1.2. Pro:
          The Torah [17] has been used as justification for enforcing menstrual exile on women (p. 63 [18]).

        1.1.1.3.2. Pro:
        Judaism permits husbands to abuse their wives [19] in some situations and does not view such beatings as grounds for divorce.

        1.1.1.3.3. Con:
        Judaic law does not prescribe specific roles for women and promotes a reverence for motherhood (pp. 48–49 [20]).

      1.1.1.4. Con:
      Judaic law was codified at a very different time and place from the modern world; many Judaic laws would be considered violations of human rights [21] in modern society.

        1.1.1.4.1. Pro:
        The Torah requires women who are victims of rape to marry their assailant [22].

        1.1.1.4.2. Con:
        Judaic law need not be, and often is not, followed to the letter. Judaic reform movements have dispensed with many of the outdated practices and distinctions, giving women first-class status.

    1.1.2. Pro:
    Following Judaism has positive benefits for the individual.

      1.1.2.1. Con:
      Converting to Judaism only makes sense for personal and emotional reasons because it imposes rules and restrictions [23] without offering any advantages to those who are not ethnically Jewish [24].

        1.1.2.1.1. Con:
        In modern congregations, the full personal and social benefits of Judaism are fully available to converts [25].

        1.1.2.1.2. Pro:
        Following Judaism can present many obstacles [26] to those who are not ethnically Jewish.

      1.1.2.2. Con:
      Jewish men exhibit a higher rate of major depression than their non-Jew peers (p. 945 [27]).

        1.1.2.2.1. Con:
        Judaism does not promote belief in Hell [28], which has been shown to have profoundly negative psychological effects [29].

        1.1.2.2.2. Pro:
        Depression can be particularly challenging for Orthodox Jews, who often hold a strong antipathy towards modern psychotherapy [30].

      1.1.2.3. Pro:
      Jewish spirituality is compatible with the realities of human life [31] and does not place unreasonable restrictions on the lifestyle or emotions of followers.

        1.1.2.3.1. Pro:
        Judaism teaches that pleasure is a sufficient motivation for sex [32] rather than requiring procreative intent.

        1.1.2.3.2. Con:
        Many traditional and orthodox branches of Judaism are largely incompatible with modern society (p. 73 [33]).

      1.1.2.4. Pro:
      It is fun to participate in Jewish culture via music, festivals, and foods that date back thousands of years.

        1.1.2.4.1. Con:
        Anyone can participate in Jewish cultural traditions [34] without believing or following the religion.

        1.1.2.4.2. Pro:
        The community and cultural aspects of Judaism hold social value independent of religious doctrine.

    1.1.3. Pro:
    Judaism is a complete and well-established system of belief.

      1.1.3.1. Con:
      Despite the importance of the messiah concept in Judaism, there is a lack of consensus and clarity [35] in Jewish teachings on the subject.

        1.1.3.1.1. Con:
        The eventual coming [36] of a Messiah is never mentioned in the Torah, indicating that it is likely a later belief.

        1.1.3.1.2. Pro:
        Modern scholars view the lack of Torah references to a Messiah as reason to discount the concept, while traditional Judaism [37] maintains that the Messiah has always been an article of faith.

      1.1.3.2. Con:
      In some places, such as the US, a low birth rate, increased intermarriage, and successful assimilation are projected to drastically reduce the number of Jews [38] in the coming decades.

        1.1.3.2.1. Con:
        The total number of Jews in the world has continued to increase [39], so there is little danger of Judaism becoming extinct.

        1.1.3.2.2. Pro:
        In countries other than Israel and the US [40], it may become increasingly difficult for people to find a Jewish community in which they can participate.

      1.1.3.3. Pro:
      Judaism allows for intellectual and spiritual differences among adherents, with some denominations [41] even allowing agnosticism.

        1.1.3.3.1. Pro:
        Some branches of Judaism hold that religion can – and should – change with the times [42] to better reflect the realities of modern life.

        1.1.3.3.2. Con:
        The diversity of Jewish belief has contributed to greater division amongst Jewish communities (pp. 9–10 [43]).

      1.1.3.4. Pro:
      Judaism is truly ancient, with origins going back to the Bronze Age [44], before the widespread use of writing.

        1.1.3.4.1. Con:
        The long history of Judaism as a predominantly oral tradition [45] undermines claims of scriptural accuracy and authenticity.

        1.1.3.4.2. Pro:
        Jews have survived persecution and attacks [46] throughout history, showing that the religion can survive through anything.

        1.1.3.4.3. Pro:
        Judaic teachings and scriptures have been well preserved thanks to the successful maintenance [47] of the Hebrew language since ancient times.

    1.1.4. Con:
    There is no evidence to support the assertions of Judaism.

      1.1.4.1. Pro:
      The teachings of Judaism promote belief in angels [48].

        1.1.4.1.1. Con:
        Belief in angels is not a requirement in Judaism, and many devout Jews do not believe [49] in their literal existence.

        1.1.4.1.2. Pro:
        Angels play a key role in Jewish scripture; to doubt their existence would undermine the authority of the Torah and Talmud [50].

      1.1.4.2. Con:
      Many Jews eschew dogmatic belief and rely on rationality and common sense over strict teachings and interpretations (p. 239 [51]).

        1.1.4.2.1. Pro:
        Modern forms of Judaism accept scientific evidence [52] and do not insist on the literal interpretation of scripture.

          1.1.4.2.1.1. Pro:
          There is a sigificant proportion [53] of Jews in the scientific community, demonstrating the compatibility of their beliefs with empiricism.

        1.1.4.2.2. Con:
        Modern Orthodox Jewish communities eschew some scientific practices, such as treatment of mental health issues (p. 74 [54]).

      1.1.4.3. Pro:
      A number of events in the Torah lack sufficient evidence to justify belief.

        1.1.4.3.1. Pro:
        Jewish scripture contains many examples of miracles [55] that are both improbable and lack empirical evidence.

        1.1.4.3.2. Con:
        The principal articles of Jewish faith do not rest on the historicity of the Torah [56].

        1.1.4.3.3. Pro:
        The Exodus described in the Torah [57] lacks archaeological evidence.

      1.1.4.4. Con:
      The Jewish understanding of the creation narrative supports the theory of evolution (p. 4 [58]).

        1.1.4.4.1. Pro:
        Most modern branches of Judaism do not find the theory of evolution [59] problematic in respect to their religious beliefs.

        1.1.4.4.2. Con:
        Traditional Jews rely on a literal reading of the Torah [60] and reject the theory of evolution, considering it opposed to their faith.

    1.1.5. Con:
    Judaism is a source of human conflict.

      1.1.5.1. Pro:
      Judaism has been responsible for a number of wars and armed conflicts.

        1.1.5.1.1. Con:
        Judaism is a religion of peace [61] and strongly advocates avoiding violence, unless as a last resort [62].

        1.1.5.1.2. Con:
        Some wars are fought for valid reasons and are necessary. This is demonstrated by the many wars God prompted the Jews to fight on His behalf in the Old Testament.

          1.1.5.1.2.1. Con:
          The ancient Jewish people were responsible for a number of massacres, including the slaughter of the Bashan [63] people.

        1.1.5.1.3. Pro:
        The Jewish democratic state [64] of Israel regularly performs raids in the West Bank [65], during which many non-combatant Palestinians have been killed.

        1.1.5.1.4. Pro:
        Jewish terrorist groups, such as the Sicarii [66], the Lehi [67], and the Jewish Defense League [68], have carried out fatal attacks.

          1.1.5.1.4.1. Con:
          The actions of these parties are in no way condoned or encouraged by Jewish community leadership.

        1.1.5.1.5. Pro:
        The Judean Civil War [69] was a war between the Jewish Pharisees and Sadducees.

      1.1.5.2. Pro:
      The idea that the Jewish people are chosen by God [70] is divisive. It is dangerous to normalise a belief that membership in an ethnic, religious, or linguistic group confers special status.

        1.1.5.2.1. Con:
        Judaism includes the Noahide Laws [71], which are meant to be followed by all righteous non-Jewish people. Therefore, Judaism includes a system for both Jews and non-Jews that expects different things from each group.

          1.1.5.2.1.1. Con:
          It is unclear why any non-Jew would have reason to follow Judaic laws.

        1.1.5.2.2. Pro:
        Ethnoreligious [72] interpretations of Judaism have been used in support of anti-Semitic ideology.

      1.1.5.3. Con:
      Jewish people do not proselytise [73].

        1.1.5.3.1. Pro:
        Judaism doesn't actively proselytise [74], which encourages people to choose a path that makes sense to them rather than conform to pressure.

        1.1.5.3.2. Con:
        Membership in the Jewish community has traditionally been considered a matrilineally passed trait, implying that the religion is only open to those from a specific ethnic background (pp. 475–6 [75]).

      1.1.5.4. Con:
      Judaism has no history of abuses of power.

        1.1.5.4.1. Pro:
        Judaism has never killed heretics, burned heretical documents, or persecuted religious minorities.

        1.1.5.4.2. Con:
        Judaic law supports the death penalty [76] for both significant and trivial offenses.

          1.1.5.4.2.1. Con:
          The punishments mentioned in the Torah are the maximum allowable punishments [77], not the standard or common punishments. Although allowed by law, 'death sentences were rarely [78] carried out by Jewish courts'.

          1.1.5.4.2.2. Con:
          In Israel, the only country governed by Judaic law, the death penalty has been all but abolished since 1954 [79] except in cases of genocide.

    1.1.6. Con:
    Judaism takes advantage of its followers.

      1.1.6.1. Pro:
      There have been widespread instances of sexual abuse [80] by religious leaders in some Jewish communities [81].

        1.1.6.1.1. Pro:
        Victims of abuse in traditional, closed Jewish communities are often discouraged [82] from seeking help and support from authorities. This allows the perpetrators to continue their abuse without facing repercussions.

        1.1.6.1.2. Con:
        Numerous Jewish organizations have been founded to identify and prevent [83] cases of abuse and provide support [84] to victims [85].

      1.1.6.2. Con:
      Jewish lenders are forbidden from collecting interest from Jewish borrowers [86], which maintains a focus on developing good relationships.

        1.1.6.2.1. Pro:
        Modern organisations, such as the Jewish Free Loan Association [87], offer interest-free emergency loans to Jews and non-Jews alike.

        1.1.6.2.2. Con:
        Scholars have argued that the Jewish prohibition against charging interest should be equally applied [88] to those of Abrahamic faiths or to any who treat Judaism with respect.

      1.1.6.3. Con:
      Virtually all Jewish communities have a tzedakah fund [89] set aside to help members who find themselves in financial difficulty.

        1.1.6.3.1. Con:
        Some rabbis fraudulently misappropriate charitable donations [90] made to their synagogue, so support for members in need may be unavailable.

        1.1.6.3.2. Pro:
        Tzedekah funds are often used to support a wide range of humanitarian and social causes [91] in the wider community.

      1.1.6.4. Pro:
      Rabbis have encouraged members of their communities to participate in fraudulent financial practices [92], putting them at risk of serious consequences.

        1.1.6.4.1. Pro:
        Rabbi Yisroel Goldstein convinced members of his congregation to participate in tax fraud [93] by helping them claim tax deductions for USD $6.2 million of fake donations in exchange for 10% of their reduced taxes.

        1.1.6.4.2. Con:
        Most modern rabbis draw competitive salaries [94] from their congregations, and have little need [95] to abuse their position for financial gain.

  1.2. Thesis:
  Vodou [96]

    1.2.1. Pro:
    Following Vodou has positive benefits for the individual.

      1.2.1.1. Pro:
      Vodou has helped enslaved African people to maintain their beliefs and identity [97] and can help followers understand and manage the suffering brought on by oppressive circumstances.

        1.2.1.1.1. Pro:
        Vodou has provided enslaved people with a means of resistance and resilience, operating as both a religion and a means of survival (p. 3 [98]).

        1.2.1.1.2. Con:
        The West African roots [99] of Vodou belief do not adequately represent the range of identities and beliefs held by the different ethnocultural groups [100] affected by the Atlantic slave trade.

      1.2.1.2. Pro:
      Vodou supports the reclamation of personal power [101] and agency [102] over one's life.

        1.2.1.2.1. Con:
        By placing a high value on individual power, Vodou can promote self-serving behaviour and victim blaming [103].

        1.2.1.2.2. Pro:
        Vodou beliefs and rituals helped restore the agency of enslaved African peoples to such an extent that they were able to overthrow colonial oppression (pp. 24–25 [104]).

      1.2.1.3. Con:
      Vodou belief in divine punishment and the marginalisation of the religion can make Vodou adherents more prone to PTSD and depression (p. 4 [105]).

        1.2.1.3.1. Pro:
        Even in Haiti, Vodou practitioners are often harassed or even attacked [106] for their beliefs.

        1.2.1.3.2. Con:
        High levels of depression in Haiti are attributable to poverty, violence, and political disorder rather than belief in Vodou (pp. vii–viii [107]).

      1.2.1.4. Con:
      Belief in Vodou discourages followers from seeking modern solutions [108] to common problems.

        1.2.1.4.1. Pro:
        The belief in supernatural causes associated with Vodou can disincentivise followers from seeking biomedical treatment for mental health issues (p. 3 [109]).

        1.2.1.4.2. Con:
        Modern solutions are beyond the financial means of many Haitians, who rely on Vodou priests [110] for a wide range of social services.

    1.2.2. Pro:
    Vodou is a complete and well-established system of belief.

      1.2.2.1. Con:
      Vodou is not a distinct religion; it is a syncretic tradition that blends Christianity with Western [111] and Central African [112] beliefs.

        1.2.2.1.1. Pro:
        The adoption of Christian elements in Vodou was driven by the desire to avoid religious oppression rather than by acceptance of Christian doctrine (p. 11 [113]).

          1.2.2.1.1.1. Con:
          The adoption of Christian beliefs in Vodou often extends only to names, while the underlying beliefs remain unchanged (pp. 1–2 [114]).

        1.2.2.1.2. Con:
        Most religions include elements adopted from other traditions [115] via intercultural contact. The adoption of beliefs and practices from other religions does not diminish the legitimacy or authenticity of Vodou as a distinct religion (p. 3 [116]).

      1.2.2.2. Pro:
      Vodou has increasingly focused on the establishment of official organisations, churches, and teachings (p. 27 [117]).

        1.2.2.2.1. Pro:
        Since 2003, when Vodou was been granted official religious status by the Haitian government; Vodou temples have instituted literacy projects [118] to overcome the discrimination faced by followers in Christian schools.

        1.2.2.2.2. Con:
        Many international Vodou temples have been founded as tourist destinations and focus on creating exoticised stereotypes of Vodou practices rather than authentic encounters with the religion (pp. 24–25 [119]).

      1.2.2.3. Con:
      There is no comprehensive history of Vodou practices, and it lacks authoritative sources (p. 1 [120]).

        1.2.2.3.1. Pro:
        Vodou's lack of centralised, authoritative sources contributes to its continued misrepresentation [121] in Western pop culture.

        1.2.2.3.2. Con:
        Scholars have increasingly sought to accurately document Vodou beliefs and practices [122] and establish a more objective context [123] for its history.

      1.2.2.4. Pro:
      Vodou beliefs are based upon traditional African beliefs, such as the Vodun religion [124], and are thus a manifestation of established ancient belief systems.

        1.2.2.4.1. Pro:
        The West African roots of Vodou extend back for thousands of years [125] prior to the Atlantic slave trade.

        1.2.2.4.2. Con:
        Despite drawing on traditional African and Catholic sources, Vodou is a distinct tradition that was first established in 17th century Haiti [126].

    1.2.3. Pro:
    Following Vodou is beneficial to society.

      1.2.3.1. Con:
      Some Vodou rituals involve animal sacrifice [127]. This disregard for life is inhumane and increases harm in the universe.

        1.2.3.1.1. Con:
        Animal sacrifice within Vodou is usually performed during the ritual preparation of sacred meals [128]. In this way, it does not differ significantly from other forms of meat consumption.

        1.2.3.1.2. Pro:
        Animals in Vodou ritual slaughter [129] are often tortured and killed, subjecting them to pain and trauma.

      1.2.3.2. Pro:
      Vodou promotes equality.

        1.2.3.2.1. Pro:
        Vodou is accepting of LGBTQ+ [130] individuals.

        1.2.3.2.2. Pro:
        Vodou accepts and encourages both men and women into leadership [131].

        1.2.3.2.3. Con:
        Vodou reinforces cultural and economic divisiveness between the educated, urban class and rural residents (pp. 16, 32 [132]).

      1.2.3.3. Pro:
      Vodou values promote community cohesion (p. 5 [133]).

        1.2.3.3.1. Pro:
        Vodou has provided communities with resilience and organisation in times of oppression (p. 70 [134]).

        1.2.3.3.2. Con:
        The need for social inclusion is driving poverty [135] in many traditional vodou communities.

      1.2.3.4. Con:
      Vodou practitioners often act as a clandestine justice system [136] and have been known to employ poisons [137] to punish offenders.

        1.2.3.4.1. Con:
        Some victims of sexual assault have successfully pursued justice for their attackers [138] via Vodou rituals.

        1.2.3.4.2. Pro:
        At times, Vodou priests have been enlisted and deployed by colonial leaders as extrajudicial spies and assassins [139].

    1.2.4. Con:
    Vodou takes advantage of its followers.

      1.2.4.1. Pro:
      Vodou beliefs and practices have been widely exploited for commercial gain (pp. 12–13 [140]).

        1.2.4.1.1. Pro:
        Commercialised, tourist Vodou often reinforces stereotypical racist views of followers as primitive and animalistic (pp. 10–11 [141]).

        1.2.4.1.2. Con:
        The 60,000 Vodou priests in Haiti act as a primary social support system [142] and source of humanitarian aid [143] in their communities, where other forms of help are often unavailable.

      1.2.4.2. Con:
      Vodou priests provide medical services [144] to their communities.

        1.2.4.2.1. Pro:
        Vodou temples played a central role in helping Haitians through the coronavirus pandemic [145].

        1.2.4.2.2. Con:
        Vodou's widespread role in providing medical services is attributable to adherents' lack of access to modern medical care [146] rather than by efficacious medical practices.

      1.2.4.3. Pro:
      There have been allegations of sexual abuse [147] against Vodou priests.

        1.2.4.3.1. Pro:
        Vodou curses have been used to intimidate sex trafficking victims [148] into complying with their captors.

        1.2.4.3.2. Con:
        The incidence of rape in Haiti has often been greatly exaggerated by journalists and aid workers [149] in support of their agendas.

      1.2.4.4. Con:
      Rather than preying on Haitians affected by the 2010 earthquake, Vodou has, instead, played a key role in rebuilding efforts [150] by acting as a source of cultural tourism.

        1.2.4.4.1. Pro:
        Haitian travel agencies and websites often promote excursions where tourists can participate in Vodou [151] rituals and dances.

        1.2.4.4.2. Con:
        As a cultural tradition opposed to social progress [152], Vodou has contributed to Haitian poverty and vulnerability to natural disasters.

    1.2.5. Con:
    Vodou is a source of human conflict.

      1.2.5.1. Con:
      Vodou has often been unfairly scapegoated [153] by other religions and secular society.

        1.2.5.1.1. Pro:
        The US military misrepresented Vodou practices [154] as a pretext for continuing their occupation of Haiti, resulting in human rights abuses.

        1.2.5.1.2. Pro:
        Occurrences of cannibalism [155] have been falsely attributed to Vodou by authorities.

        1.2.5.1.3. Con:
        Though uncommon, the existence of several high-profile [156] Vodou murders [157] have understandably cast an indelible shadow over the religion.

      1.2.5.2. Pro:
      Vodou practitioners have contributed to inter-religious conflict by claiming to be Catholic yet secretly continuing Vodou practices [158] that are opposed by the Catholic church.

        1.2.5.2.1. Con:
        Many Vodou practitioners openly follow [159] Christianity whilst privately maintaining belief in Vodou to avoid continuing oppression from Catholic missionaries.

        1.2.5.2.2. Pro:
        A number of Vodou beliefs and practices are directly opposed to the teachings of Christianity [160].

      1.2.5.3. Pro:
      Vodou played a central role in starting the Haitian Revolution [161].

        1.2.5.3.1. Con:
        The unification provided by Vodou helped make the overthrow of barbaric colonial practices [162] possible.

        1.2.5.3.2. Pro:
        The Haitian Revolution resulted in the death of over 75,000 French and 350,000 Haitian people [163].

      1.2.5.4. Con:
      Vodou is tolerant of other religions.

        1.2.5.4.1. Pro:
        Despite widespread persecution of Vodou by religious authorities, its followers have remained tolerant and peaceful [164].

        1.2.5.4.2. Con:
        Most Vodou followers claim affiliation with at least one other religion [165].

    1.2.6. Con:
    There is no evidence to support the assertions of Vodou.

      1.2.6.1. Pro:
      Spirit possession [166] by supernatural entities is a central belief and practice of Vodou.

        1.2.6.1.1. Con:
        Vodou spirit possession often serves a cathartic role, helping practitioners to cope with chaotic and difficult circumstances (p. 2 [167]).

        1.2.6.1.2. Pro:
        Vodou promotes belief in supernatural beings, known as lwa [168], who intercede between a supreme God and humanity.

      1.2.6.2. Pro:
      Vodou promotes the belief that a dead person can be reanimated as a zombi [169].

        1.2.6.2.1. Con:
        Zombi are more accurately explained as a myth based upon Haitian shamanism and subconscious fear about slavery [170] than a Vodou teaching.

        1.2.6.2.2. Pro:
        Research attempting to offer scientific explanations of the creation of zombies has been widely discredited [171].

      1.2.6.3. Con:
      There is evidence that, in some cases, Vodou hexes have resulted in psychogenic death (p. 14 [172]).

        1.2.6.3.1. Con:
        Many supposed cases of psychogenic death have later been revealed as poisonings (pp. 8–9 [173]).

        1.2.6.3.2. Pro:
        Psychogenic death is explainable by science [174], and there is ample evidence of its existence.

      1.2.6.4. Con:
      Vodou adherents are often open to scientific evidence and promote evidence-based ecological policies [175].

        1.2.6.4.1. Pro:
        Vodou belief supports responsible management of natural resources [176].

        1.2.6.4.2. Con:
        Given the severe ongoing deforestation of Haiti [177], there is little evidence that belief in Vodou results in better environmental practices (p. 1 [178]).

  1.3. Thesis:
  Buddhism [179]

    1.3.1. Pro:
    Buddhism is a complete and well-established system of belief.

      1.3.1.1. Pro:
      There are distinct lineages [180] of Buddhist teachers, and each successive generation is required to achieve the same level of attainment as its predecessor. This promotes an orderly and uniform succession and transmission [181] of knowledge.

        1.3.1.1.1. Pro:
        Buddhism has an extensive collection of canonical texts [182].

          1.3.1.1.1.1. Con:
          Canonical Buddhist texts differ widely by region and language [183].

          1.3.1.1.1.2. Pro:
          The Pali Cannon [184] was written shortly after the death of the Buddha, and accurately represents the original teachings of Buddhism.

        1.3.1.1.2. Con:
        The different branches of Buddhism disagree on central matters [185], such as the nature of the Buddha, which shows inconsistency.

          1.3.1.1.2.1. Pro:
          Theravada [186] Buddhism teaches that enlightenment is only possible for ascetics, whereas Mahayana [187] Buddhism teaches that enlightenment can be achieved by all.

          1.3.1.1.2.2. Con:
          Despite their differences in teachings and interpretations, the different Buddhist traditions retain the same core elements [188].

      1.3.1.2. Pro:
      Buddhism has an organised structure [189], devoted temples [190], and a variety of established institutions [191].

        1.3.1.2.1. Pro:
        The Sangha, or Buddhist community [192], has been an essential pillar of Buddhism since its inception.

          1.3.1.2.1.1. Con:
          Monastic Buddhism and its institutions are later developments [193] and were not practised or recommended by the Buddha.

          1.3.1.2.1.2. Pro:
          Buddhist sanghas continue to fulfil a number of important functions [194] in modern society.

        1.3.1.2.2. Con:
        The numerous subtypes and schools [195] of Buddhism do not share a common organisational structure, and they operate and teach independently of each other.

          1.3.1.2.2.1. Pro:
          Although many people consider the Dalai Lama to be a leader of Buddhism, his expertise only extends to Tibetan Buddhism [196], and he is not the head of his lineage [197].

          1.3.1.2.2.2. Con:
          Regardless of their independent organisational structures, the three primary Buddhist schools [198] teach the same core doctrines.

      1.3.1.3. Con:
      Buddhism is more accurately considered a spiritual philosophy [199] than a religion in the commonly understood sense.

        1.3.1.3.1. Con:
        The teachings of Buddhism concern supernatural matters that fall outside the domain of philosophy (p. 7 [200]).

          1.3.1.3.1.1. Pro:
          Buddhist teachings are concerned with the nature of the afterlife and spiritual planes [201] of existence.

          1.3.1.3.1.2. Con:
          Although the Buddhist concept of karma constitutes a supernatural force [202], it is consistent with the philosophic concept of causation [203].

        1.3.1.3.2. Pro:
        Buddhist practice is based on experience [204] rather than dogma and theology.

          1.3.1.3.2.1. Con:
          Adherence to Buddhism requires faith [205] in its core teachings.

          1.3.1.3.2.2. Pro:
          The foundational beliefs of Buddhism are based on empirical observation [206].

      1.3.1.4. Con:
      The two truths doctrine [207] can be exploited by adherents to twist Buddhist teachings and change their meaning.

        1.3.1.4.1. Con:
        Conventional truth and absolute truth are demonstrably different [208].

          1.3.1.4.1.1. Pro:
          Individual perceptions and representations [209] of an object are not the thing itself.

          1.3.1.4.1.2. Con:
          The Buddhist understanding of truth is inherently paradoxical [210] in that it requires the integration of both conventional and absolute truth [211].

        1.3.1.4.2. Pro:
        While some Buddhist teachings refer to conventional truths, others refer to absolute truth [212] or the reconciliation of both forms. This can easily become confusing for followers.

          1.3.1.4.2.1. Pro:
          It is difficult for many, particularly those steeped in individualistic Western ideals, to understand the Buddhist concept of emptiness [213] that underlies the two truths doctrine.

          1.3.1.4.2.2. Con:
          A failure to distinguish between conventional and absolute truth creates confusion [214]; Buddhist teachings help to alleviate such confusion.

    1.3.2. Pro:
    Following Buddhism has positive benefits for the individual.

      1.3.2.1. Con:
      Some Buddhist traditions teach that irrationality plays a central role in human creativity [215] and place a high value on non-dual mental states. This does not encourage critical thinking and reason.

        1.3.2.1.1. Con:
        The Zen Buddhist perspective on creativity is consistent with a modern psychological understanding of intuition (p. 2 [216]).

          1.3.2.1.1.1. Pro:
          Zen practice promotes intuitive and spontaneous action [217], which are essential to creative endeavours.

          1.3.2.1.1.2. Con:
          While cultivating intuition can be useful, it is not a replacement for rational analysis [218], particularly in practical matters.

        1.3.2.1.2. Pro:
        Zen koans are specifically intended to focus the attention of practitioners on irrational paradoxes that offer little pragmatic value (p. 31 [219]).

          1.3.2.1.2.1. Pro:
          Koans have been used as a method of gatekeeping and a substitute for more substantive teaching methods [220].

          1.3.2.1.2.2. Con:
          Koan meditation resulted in self-reported increases in emotional regulation, concentration, and awareness of cognitive bias (p. 151 [221]).

      1.3.2.2. Con:
      The Buddhist concept of acceptance [222] can lead to the enabling of negative behaviours, such as abuse [223].

        1.3.2.2.1. Pro:
        The value Buddhism places on enduring suffering and accepting one's fate can make it difficult to address domestic violence in some communities (p. 20 [224]).

          1.3.2.2.1.1. Pro:
          Buddhist teachings can lead victims of abuse to believe that their suffering is a result of bad actions committed in previous lives (pp. 26–27 [225]).

          1.3.2.2.1.2. Con:
          Increasing acceptance of Buddhist nuns [226] has led to the establishment of many women's shelters [227] and other resources for domestic violence survivors [228].

        1.3.2.2.2. Con:
        Acceptance of a negative situation does not necessarily mean resignation [229].

          1.3.2.2.2.1. Pro:
          Accepting that a problem exists [230] is often a difficult first step towards healing for victims, enablers, and abusers alike.

          1.3.2.2.2.2. Con:
          Some Buddhist teachers have recommended prayer [231] as an effective method for addressing domestic violence, which is unproven and keeps victims in harm's way.

      1.3.2.3. Pro:
      Buddhism teaches its followers how to identify [232] and eliminate the sources [233] of suffering [234], which is a universal human problem.

        1.3.2.3.1. Pro:
        By focusing on human suffering, Buddhism directly addresses issues at the core of human experience, such as our knowledge of our own mortality [235], and teaches adherents ways to improve their existence.

          1.3.2.3.1.1. Pro:
          Suffering is a self-evident, verifiable [236] phenomenon.

          1.3.2.3.1.2. Con:
          Buddhism's focus on suffering is pessimistic and world-denying (p. 55 [237]).

            1.3.2.3.1.2.1. Pro:
            The cessation of desire is not necessarily beneficial to humans; even if desire sometimes leads to suffering, it also leads to many positive experiences [238].

        1.3.2.3.2. Con:
        The Buddhist goal of ending suffering through the denial of selfhood [239] is circular and unrealistic.

          1.3.2.3.2.1. Con:
          Buddhism does not deny the existence of a self; it asserts that the self is impermanent [240] and that clinging to such impermanent states gives rise to suffering.

          1.3.2.3.2.2. Pro:
          Suffering is a natural part of existence and will never go away. By promising an end to suffering, Buddhism sets a unrealistic goal that leads to unhealthy attitudes and feelings of failure and ineptitude.

      1.3.2.4. Pro:
      Buddhists strive to eliminate extremes in their lives and maintain a healthy moderation. The Middle Way [241] leads people to live in peace and equilibrium.

        1.3.2.4.1. Pro:
        The meditation practices [242] of some Buddhist traditions are associated with a number of psychological benefits for practitioners.

          1.3.2.4.1.1. Pro:
          Zen meditation has been demonstrated to measurably improve practitioners' creative problem-solving ability (pp. 6–7 [243]).

          1.3.2.4.1.2. Con:
          The benefits of meditation are not dependent upon belief in Buddhist doctrine and can be achieved in a secular context [244].

        1.3.2.4.2. Con:
        The Middle Way is not an exclusively Buddhist doctrine; such practices can be integrated with many different belief systems [245].

          1.3.2.4.2.1. Pro:
          Numerous religions and philosophies have concepts equivalent to the Middle Way [246].

          1.3.2.4.2.2. Con:
          The Buddhist formulation of the Middle Way is distinct from similar concepts in other systems, as it is codified in a set of specific moral principles [247].

    1.3.3. Pro:
    Following Buddhism is beneficial to society.

      1.3.3.1. Con:
      Some Buddhist denominations encourage detachment from politics and social matters [248] in the pursuit of personal enlightenment. Such apathy harms the world.

        1.3.3.1.1. Pro:
        It can be difficult for Buddhist practitioners to learn the difference between equanimity and indifference [249].

          1.3.3.1.1.1. Pro:
          The teachings of Buddhism can easily be perceived as recommending withdrawal [250] from essential elements of human life.

          1.3.3.1.1.2. Con:
          Buddhist equanimity requires balanced engagement with the world [251], whereas indifference implies a withdrawal.

        1.3.3.1.2. Con:
        A non-attached perspective helps Buddhists evaluate political ideas and systems from an unbiased, novel perspective [252].

          1.3.3.1.2.1. Pro:
          Buddhist teachings about detachment refer to the cultivation of a clear perspective [253], free of attachment to the feelings and beliefs that generate bias.

          1.3.3.1.2.2. Con:
          The principles underlying Buddhist social theory are often seen as idealistic and detached from the realities of modern politics (p. 90 [254]).

      1.3.3.2. Pro:
      Buddhist belief supports positive, ethical behaviours [255].

        1.3.3.2.1. Con:
        The ethics of Buddhism are determined by what is useful in achieving enlightenment [256] rather than by what is morally good [257].

          1.3.3.2.1.1. Con:
          Following the teachings of Buddhism promotes the development of socially positive qualities [258], including generosity and virtue.

          1.3.3.2.1.2. Pro:
          Buddhism's left-hand path [259] embraces, rather than rejects, passion, desire, and taboo-breaking as means of spiritual development (p. 27 [260]).

        1.3.3.2.2. Pro:
        The primary basis of Buddhist ethics is avoiding things that cause harm [261] to oneself or others.

          1.3.3.2.2.1. Pro:
          Buddhism offers clear, rational, and actionable rules [262] for living and avoiding harm.

          1.3.3.2.2.2. Con:
          Despite Buddhism's injunction to avoid harming living beings [263], many branches of Buddhism are not opposed to the eating of animals [264].

      1.3.3.3. Pro:
      Buddhism is opposed to consumerism and over-consumption [265], which are harmful to society and the environment [266].

        1.3.3.3.1. Pro:
        Education and activism by Buddhist monks have proven useful in environmental conservation efforts (p. 5067 [267]).

          1.3.3.3.1.1. Pro:
          The principle of interconnectedness espoused by Buddhism helps promote sustainability [268].

          1.3.3.3.1.2. Con:
          While Buddhism promotes environmental conservation in theory, the environmental degradation of many Buddhist nations [269] shows that such beliefs may not manifest in practice.

        1.3.3.3.2. Con:
        The philosophical foundations of Buddhism are at odds with holistic views of ecology, which rely on specific forms of self-identification (p. 290 [270]).

          1.3.3.3.2.1. Pro:
          The non-existence of selfhood [271] is a central tenet of Buddhism.

          1.3.3.3.2.2. Con:
          The Buddhist principle of dependent origination [272] promotes an awareness of interdependence that aligns well with deep ecology [273] (p. 110 [274]).

      1.3.3.4. Con:
      The doctrines of karma and rebirth [275] have been used to justify caste societies.

        1.3.3.4.1. Pro:
        Despite the Buddha's opposition to the caste system, a number of Buddhist countries have maintained the practice [276].

          1.3.3.4.1.1. Pro:
          Occupations associated with death, such as butchers, are still treated as lower castes [277] in some Buddhist countries, such as Japan, Sri Lanka, and Tibet [278].

          1.3.3.4.1.2. Con:
          The Buddha expressly opposed caste systems [279]; if some societies choose to continue them, then this is a reflection of them rather than Buddhism itself.

        1.3.3.4.2. Con:
        The Buddha taught five modes of conditionality, of which karma is only one [280]; Buddhist teachings are fundamentally opposed to the caste system enshrined in Hinduism.

          1.3.3.4.2.1. Con:
          Evidence from early sources suggests that the Buddha did not oppose the hereditary class system in India (p. 68 [281]).

          1.3.3.4.2.2. Pro:
          Buddhism became immensely popular among lower-caste Southeast Asians [282], whose concerns and histories had largely been erased under Brahminism [283].

    1.3.4. Con:
    There is no evidence to support the assertions of Buddhism.

      1.3.4.1. Pro:
      Many Buddhist beliefs have little grounding in reality; such beliefs are likely to be undermined by personal experience.

        1.3.4.1.1. Pro:
        Many branches of Buddhism promote belief in a variety of supernatural beings [284].

          1.3.4.1.1.1. Con:
          The Buddhist worldview differs dramatically [285] from that of scientific naturalism and does not distinguish between psychological and material phenomena.

          1.3.4.1.1.2. Pro:
          Some branches of Buddhism have inherited supernatural beliefs and practices [286] from earlier indigenous religions.

        1.3.4.1.2. Con:
        Some Buddhist principles, practices, and metaphysics are supported by modern findings in quantum physics [287], mathematics [288], and psychology [289]. This cohesion with reality reduces cognitive dissonance [290].

          1.3.4.1.2.1. Con:
          There is no connection between Buddhism and quantum mechanics [291] apart from the counterintuitive nature of some of their claims.

          1.3.4.1.2.2. Pro:
          Both Buddhism and quantum physics hold that there is no fundamental basis of reality, but rather that reality is a system of interacting objects and forces (p. 47 [292]).

      1.3.4.2. Con:
      Buddhism eschews a complex metaphysical system that could contradict empirical evidence and thereby remains compatible with scientific discovery. Indeed, many Buddhists find little to no conflict [293] between their faith and scientific research.

        1.3.4.2.1. Con:
        The Buddha's original teachings were characterized by pragmatism, but scholarly discussion of Buddhism throughout history has given rise to extended metaphysical exegesis [294].

          1.3.4.2.1.1. Pro:
          Buddhist scholars have spent a great deal of time and effort discussing questions, such as the nature of absolute truth, that they acknowledge cannot be answered (pp. 69–70 [295]).

          1.3.4.2.1.2. Con:
          Many Buddhists continue to approach their religion pragmatically [296], focusing on simple practices that can improve their existence.

        1.3.4.2.2. Pro:
        Buddhism has shown a willingness to change beliefs in light of evidence; for example, the Dalai Lama has acknowledged [297] that Buddhism remains open to change based on scientific discoveries.

          1.3.4.2.2.1. Con:
          Insofar as Buddhism continues to teach unfalsifiable doctrines, such as the existence of hells [298], it cannot be considered to be based on evidence.

          1.3.4.2.2.2. Pro:
          Buddhism encourages its adherents to question authority, even the authority of its own teachings [299], and discover truth through their own experiences and observations.

      1.3.4.3. Con:
      The Buddhist concept of rebirth is supported by multiple studies [300].

        1.3.4.3.1. Con:
        The Buddhist concept of rebirth relies upon supernatural causes that lack evidence [301].

          1.3.4.3.1.1. Con:
          Some modern schools of Buddhism, such as Triratna [302], do not support the doctrine of literal rebirth, instead teaching the concept as a spiritual metaphor.

          1.3.4.3.1.2. Pro:
          In order to scientifically study and understand rebirth, we would first need to discover the underlying metaphysics [303], such as the existence and nature of identity, and determine [304] what would qualify as sufficient evidence.

        1.3.4.3.2. Pro:
        Dr. Ian Stevenson [305], Dr. Jim Tucker [306], and Bhikkhu Analayo [307] have scientifically researched rebirth and amassed a considerable amount of evidence of mental or physical attributes being carried between lives.

          1.3.4.3.2.1. Con:
          The Buddha himself opposed speculation about previous lives, as he considered it a fruitless endeavor (p. 5 [308]).

          1.3.4.3.2.2. Pro:
          The Buddhist concept of rebirth does not involve a supernatural soul [309] and, as such, is well suited to scientific investigation.

      1.3.4.4. Pro:
      There is no proof that enlightenment [310] or karma [311] exist; one should not accept these teachings without evidence.

        1.3.4.4.1. Pro:
        Karma implies that a person is repaid proportionally for the good or bad they do, yet many bad people lead easy lives [312], and many good people have lives full of difficulty and suffering.

          1.3.4.4.1.1. Con:
          People who have done good things yet had terrible lives (or vice versa) may be experiencing karma [313] from their past lives [314].

          1.3.4.4.1.2. Con:
          It is exceedingly difficult to truly know the inner workings and private thoughts of another; such people may inwardly suffer [315] the effects of their actions.

          1.3.4.4.1.3. Pro:
          Karma is presented as the spiritual aspect of the law of cause and effect [316], so it is reasonable to expect that it should operate similarly for all.

        1.3.4.4.2. Con:
        Karma [317] refers to thoughts and actions that lead to future consequences; many modern psychological theories coincide with this idea. Just because science doesn't use the same language to describe karma, doesn't mean it doesn't exist.

          1.3.4.4.2.1. Con:
          Observations from psychology are insufficient evidence for establishing a proposed universal law [318].

          1.3.4.4.2.2. Pro:
          Bowen's Family Systems Theory describes how dysfunction in a family can be transmitted from generation to generation [319].

    1.3.5. Con:
    Buddhism takes advantage of its followers.

      1.3.5.1. Pro:
      Some Buddhist monks beg for their food [320] rather than purchasing or growing it; such behaviour exploits others by allowing monks to prosper whilst offering little in return.

        1.3.5.1.1. Con:
        The practice of alms-giving does not lead to prosperity for Buddhist monks; many rely on such giving for their basic subsistence [321].

          1.3.5.1.1.1. Pro:
          Monks who practice bindabat [322] collect food each morning; this is often their only meal of the day.

          1.3.5.1.1.2. Con:
          While the rules strictly prohibit Buddhist monks from accepting or using money, the overwhelming majority [323] of them continue to do so.

        1.3.5.1.2. Pro:
        Some Buddhist temples have been caught secretly amassing great wealth [324] at the expense of followers whilst presenting an image of ascesticism [325].

          1.3.5.1.2.1. Pro:
          Many Buddhist temples have been converted into money-making ventures [326] that profit from tourism and believers alike.

          1.3.5.1.2.2. Con:
          The breakdown of the traditional Buddhist merit economy [327] can leave temples in dire financial situations.

      1.3.5.2. Pro:
      There have been many reports of corruption and abuse by Buddhist monks [328] in a number of countries.

        1.3.5.2.1. Pro:
        Some Buddhist teachers have used their position to sexually exploit their students [329].

          1.3.5.2.1.1. Pro:
          Students in the UK Rigpa Fellowship were physically, sexually and emotionally abused by senior staff [330], and the trustees failed to take action after discovering this.

          1.3.5.2.1.2. Con:
          The principles of Buddhism strictly forbid any form of sexual misconduct [331], so such teachers are not acting in accord with the teachings of the faith.

        1.3.5.2.2. Con:
        Many Buddhist leaders have openly acknowledged concerns over sexual abuse and have provided victims and their advocates with a platform to raise their concerns [332].

          1.3.5.2.2.1. Pro:
          Shambhala International, one of the world's largest Buddhist organisations, has openly acknowledged its failures [333] in addressing sexual abuse by leaders.

          1.3.5.2.2.2. Con:
          The Dalai Lama has been accused of inaction regarding sexual abuse [334] in Tibetan Buddhism after acknowledging that he has long been aware of it occurring [335].

      1.3.5.3. Con:
      Buddhist organisations often participate in charity and humanitarian aid [336].

        1.3.5.3.1. Pro:
        The teachings of Buddhism directly promote compassion [337] and charity [338].

          1.3.5.3.1.1. Pro:
          Buddhism promotes charity to all, regardless of ethnicity or religious affiliation [339].

          1.3.5.3.1.2. Con:
          There is no evidence to suggest that Buddhist societies are more compassionate than their counterparts (p. 12 [340]).

        1.3.5.3.2. Con:
        Numerous charity scams [341] have been perpetrated by Buddhist clergy.

          1.3.5.3.2.1. Pro:
          The Buddhist practice of merit-making [342] through donations to religious centers has often been abused by corrupt clergy.

          1.3.5.3.2.2. Con:
          The renunciation of material wealth [343] is a central tenet of Buddhist clergy; examples of scams are the odd exception rather than the rule.

      1.3.5.4. Con:
      Buddhist sanghas often act as spiritual advisors [344] to followers during difficult times.

        1.3.5.4.1. Pro:
        A sangha can act as a supportive surrogate community [345] for those without family or who are otherwise isolated.

          1.3.5.4.1.1. Pro:
          Sanghas provide followers with positive peer pressure, encouragement, and role models [346], helping them to achieve their spiritual goals.

          1.3.5.4.1.2. Con:
          The inherent power differential between students and teachers in sanghas can easily contribute to spiritual abuse and the silencing of victims [347].

        1.3.5.4.2. Con:
        Experts have noted widespread nationalism and sexism and a lack of critical thinking [348] in sanghas.

          1.3.5.4.2.1. Pro:
          Buddhist sanghas have often overlooked the failure of male monks to address their own sexual desires, instead blaming women as a source of sexual temptation [349].

          1.3.5.4.2.2. Con:
          Many sanghas promote inclusivity [350] and offer safe spaces and meetings for women [351], transgender [352] people, and other marginalised groups.

    1.3.6. Con:
    Buddhism is a source of human conflict.

      1.3.6.1. Con:
      Buddhism is, in nature and in history, non-exclusive to other religions. Thus, it does not have to be one's sole faith.

        1.3.6.1.1. Pro:
        The syncretism [353] of Buddhism and Shinto in Japan is due to the metaphysical flexibility of Buddhism.

          1.3.6.1.1.1. Pro:
          Buddhism and Shintoism have long been intertwined in Japanese religious belief [354].

          1.3.6.1.1.2. Con:
          Despite some moves toward syncretism, Shinto and Buddhism largely remained distinct traditions in Japan and were formally separated in 1868 [355].

        1.3.6.1.2. Pro:
        Some branches of Buddhism are formless and non-dogmatic [356] and can easily exist alongside other religious beliefs.

          1.3.6.1.2.1. Pro:
          Zen Buddhism can be performed purely as practice, without any beliefs or doctrines [357] at all, making it easy for anyone to follow.

          1.3.6.1.2.2. Con:
          Over time, many branches of Buddhism have developed dogmatic and esoteric [358] teachings that are difficult to integrate with the teachings of other religions.

        1.3.6.1.3. Con:
        Buddhism and Hinduism are incompatible, as they hold conflicting beliefs on the existence of an unchanging soul [359], which is a key concept in Hinduism.

          1.3.6.1.3.1. Con:
          There is no indication that the Buddha formally renounced Hinduism [360]; it may be more accurate to consider him a reformer [361] than the founder of a new religion.

          1.3.6.1.3.2. Pro:
          Buddhism as a distinct religion arose from its founder, Siddhartha Gautama [362] (the Buddha), rejecting key tenets of the Hindu religion [363].

        1.3.6.1.4. Con:
        The current (14th) Dalai Lama opposes this view, saying that while human society must have multiple religions, individuals should follow a single religion [364].

          1.3.6.1.4.1. Pro:
          One cannot be Buddhist and Christian [365] at the same time, because the two religions have incompatible core beliefs [366], such that faith in one inherently detracts from experiencing the other.

          1.3.6.1.4.2. Con:
          Many people have adopted Buddhist beliefs and practices to good effect [367] while maintaining their original faith.

      1.3.6.2. Pro:
      Some Buddhist sects espouse violence [368] against Muslims.

        1.3.6.2.1. Pro:
        Buddhist religious leaders have supported violence [369] against the Islamic minority of Myanmar.

          1.3.6.2.1.1. Pro:
          Buddhism has played a central role in the development of ethnic nationalism [370] that underlies the ethnic cleansing atrocities in Myanmar.

          1.3.6.2.1.2. Con:
          Some Muslim groups in Myanmar are accepted, while others are not; this indicates that the conflict is fueled by ethnicity rather than religion [371].

        1.3.6.2.2. Con:
        Religious violence against Muslims is associated with Buddhist extremist groups [372] rather than the religion as a whole.

          1.3.6.2.2.1. Con:
          Myanmar is overwhelmingly a Buddhist country [373]; the state-sponsored violence against Muslims indicates a willingness on the part of Buddhists to overlook such atrocities [374].

          1.3.6.2.2.2. Pro:
          Religious violence of any form has been widely disavowed by the larger Buddhist community [375].

      1.3.6.3. Pro:
      Zen Buddhism has long been associated with militarism and nationalism [376].

        1.3.6.3.1. Pro:
        Zen Buddhism was associated with and supported Japanese militarism [377] prior to and during WWII.

          1.3.6.3.1.1. Con:
          Japanese Zen Buddhists have apologised [378] for their actions during WWII. Such contrition should be valued highly.

          1.3.6.3.1.2. Pro:
          Zen schools continued to provide ethical support for Japanese military aggression in spite of atrocities at odds with the spirit of Buddhism [379].

        1.3.6.3.2. Con:
        The establishment of Zen Buddhism is associated with the development of martial arts [380] focused on self-defense rather than offensive action [381].

          1.3.6.3.2.1. Pro:
          The Taoist principle of wu wei adopted by Zen Buddhism supports the goal of promoting non-violence and minimizing harm whenever possible (pp. 253–254 [382]).

          1.3.6.3.2.2. Con:
          At times, Zen monks have actively participated in warfare [383], which directly contradicts the Buddha's teachings [384].

      1.3.6.4. Con:
      Buddhism is a religion of peace.

        1.3.6.4.1. Pro:
        Buddhism rejects all forms of terrorism and violence (pp. 91–92 [385]).

          1.3.6.4.1.1. Pro:
          Buddhism both inherited and expanded upon ahimsa [386], the Hindu principle of non-violence.

          1.3.6.4.1.2. Con:
          Despite the popular perception of Buddhism as pacifistic, at times, it has been as violent as any other religion [387].

          1.3.6.4.1.3. Con:
          Some Buddhist sutras provide clear support for war, torture, and violent punishment under certain circumstances (p. 1 [388]).

        1.3.6.4.2. Pro:
        Buddhist teachings on the non-duality of human experience are conducive to conflict transformation and resolution (p. 8 [389]).

          1.3.6.4.2.1. Con:
          In some conflicts, one party is clearly wrong or is operating in bad faith [390]; in such situations, attempts to non-dualistically identify with the other party may be of little use.

          1.3.6.4.2.2. Pro:
          The Buddhist concept of emptiness [391] helps reframe conflict in ways that contribute to its elimination or resolution (p. 162 [392]).

        1.3.6.4.3. Con:
        The ideal of non-violence in Buddhism is too lofty and impractical [393] to be helpful.

          1.3.6.4.3.1. Pro:
          The pacifistic response of Tibetan Buddhist people to their violent occupation by China [394] has done little to improve their situation (p. 1 [395]).

          1.3.6.4.3.2. Con:
          Buddhism does not preach absolute pacifism [396], and accepts the necessity of violent self-defence [397] under the right conditions.

  1.4. Thesis:
  People should not follow religion.

    1.4.1. Pro:
    There is no evidence to support the assertions made by religion.

      1.4.1.1. Pro:
      Since the existence of divine beings cannot be empirically [398] or logically [399] proven or disproven, we do not know whether god(s) or a higher power exists or doesn't exist.

        1.4.1.1.1. Con:
        Belief in God is reasonable given the complexity and consistent order of life and the universe.

          1.4.1.1.1.1. Con:
          Complexity is subjective, measured in respect to individual perceptions of what is simple and what isn't (p. 9 [400]). Natural order (i.e., the laws of physics, etc.) is neither complex nor simple [401], it just is.

          1.4.1.1.1.2. Pro:
          The precision, consistency, and patterns of the natural world are evidence of an intelligent [402] cause [403] that both encompasses and exceeds it.

            1.4.1.1.1.2.1. Pro:
            Fine tuning offers evidence for God beyond personal subjective experiences (pp. 1–2 [404]).

            1.4.1.1.1.2.2. Con:
            Under a worldview based on methodological naturalism [405], the complexity of life and its awesomeness are not evidence of the divine origin of the universe or the existence of the supernatural.

        1.4.1.1.2. Pro:
        A great deal of research [406] and evidence suggests religions and gods are human inventions.

          1.4.1.1.2.1. Pro:
          The oldest archaeological evidence of religious practices [407] dates to about 70,000 years ago, whereas there is evidence that modern humans [408] have been in existence for 300,000 years.

          1.4.1.1.2.2. Con:
          Religions and gods have divine or supernatural origins [409] that have been revealed to or discovered by humans.

            1.4.1.1.2.2.1. Con:
            There is no evidence that gods and religion are not human creations apart from claims made by religions themselves.

        1.4.1.1.3. Pro:
        The concept of 'god' is superfluous [410] to our understanding of the universe.

          1.4.1.1.3.1. Con:
          The concept of 'god' is a symbol of higher consciousness (p. 6 [411]).

            1.4.1.1.3.1.1. Con:
            The concept of 'god' as a symbol of higher consciousness is distinctly different from the personified [412] concept taught by religions.

          1.4.1.1.3.2. Pro:
          Most experiences of a 'god' or spiritual entity can be explained [413] by reference to the internal processes of the mind.

        1.4.1.1.4. Con:
        The reason to believe there is a God is teleologic: there must be a prime mover [414].

          1.4.1.1.4.1. Con:
          The argument for a prime mover is fallacious [415], and includes a presupposition [416] that god exists within its formulation.

          1.4.1.1.4.2. Pro:
          Whatever begins to exist has a cause (p. 2 [417]).

            1.4.1.1.4.2.1. Con:
            There is no reason why a first cause must be God. It is equally likely to be random, faulty, or even the universe itself.

      1.4.1.2. Con:
      Religious assertions are supported by experiential rather than experimental evidence (p. 448 [418]).

        1.4.1.2.1. Pro:
        The changes in one's motivations and character [419] that result from religious experience—and the ways in which these changes conform to religious teachings—are evidence that there is an underlying truth to religious assertions.

          1.4.1.2.1.1. Pro:
          Many sciences routinely perform qualitative studies of human experience [420].

          1.4.1.2.1.2. Con:
          Personal changes attributed to religious experience could easily be the result of other factors, particularly given the impossibility of establishing supernatural causality (p. 14 [421]).

        1.4.1.2.2. Con:
        Experiential evidence is subject to individual limitations and perceptions and, as such, is of limited use in determining objective truth.

          1.4.1.2.2.1. Pro:
          Religions often use experiential evidence to make assertions that require objective, qualitative support [422].

          1.4.1.2.2.2. Con:
          Empirical evidence is also subject to observer-related biases [423].

      1.4.1.3. Con:
      Religion need not be objectively true in order to be beneficial.

        1.4.1.3.1. Pro:
        The practices [424] and social [425] elements of a religion can offer benefits to followers regardless of whether its teachings can be proven true.

          1.4.1.3.1.1. Pro:
          Many of religion's benefits rest on the structure and community [426] it provides rather than on their objective truth.

          1.4.1.3.1.2. Con:
          If the point of religion is simply to create comforting beliefs with no regard for truth [427], then humanity should create new religions that are more effective in this regard.

        1.4.1.3.2. Con:
        Religious support of irrational beliefs undermines critical thinking and leads to unreasonable public policies (pp. 4–5 [428]).

          1.4.1.3.2.1. Con:
          Key studies linking increased religiosity with decreased critical thinking have been debunked [429].

          1.4.1.3.2.2. Pro:
          Children who are raised religiously are less able to determine fact from fiction (pp. 18–19 [430]).

      1.4.1.4. Pro:
      Belief should be based on verifiable evidence. Since there is no substantial evidence to support the assertions of any particular religion, it is better to not follow one (p. 17 [431]).

        1.4.1.4.1. Con:
        By definition, a position of faith is impossible to confirm [432], making it unreasonable to expect confirmation, or to condemn for lack of confirmation.

          1.4.1.4.1.1. Pro:
          Belief [433] is defined as 'the feeling of being certain that something exists or is true' and, as a feeling, is not necessarily based on evidence.

          1.4.1.4.1.2. Con:
          It is reasonable to expect evidence for beliefs, and to condemn beliefs that are presented without evidence. Insofar as faith, by definition, requires such beliefs [434], it is condemnable.

        1.4.1.4.2. Pro:
        Nearly every religion asserts [435] that it is supported by facts [436] without providing actual evidence [437] (p. 2 [438]). Asserting validity is a poor argument in the absence of rigorous, comparative data points.

          1.4.1.4.2.1. Pro:
          Religions rely on unfalsifiable claims [439], making it impossible to meaningfully differentiate between different beliefs.

          1.4.1.4.2.2. Con:
          This is a characteristic of human belief rather than a phenomena particular to religion; secular beliefs are often accepted without evidence [440].

    1.4.2. Pro:
    Religions are a source of human conflict.

      1.4.2.1. Con:
      So long as an individual's religious beliefs do not harm [441] or otherwise encroach on the freedoms [442] or rights of others, they should be free to believe what they choose.

        1.4.2.1.1. Pro:
        The right to choose one's religious beliefs is one form of freedom of thought and conscience [443], which is an essential human right.

          1.4.2.1.1.1. Con:
          Having the freedom to follow a religion does not necessarily mean that one should do so.

          1.4.2.1.1.2. Pro:
          Freedom of religion is enshrined as a human right in the UN's Universal Declaration of Human Rights [444].

        1.4.2.1.2. Con:
        Religious beliefs often encourage and excuse harmful behaviours [445] that infringe on the rights of others.

          1.4.2.1.2.1. Pro:
          Religious extremism is often a source of violence and hate crimes [446].

          1.4.2.1.2.2. Con:
          Most religions teach some version of the Golden Rule [447], so they cannot reasonably be blamed for the actions of those who fail to abide by the concept.

      1.4.2.2. Pro:
      Many religions throughout history have persecuted [448] non-believers, dissenters, and minority groups.

        1.4.2.2.1. Con:
        Many religions have a long history of tolerance for other beliefs [449] and interfaith dialogue [450].

          1.4.2.2.1.1. Pro:
          Modern religious organizations have made significant progress in advancing mutual understanding and respect [451] between different faiths.

          1.4.2.2.1.2. Con:
          The very idea that other faiths require tolerance reveals how religions inherently promote the idea of their superiority [452] over other groups.

        1.4.2.2.2. Pro:
        Belief systems can cause the persecution of innocents, such as people with albinism (p. 212 [453]).

          1.4.2.2.2.1. Pro:
          Individuals with red hair have been subject to widespread religious persecution [454] across numerous cultures.

          1.4.2.2.2.2. Con:
          Discrimination based on physical differences has been a common occurrence throughout human history in both religious and secular contexts (pp. 14, 16 [455]).

        1.4.2.2.3. Pro:
        Homophobia around the world is largely the product of religious bigotry (p. 1974 [456]).

          1.4.2.2.3.1. Con:
          Research and psychoanalytic theory agree that homophobia is largely a result of repressed homosexual arousal [457] rather than religious beliefs (p. 20 [458]).

            1.4.2.2.3.1.1. Con:
            Religious individuals often repress their sexuality to better conform with the values and expectations of their faith (pp. 89–90, 92 [459]).

          1.4.2.2.3.2. Pro:
          LGBTQ+ individuals are often rejected or shunned [460] by religious family members, which can have deleterious effects on their well-being (p. 8 [461]).

      1.4.2.3. Con:
      Peace is a central concept in most religions (pp. 20–21 [462]).

        1.4.2.3.1. Pro:
        Religious beliefs and leaders can play a crucial role in peacekeeping efforts [463].

          1.4.2.3.1.1. Pro:
          Religion can contribute to peacekeeping efforts by encouraging self-reflection over emotional responses (p. 2 [464]).

          1.4.2.3.1.2. Con:
          Religious leaders often contribute to the escalation of conflict by preaching intolerance [465].

        1.4.2.3.2. Con:
        Religious differences have often contributed to the dehumanisation of different social and ethnic groups, which is a common element of large scale conflict (pp. 2, 10–11 [466]).

          1.4.2.3.2.1. Pro:
          Religion is often used as an instrument of war by reinforcing the otherness of those from different faiths (p. 1 [467]).

          1.4.2.3.2.2. Con:
          The humanisation of those from other faiths is a core element of interfaith dialogue (p. 1 [468]).

      1.4.2.4. Pro:
      Many wars [469] have historically been fought over religious causes.

        1.4.2.4.1. Pro:
        Religion remains a leading cause of violent conflict [470] in the modern world.

          1.4.2.4.1.1. Con:
          Many conflicts presented as religious in nature are actually the result of secular concerns [471]. For example, religion has often been used as an excuse [472] for justifying political and resource-motivated wars.

          1.4.2.4.1.2. Pro:
          Religious beliefs contribute to inflexibility, nationalism, and escalation [473] of conflict.

        1.4.2.4.2. Con:
        The actions of religious believers do not necessarily conform with the teachings of their religion [474].

          1.4.2.4.2.1. Pro:
          Religious people often participate in armed conflict in spite of religious teachings that promote peace and set high standards for the justification of violence (pp. 11, 19–21 [475]).

          1.4.2.4.2.2. Con:
          There have been numerous holy wars that were motivated by religious teachings [476].

    1.4.3. Pro:
    Religions take advantage of their followers.

      1.4.3.1. Pro:
      In many cases, religions have been used to legitimise socio-economic inequality (p. 2 [477]); Karl Marx characterised religion as a form of social control [478] that discourages opposition to inequality.

        1.4.3.1.1. Pro:
        Religiosity is negatively correlated with economic prosperity for both individuals and countries (p. 164 [479]).

          1.4.3.1.1.1. Con:
          Religion's role in helping poor people and countries cope with difficult circumstances leads to increased emotional well-being [480].

          1.4.3.1.1.2. Pro:
          Religious belief often interferes with interventions and behaviours that can alleviate poverty, such as education and personal finance (p. 6 [481]).

        1.4.3.1.2. Con:
        The teachings of many religions promote economic equality and helping the less fortunate (pp. 15–16 [482]); most religions promote charitable giving [483] to support those in need.

          1.4.3.1.2.1. Con:
          There is evidence [484] that the children of non-believers are more generous than their religious counterparts.

          1.4.3.1.2.2. Pro:
          Individuals with a religious affiliation tend to donate more to charity [485] than those without an affiliation (p. 5 [486]).

      1.4.3.2. Con:
      Religions function as social support systems [487] for their followers during difficult times.

        1.4.3.2.1. Pro:
        The structure and community offered by religion can improve mental health [488] during stressful life events.

          1.4.3.2.1.1. Pro:
          A positive sense of community is associated with lower occurrence and symptoms of depression, anxiety, and stress (p. 1 [489]).

          1.4.3.2.1.2. Con:
          Religious communities often reinforce stigmas about mental health and operate as a barrier to effective treatment (p. 846 [490]).

        1.4.3.2.2. Con:
        Many religions employ coercive shunning and social exclusion [491] of former or incalcitrant members.

          1.4.3.2.2.1. Pro:
          Religious shunning can have profoundly negative effects [492] on an individual's well being and mental health.

          1.4.3.2.2.2. Con:
          Most religious shunning originates in doctrinal disputes; religious organisations and individuals have the right to practise their beliefs and disassociate themselves from those who disagree (p. 293 [493]).

      1.4.3.3. Con:
      Religious organisations play a central role in providing medical care, education, and humanitarian aid throughout the world.

        1.4.3.3.1. Pro:
        A large proportion of hospitals [494] are operated by faith-based organisations (FBOs), particularly in developing countries (p. 6 [495]).

          1.4.3.3.1.1. Con:
          Systematic reviews have concluded that the proportion of hospitals operated by FBOs has often been significantly overestimated (p. 6 [496]).

          1.4.3.3.1.2. Pro:
          FBOs have supported public health initiatives that directly benefit disadvantaged and high-risk populations (p. 341 [497]).

        1.4.3.3.2. Con:
        Religious groups often combine humanitarian aid with proselytising, which carries numerous ethical risks (pp. 623–624 [498]).

          1.4.3.3.2.1. Con:
          The right of religious groups and individuals to proselytise is a manifestation of their right to religious expression (p. 43 [499]).

          1.4.3.3.2.2. Pro:
          Religious hospitals often deny care for treatments that they oppose and give religiously biased medical advice despite receiving public funds (p. 1 [500]).

      1.4.3.4. Pro:
      The power dynamics [501] of religious institutions [502] often create opportunities for child abuse [503] and spiritual abuse [504].

        1.4.3.4.1. Con:
        Religions do not endorse abuse, which directly contradicts religious teachings [505]. Individual perpetrators rather than religious institutions should be held accountable for this.

          1.4.3.4.1.1. Con:
          Religions need not expressly condone abuse to contribute to it [506]; for example, religiosity is positively correlated with higher incidence of child sexual abuse [507] by relatives.

          1.4.3.4.1.2. Pro:
          Many religions have moved to improve the reporting of instances of abuse and hold offenders accountable [508].

        1.4.3.4.2. Pro:
        Religious abuse can cause mental trauma in children (p. 21 [509]).

          1.4.3.4.2.1. Pro:
          The trauma experienced by abused children has measurable, negative effects on their long-term well-being (p. 8 [510]).

          1.4.3.4.2.2. Con:
          Religion can be a source of resilience and personal growth [511] for those who have experienced traumatic events (pp. 37–38, 41 [512]).

    1.4.4. Con:
    Religions are complete and well-established systems of belief.

      1.4.4.1. Con:
      Many of the core claims of different religions directly contradict each other, yet they simultaneously claim absolute truth.

        1.4.4.1.1. Con:
        The claims of different religions correspond with, and are based upon, distinct worldviews [513], so the fact that religious truth claims are mutually exclusive is not problematic.

          1.4.4.1.1.1. Pro:
          Belief plays a key role in determining the reality of individuals and societies regardless of the truth of such beliefs (pp. 7–9 [514]).

          1.4.4.1.1.2. Con:
          The worldviews of most religions share a number of common characteristics [515].

        1.4.4.1.2. Pro:
        Religious pluralism is deductively false, as it inherently requires the acceptance of contradictory assertions [516].

          1.4.4.1.2.1. Pro:
          It is logically impossible for monotheism, polytheism, pantheism, and atheism to simultaneously be true, yet each of these beliefs are held to be true [517] by different religions.

          1.4.4.1.2.2. Con:
          All religions need not be true in order for one religion to be true; this is why people generally believe in one religion rather than many.

      1.4.4.2. Pro:
      Religion is ubiquitous in human society (p. 3 [518]).

        1.4.4.2.1. Pro:
        84% of the world's population [519] identifies as religious.

          1.4.4.2.1.1. Pro:
          As much as 64% [520] of the global population believes in God.

          1.4.4.2.1.2. Con:
          If 16% of the world's population does not identify as religious, then irreligion is also ubiquitous.

        1.4.4.2.2. Con:
        Religion being a universal element of human society does not mean that it is positive; poverty is also ubiquitous in human society (p. 2 [521]).

          1.4.4.2.2.1. Pro:
          Arguing that one should believe in a religion because it is a common social practice is an appeal to popularity [522].

          1.4.4.2.2.2. Con:
          If following a religion held no value for people, then religious belief would be far less common than it is.

      1.4.4.3. Pro:
      Religious traditions form the basis of many social practices and beliefs.

        1.4.4.3.1. Pro:
        Many common cultural practices throughout various societies are religious in origin (pp. 4–5 [523]).

          1.4.4.3.1.1. Pro:
          Religion plays a key role in the formation and expression of cultural identity [524].

          1.4.4.3.1.2. Con:
          Many religious teachings are simply enshrinements of existing cultural practices and values [525].

        1.4.4.3.2. Con:
        Culture encompasses religion [526] and has a greater effect than religion on social customs.

          1.4.4.3.2.1. Pro:
          Followers of the same religion from different cultures often have widely divergent practices, such as marriage traditions [527].

          1.4.4.3.2.2. Con:
          Religion is central to the development of community [528] and is the only thing capable of unifying the diverse elements of human existence [529].

      1.4.4.4. Con:
      Many religious concepts are so internally contradictory [530] that logic and reason make belief impossible; e.g., a god [531] who is invisible and non-physical but affects the physical world; who is loving and all-powerful but does nothing about evil.

        1.4.4.4.1. Con:
        Religious teachings that appear contradictory may be expressing truths that exceed the rational capacity of humans (p. 1061 [532]).

          1.4.4.4.1.1. Con:
          The parent claim is an appeal to mystery [533].

          1.4.4.4.1.2. Pro:
          Human understanding is inherently limited [534] to the extent of human perceptions and ability to process information.

        1.4.4.4.2. Pro:
        According to the coherence theory of truth [535], the internal consistency of a set of beliefs is a necessary condition of its truth.

          1.4.4.4.2.1. Pro:
          Commitment to religious belief has been strongly correlated with belief inconsistency and dogmatism (pp. 5, 7–8 [536]).

          1.4.4.4.2.2. Con:
          A belief is true insofar as it corresponds [537] with the way that things are; its consistency with other beliefs is irrelevant to its truth.

    1.4.5. Con:
    Following a religion has positive benefits for individuals.

      1.4.5.1. Pro:
      According to an argument commonly known as Pascal's Wager [538], it is better to follow a religion, so as to reap the rewards of believing and acting correctly.

        1.4.5.1.1. Pro:
        Believing in a religion that turns out to be untrue is safer than not believing [539] in a religion that turns out to be true.

          1.4.5.1.1.1. Con:
          If God doesn't judge humanity based on belief, then any perceived gain from believing is lost. The Atheist's Wager [540] counters Pascal's Wager by showing that morality is more important than faith whether a benevolent god exists or not.

          1.4.5.1.1.2. Pro:
          If a religion turns out to be true, and one does not believe, then one could be subject to severe consequences [541].

        1.4.5.1.2. Con:
        Pascal's wager is problematic [542] insofar as it asserts, without evidence, that one can choose what one believes and irrationally assumes that one of the many possible Gods is the correct one.

          1.4.5.1.2.1. Con:
          Humans are capable of choosing what they believe [543] by focusing on different thoughts and sensory information.

          1.4.5.1.2.2. Pro:
          Once can choose to feign belief [544] in God, but this does not constitute actual belief.

      1.4.5.2. Con:
