      Belief systems can be a threat to human health, e.g., the anti-vaccination movement and the condom controversy [545] (p. 1 [546]).

        1.4.5.2.1. Con:
        Medical intervention [547] has often posed threats to human health, such as hospital-acquired infections and surgical errors, so religions are right to urge caution before undergoing treatment.

          1.4.5.2.1.1. Pro:
          Many religions oppose the use of addictive or intoxicating substances, such as alcohol [548] or painkillers [549], which may be present in medications.

          1.4.5.2.1.2. Con:
          Some religions object to simple, well-tested, and effective treatments, such as blood transfusions (p. 347 [550]).

        1.4.5.2.2. Pro:
        Belief in unfounded religious assertions has demonstrably harmed people, for example, in cases where faith healing [551] is used in place of modern medicine (p. E709 [552]).

          1.4.5.2.2.1. Pro:
          Some religious parents reject proper medical care [553] for themselves or their children when it conflicts with religious doctrines, and many children have died from treatable conditions [554] when their parents insist on faith healing rather than modern medicine.

          1.4.5.2.2.2. Con:
          Believing something that may not be true is different than not believing in something that is true. It is a false dichotomy to say that someone can believe in prayer but not medicine; people who refuse medicine for religious reasons are not suffering from faith but from a lack of rational thought.

      1.4.5.3. Con:
      Religion is irrelevant, and thinking about it consumes precious time that could be better spent on other pursuits.

        1.4.5.3.1. Con:
        Knowledge of religion is essential to the understanding of human history [555] and current politics (pp. 1, 23 [556]).

          1.4.5.3.1.1. Pro:
          Religion is a key element of identity development and has played a central role in numerous historical conflicts (p. 2 [557]).

          1.4.5.3.1.2. Con:
          The moral values espoused by religion have been supplanted by secular values [558] that can accomplish the same ends without the superstition, intolerance, and dogma associated with religious belief (p. 167 [559]).

        1.4.5.3.2. Pro:
        Religion has become increasingly irrelevant [560] since the Enlightenment, as science has been able to successfully address many topics formerly considered the domain of religion.

          1.4.5.3.2.1. Pro:
          Science can reliably and rationally explain the processes of the natural world [561], which were formerly addressed by religion [562].

          1.4.5.3.2.2. Con:
          Science is incapable of addressing a number of the topics discussed by religion, including morality, values, and the supernatural (p. 19 [563]).

      1.4.5.4. Pro:
      The concepts and practices taught by religion can provide psychological benefits [564].

        1.4.5.4.1. Pro:
        Religions provide their followers with a sense of meaning and purpose [565] that helps them deal with difficult situations.

          1.4.5.4.1.1. Pro:
          Religion is unique among human endeavors, in that it asserts that there is a larger meaning to life [566].

          1.4.5.4.1.2. Con:
          Non-religious children have better long-term development outcomes than religious children after experiencing the death of a family member (p. 28 [567]).

        1.4.5.4.2. Con:
        The psychological and personal development benefits of religions are often incidental to the religion. Other social [568] and psychological [569] activities can deliver the same benefits in a more thoughtful and effective way.

          1.4.5.4.2.1. Pro:
          Modern psychology and psychiatry are more effective than religion [570] in addressing mental health concerns.

          1.4.5.4.2.2. Con:
          Religious involvement during childhood and adolescent development is correlated with better outcomes in adulthood [571].

    1.4.6. Con:
    Following religion is beneficial to society.

      1.4.6.1. Con:
      Religion has slowed technological and medical [572] progress (p. 2 [573]).

        1.4.6.1.1. Pro:
        Religious objections to specific advances, such as stem cell research [574], have continued to impede medical progress.

          1.4.6.1.1.1. Pro:
          Stem cell research can offer significant benefits to society [575].

          1.4.6.1.1.2. Con:
          Many presumably religious objections over stem cell research are actually predicated on empirical observation and secular ethics [576].

        1.4.6.1.2. Con:
        Religious institutions and individuals have been responsible for a great deal of scientific inquiry [577] throughout history.

          1.4.6.1.2.1. Pro:
          The development of the experimental approach to science [578] was motivated by religion.

          1.4.6.1.2.2. Con:
          Religious belief remains a key motivation in the rejection of well-established scientific theories such as evolution [579].

        1.4.6.1.3. Pro:
        The centrality of belief in supernatural causes within many religions impoverishes scientific and critical thinking (p. 1 [580]).

          1.4.6.1.3.1. Con:
          Religious belief, as opposed to scientific belief, does not need to be based on evidence [581].

          1.4.6.1.3.2. Pro:
          If the cause of an event is claimed to be supernatural, there is no motivation to provide a rational explanation for why the event occurred.

      1.4.6.2. Pro:
      Societies without an objective standard, such as that offered by religion, lack an objective rationale for morality [582].

        1.4.6.2.1. Pro:
        The atheistic view of morality as an evolved social construct implies that it is subject to change.

          1.4.6.2.1.1. Con:
          As a human construct, morality would not exist without humans; if humans did not exist it would be meaningless to ascribe any negative value to the absence of morality.

          1.4.6.2.1.2. Pro:
          Theistic views of morality are flexible enough to account for cultural differences, yet remain rooted in an unchanging and objective source—God—and therefore are not at risk of fading.

            1.4.6.2.1.2.1. Con:
            If God does not exist, then theistic views of morality are not rooted in an unchanging and objective source, but rather in fiction, making them worse explanations for morality.

        1.4.6.2.2. Con:
        Moral relativism [583] allows for more diverse rationales for morality and is often preferred [584] over moral objectivism.

          1.4.6.2.2.1. Pro:
          Morality can vary considerably [585] depending on a number of factors, including culture, context, and individual perspective [586].

          1.4.6.2.2.2. Con:
          Moral relativism results in irrational conclusions [587] since it requires that different, opposed moral values be considered equally valid.

        1.4.6.2.3. Con:
        Morality arises from social interactions. Religious belief systems are not necessary for the development of morality (p. 9 [588]).

          1.4.6.2.3.1. Pro:
          Humans have always lived in societies, and the rationale for morality is probably that it makes societies healthier (p. 169 [589]).

          1.4.6.2.3.2. Con:
          There are no empirical means of determining morality without making non-empirical assertions [590], so basing morality on philosophy is logically equivalent to basing it on religion.

          1.4.6.2.3.3. Con:
          Societies that have morals but no religion borrow their concept of morality [591] from religion.

          1.4.6.2.3.4. Pro:
          It would be more beneficial for society to follow no religion, since humans could then develop moral and philosophical ideas unencumbered by religious obligations and convictions [592].

      1.4.6.3. Pro:
      Religions play an essential role in the formation of social bonds, which supports the development of human society (p. 46 [593]).

        1.4.6.3.1. Pro:
        Religious traditions provide intergenerational continuity, which benefits society (p. 4 [594]).

          1.4.6.3.1.1. Pro:
          Intergenerational continuity promotes social cohesion, which is particularly important given the modern changes to family structures and demographics (pp. 12, 36 [595]).

          1.4.6.3.1.2. Con:
          Intergenerational continuity is not necessarily beneficial; for example, harsh parenting styles have been shown to predict similarly harsh parenting in the next generation and an increase in externalizing behaviour [596] (p. 12 [597]).

        1.4.6.3.2. Con:
        In diverse modern societies, religion is increasingly seen as a divisive force [598].

          1.4.6.3.2.1. Pro:
          Claims made by religions regarding the possession of exclusive and universal truth are inherently divisive (p. 484 [599]).

          1.4.6.3.2.2. Con:
          Religion has been the primary driving force behind humanity's success, as it has enabled the creation of larger, more organised social groups [600].

      1.4.6.4. Pro:
      Belief systems are necessary to motivate important social change.

        1.4.6.4.1. Con:
        By operating as an institutional source of moral values, religions tend to discourage social change [601].

          1.4.6.4.1.1. Pro:
          Religion prevents social change by providing followers support and consistency during disruptive events [602] that would otherwise result in needed social change.

          1.4.6.4.1.2. Con:
          Religion often acts as a catalyst of social change [603], particularly amongst disenfranchised groups.

        1.4.6.4.2. Pro:
        The US civil rights movement was based on a religious belief [604] that people of all races deserve equal rights.

          1.4.6.4.2.1. Pro:
          Christian churches were instrumental in cultivating the oppositional consciousness [605] underlying the US civil rights movement.

          1.4.6.4.2.2. Con:
          White supremacy groups, such as the KKK [606], have also been motivated by religion and used it as a justification for bigotry.

        1.4.6.4.3. Pro:
        The abolitionist movement was based on the belief of like-minded religious groups [607] that human beings should not be treated as property.

          1.4.6.4.3.1. Con:
          Prior to the abolitionist movement, religion supported and profited [608] from the slave trade.

          1.4.6.4.3.2. Pro:
          Abolitionists sought to demonstrate the incompatibility of slavery with Christian doctrine [609] and were successful in recruiting many churches to their cause.

      1.4.6.5. Con:
      Religion makes people sexist [610].

        1.4.6.5.1. Pro:
        Many religions promote a patriarchal view of the world [611] that is incompatible with the equality agenda of many modern societies [612].

          1.4.6.5.1.1. Pro:
          Religions promote patriarchy [613] via essentialised portrayals of women and the promotion and justification of patriarchal laws and practices.

          1.4.6.5.1.2. Con:
          The widespread existence of patriarchal beliefs and customs in religion is a result, rather than a cause, of patriarchal society [614].

        1.4.6.5.2. Pro:
        Religion is frequently used to discriminate [615] against unmarried mothers and those of childbearing age in the workplace.

          1.4.6.5.2.1. Pro:
          Religious organisations have obtained exemptions allowing them to circumvent the rights of employees [616] who fail to abide by their faith's doctrines.

          1.4.6.5.2.2. Con:
          The principles of religious freedom and expression [617] allow individuals and organisations to act according to their beliefs.

        1.4.6.5.3. Con:
        The prosocial elements of most religions are directly opposed to hostile sexism (pp. 387, 390 [618]).

          1.4.6.5.3.1. Pro:
          Several studies have failed to find a correlation between religiosity and hostile sexism (pp. 2–3 [619]).

          1.4.6.5.3.2. Con:
          Even if they are not associated with hostile sexism, religions are directly associated with the development and promotion of benevolent sexism beliefs and practices (pp. 45–46 [620]).

  1.5. Thesis:
  Jainism [621]

    1.5.1. Pro:
    Following Jainism is beneficial to society.

      1.5.1.1. Con:
      Some sects of Jainism are inherently sexist [622], as they teach that women cannot achieve liberation without being reborn as men first.

        1.5.1.1.1. Pro:
        Some Jain texts say that menstrual blood is a sign of impurity [623] that kills micro-organisms, thus, making women more violent than men.

        1.5.1.1.2. Con:
        The exception does not define the rule. Just because one sect of a religious group does something doesn't mean that they all do.

      1.5.1.2. Pro:
      Jainism is opposed to the inequality embodied in the caste system [624].

        1.5.1.2.1. Con:
        Over 40% of surveyed Jains expressed discriminatory attitudes [625] towards certain castes.

        1.5.1.2.2. Pro:
        Jainism rejects the spiritual authority of the Brahmins, which forms the basis of the Hindu caste system [626].

      1.5.1.3. Con:
      Many Jains are opposed to intermarriage [627] with those of different faiths.

        1.5.1.3.1. Pro:
        The Indian rules on interfaith marriage subject Jains with a partner outside the faith to widespread public harassment [628].

        1.5.1.3.2. Con:
        Marriage for Jains is predominantly a civil rather than religious matter; as such, many Jain communities do not oppose intermarriage (p. 36 [629]).

      1.5.1.4. Pro:
      Jainism teaches a beneficial moral code.

        1.5.1.4.1. Con:
        The Jain practice of santhara [630], or fasting to death, is unethical because it is a form of suicide.

          1.5.1.4.1.1. Con:
          The Jain santhara [631] ritual teaches people how to die with equanimity.

        1.5.1.4.2. Pro:
        Jains take a vow to tell the truth and never steal [632].

    1.5.2. Pro:
    Following Jainism has positive benefits for the individual.

      1.5.2.1. Con:
      The Jain diet is an extremely restrictive [633] form of vegetarianism that can be difficult to follow.

        1.5.2.1.1. Con:
        Vegetarian and vegan diets can provide health benefits [634].

        1.5.2.1.2. Pro:
        It can be difficult, expensive, and time consuming [635] to follow a Jain diet, particularly when away from home.

      1.5.2.2. Con:
      The extreme asceticism [636] required of Jains is incompatible with the enjoyment of modern life.

        1.5.2.2.1. Pro:
        Adhering to the strict requirements of Jainism requires one to renounce many aspects of modern society [637].

        1.5.2.2.2. Con:
        Detachment from modern life allows Jain ascetics to focus more intently on their spiritual development [638].

      1.5.2.3. Pro:
      Jainism places a high value on education as a method of personal development (p. 6 [639]).

        1.5.2.3.1. Pro:
        Jainism has contributed to the spread of universal education from the fourth century BCE [640] onward (p. 28 [641]).

        1.5.2.3.2. Con:
        Jain philosophy views conflicting perspectives as indicative of a higher truth to be discovered (pp. 88–89 [642]); while this position is useful for producing pluralism, such a position can be problematic when teaching about controversial topics.

      1.5.2.4. Pro:
      Jainism provides followers with a sense of membership in an accepting and inclusive community (pp. 7–8 [643]).

        1.5.2.4.1. Con:
        Some Jain teachings are unabashedly misogynistic [644].

        1.5.2.4.2. Pro:
        Jainism promotes the equality and acceptance of LGBTQ+ persons [645].

    1.5.3. Pro:
    Jainism is a complete and well-established system of belief.

      1.5.3.1. Pro:
      Jainism has a large organisational structure with numerous temples [646] and centres around the world [647].

        1.5.3.1.1. Pro:
        Jainism uses the local language of the community [648], rather than forcing followers to adapt to a foreign tongue.

        1.5.3.1.2. Con:
        Some scholars have argued that Jainism faces a serious threat of extinction in coming years due to a decline in its membership (pp. 24–25 [649]).

      1.5.3.2. Pro:
      Jainism has official scriptures and leadership that preserve its authority (p. 3 [650]).

        1.5.3.2.1. Con:
        The different sects of Jainism disagree on which scriptures should be considered canonical [651], and some works have been lost.

        1.5.3.2.2. Pro:
        Jain scriptural authority rests on a combination of both written and oral transmissions [652], with a defined lineage of teachers.

      1.5.3.3. Con:
      The Jain doctrine of anekāntavāda [653] (non-absolutism) leads to inherent contradictions and is therefore ineffective as the basis of a system of belief (p. 15 [654]).

        1.5.3.3.1. Pro:
        Jain teachings on non-absolutism propose that truth is beyond the comprehension of humans [655], which constitutes an appeal to mystery [656].

        1.5.3.3.2. Con:
        The perceptions of individual humans are inherently subjective [657], so no human is capable of reasonably making a claim to absolute truth.

      1.5.3.4. Con:
      Jainism is considered by many to be a branch of Hinduism rather than a distinct religion (p. 26 [658]).

        1.5.3.4.1. Pro:
        Jains share many beliefs in common with Hindus and are well integrated into Hindu society [659].

        1.5.3.4.2. Con:
        Despite sharing some beliefs in common, Jainism and Hinduism are distinct faiths with different teachings and divergent histories [660].

    1.5.4. Con:
    Jainism takes advantage of its followers.

      1.5.4.1. Pro:
      There have been allegations of sexual abuse [661] perpetrated by Jain monks.

        1.5.4.1.1. Pro:
        Some Jain monks have used the treatment of depression or other conditions as a pretext for isolating and molesting victims [662].

        1.5.4.1.2. Con:
        Any form of abuse is inherently at odds with ahimsa [663], the Jain principle of non-violence.

      1.5.4.2. Con:
      Jains are responsible for a great deal of charitable giving.

        1.5.4.2.1. Pro:
        Jains regularly donate organs [664] to help those in need.

        1.5.4.2.2. Con:
        Many Jain communities continue to amass incredible wealth [665] despite the Jain teaching that wealth presents an obstacle to personal liberation [666].

      1.5.4.3. Con:
      Jain recovery programs both acknowledge and address the religion itself as a source of stigma and shame [667] for addicts.

        1.5.4.3.1. Pro:
        Higher religiosity is often associated with more negative views on addiction (p. 10 [668]); faith-based interventions can thus be essential for many religious people suffering from substance abuse.

        1.5.4.3.2. Con:
        Shame and stigma from their religious community [669] can prevent Jains from seeking treatment for substance abuse in the first place.

      1.5.4.4. Pro:
      The Bal Diksha [670] ritual, in which children take strict monastic orders, has been criticised [671] for violating children's rights.

        1.5.4.4.1. Pro:
        Bal Diksha places severe ascetic restrictions on adherents; children are not sufficiently capable of making such profound decisions [672] about their lives.

        1.5.4.4.2. Con:
        Children who choose to undergo Bal Diksha do so of their own free will, and typically consider it a way of freeing themselves from the confines and concerns of modern life [673].

    1.5.5. Con:
    Jainism is a source of human conflict.

      1.5.5.1. Pro:
      Most Indian Jains belong to a higher caste [674], indirectly supporting institutionalised inequality.

        1.5.5.1.1. Pro:
        Many Jains openly consider themselves inherently superior to those from lower castes (p. 119 [675]).

        1.5.5.1.2. Con:
        Most Jains live in India, which has an entrenched caste system [676] derived from Hinduism. As such, Jains have often been forced to accept the caste system in order to secure marriage alliances (p. 7 [677]).

      1.5.5.2. Pro:
      Some Jain kings have waged war on other kingdoms (pp. 21–22 [678]).

        1.5.5.2.1. Pro:
        Jainism has a history of passive-aggressive militancy against other faiths (p. 23 [679]).

        1.5.5.2.2. Con:
        Despite occasional military action by Jain kings, Jainism has never been widely militarised, which may be responsible for its decline relative to more militant faiths (p. 27 [680]).

      1.5.5.3. Con:
      Jainism contributes to interfaith dialogue [681], promoting harmony between different religious groups.

        1.5.5.3.1. Pro:
        Jains participate directly in interfaith dialogue [682] to increase their knowledge and widen their perspective; they also act as neutral facilitators in dialogue between other faiths.

        1.5.5.3.2. Con:
        Jain philosophy allows for contradictory claims and positions to be considered equally valid, which can serve to legitimise extremist views (p. 20 [683]).

      1.5.5.4. Con:
      Jainism is a peaceful and non-violent [684] religion.

        1.5.5.4.1. Pro:
        Jainism teaches that all living things have an equally valuable soul [685] and that non-injury (ahimsa) to others and oneself is the highest religious duty [686]. This protects not just humans, but all living things.

        1.5.5.4.2. Con:
        While Jain monks and nuns have traditionally taken vows of absolute pacifism, such restrictions have been relaxed [687] in modern times and do not apply to the laity.

    1.5.6. Con:
    There is no evidence to support the assertions of Jainism.

      1.5.6.1. Pro:
      Jains believe in rebirth [688], which is unproven.

        1.5.6.1.1. Pro:
        There is no evidence of the existence of the soul [689] as described by Jainism.

        1.5.6.1.2. Con:
        Evidence for rebirth [690] includes numerous examples of Jains who have accurately remembered details of their previous lives, as well as prodigies who have developed skills far beyond what is reasonable for children.

      1.5.6.2. Con:
      Jainism is not opposed to scientific progress, and teaches that rationality and religious belief [691] are compatible.

        1.5.6.2.1. Pro:
        Many Jain teachings correspond well with modern scientific theories [692].

        1.5.6.2.2. Con:
        The Jain belief that the universe has always existed [693] is not supported by scientific evidence [694].

      1.5.6.3. Pro:
      Jainism has continued to support the use of faith healing practices despite a lack of evidence for their efficacy (p. 89 [695]).

        1.5.6.3.1. Pro:
        Jain spiritual healing practices rely upon supernatural causes [696] that cannot be empirically demonstrated to exist.

        1.5.6.3.2. Con:
        Spiritual healing is far more important than physical healing to Jains; even if faith healing practices are less effective at curing disease, they may be better suited to improving one's spiritual state [697].

      1.5.6.4. Con:
      Jainism rejects the concept of God [698] as contradictory and lacking evidence.

        1.5.6.4.1. Pro:
        Jainism teaches that the world is governed by natural laws [699] rather than supernatural beings.

        1.5.6.4.2. Con:
        Despite eschewing belief in an omnipotent creator god, Jains venerate jinas [700] – enlightened immaterial beings – who also lack empirical support.

  1.6. Thesis:
  Shinto [701]

    1.6.1. Pro:
    Following Shinto has positive benefits for the individual.

      1.6.1.1. Con:
      Shinto is not morally opposed [702] to suicide, which may contribute to higher suicide rates.

        1.6.1.1.1. Con:
        While religious beliefs may play a small role, Japan's high suicide rate is more likely attributable to cultural factors [703], such as family honor.

        1.6.1.1.2. Pro:
        Shinto sometimes views suicide as a sacrificial expression of guilt, honor, protest, or loyalty (pp. 8–9 [704]).

      1.6.1.2. Pro:
      Shinto emphasises [705] a positive outlook on life and practising gratitude, which can have positive health benefits [706].

        1.6.1.2.1. Pro:
        Neuroscientific research [707] has shown gratitude practice to have a significant number of physical and mental health benefits, including a strengthened immune system, improved heart health, and lower blood pressure.

        1.6.1.2.2. Con:
        One can cultivate a positive outlook and practise gratitude [708] without accepting or following Shinto.

      1.6.1.3. Con:
      Shinto beliefs stigmatise negative [709] emotions. Not acknowledging such emotions can detrimental [710] to an individual's health [711].

        1.6.1.3.1. Con:
        Rather than denying knowlegde of negative emotions, Shinto advocates for reframing [712] the perspective of such emotions, a technique [713] commonly used by mental health practitioners.

        1.6.1.3.2. Pro:
        Studies indicate that unaddressed profound emotional stress and interpersonal conflict can lead to acute cardiac failure and myocardial infarction in otherwise healthy people (pp. 859–860 [714]).

      1.6.1.4. Pro:
      Participation in Shinto rites is associated with a sense of well-being and increased self-esteem [715].

        1.6.1.4.1. Pro:
        Shinto rituals promote well-being [716] by addressing the negative energies [717] that can harm both individuals and communities.

        1.6.1.4.2. Con:
        Many of the ills addressed by Shinto rituals may be better treated with modern psychotherapy compared to outdated, mystical rituals (p. 52 [718]).

    1.6.2. Pro:
    Shinto is a complete and well-established system of belief.

      1.6.2.1. Con:
      It has been argued that Shinto constitutes a collection of cultural traditions [719] rather than a distinct religion.

        1.6.2.1.1. Pro:
        Shinto lacks [720] a central moral code, dedicated scriptures, and common metaphysical concepts, such as life after death, which are often considered essential elements of religion.

        1.6.2.1.2. Con:
        Shinto includes belief in, and reverence for, deities [721] and the observance of ritual, which are hallmarks of religion.

      1.6.2.2. Pro:
      Shinto has enjoyed great longevity [722] and is profoundly integrated [723] with Japanese society.

        1.6.2.2.1. Pro:
        Shinto predates [724] historical records.

        1.6.2.2.2. Con:
        Despite its long history, modern, organised versions of Shinto [725] bear little resemblance to its shamanic origins [726].

      1.6.2.3. Con:
      Shinto lacks many common elements of religion [727], such as compulsory religious services, texts, and centralised authority.

        1.6.2.3.1. Pro:
        Shinto is often presented as deriving authority from a distinctly indigenous Japanese character, yet many notable Shinto authorities are not Japanese and hold differing interpretations (pp. 17–18 [728]).

        1.6.2.3.2. Con:
        Shinto's lack of a central authority is not necessarily problematic, as it represents a move away from the centralised, nationalistic versions of the religion [729] historically associated with militarism.

      1.6.2.4. Pro:
      Shinto has increasingly moved beyond being an exclusively Japanese phenomena and has embraced the development of online communities [730].

        1.6.2.4.1. Pro:
        Online Shinto communities allow people outside Japan, and those in areas without shrines, to connect with priests and priestesses to learn more about the religion and stay connected [731] to its practices.

        1.6.2.4.2. Con:
        Most traditional Shinto sects have expressly disavowed online communities [732].

    1.6.3. Pro:
    Following Shinto is beneficial to society.

      1.6.3.1. Con:
      Shinto does not promote a healthy view of death [733] (p. 123 [734]).

        1.6.3.1.1. Pro:
        Since Shinto teaches that the body becomes impure upon death and emphasises purity, many followers of Shinto oppose organ transplantation [735].

        1.6.3.1.2. Pro:
        The Shinto belief that any association with death creates impurity has led to severe discrimination [736] against some occupations, such as butchers and tanners, as well as their descendants.

        1.6.3.1.3. Con:
        The Shinto view of death serves to remind its followers to make the most [737] of life. In this way, it can be seen as a positive viewpoint.

      1.6.3.2. Pro:
      Shinto has a useful moral code [738].

        1.6.3.2.1. Con:
        The moral code of Shinto was not created by the religion and is entirely based upon secular ethics [739].

        1.6.3.2.2. Pro:
        Shinto [740] "has no moral absolutes and assesses the good or bad of an action or thought in the context in which it occurs." This type of pragmatic morality is useful in avoiding blanket ideological beliefs.

      1.6.3.3. Pro:
      Shinto promotes respect and reverence for nature [741], which encourages responsible environmental views.

        1.6.3.3.1. Pro:
        Shinto's promotes belief in the interconnectedness [742] of all things, which supports ecological preservation [743] and is consistent with holistic ecological practices (p. 30 [744]).

        1.6.3.3.2. Con:
        There is no evidence that Shinto has prevented common environmental harms associated with industrialisation [745].

      1.6.3.4. Con:
      Shinto beliefs do not support gender equality.

        1.6.3.4.1. Con:
        Some branches of Shinto promote equality despite race, sex, or social status (p. 10 [746]).

        1.6.3.4.2. Pro:
        Shinto promotes unequal expectations of men and women in relation to marital fidelity [747].

        1.6.3.4.3. Con:
        Both men and women [748] can become Shinto priests [749].

          1.6.3.4.3.1. Pro:
          Historically, Shinto has relied heavily on shrine maidens [750], who were considered to have the shamanic power to communicate with spirits.

        1.6.3.4.4. Pro:
        Shinto teaches that menstrual blood is spiritually unclean [751].

          1.6.3.4.4.1. Pro:
          Priestesses have been barred from Shinto shrines and holy sites [752] whilst menstruating.

          1.6.3.4.4.2. Pro:
          Modern Shinto priestesses must regulate their menstruation [753] with medication.

        1.6.3.4.5. Pro:
        Some branches of Shinto consider sexual minorities to be suffering from an acquired disorder [754].

    1.6.4. Con:
    There is no evidence to support the assertions of Shinto.

      1.6.4.1. Pro:
      There is no evidence of the existence of kami [755], the Shinto spirits that are said to inhabit both creatures and inanimate natural objects.

        1.6.4.1.1. Pro:
        While Shinto describes many varieties of kami, they are all immaterial, supernatural spirits that lack empirical validation [756].

        1.6.4.1.2. Con:
        The term kami includes beings with vastly differing natures [757]; while some kami are properly considered spirits, others are more properly conceived of as myths or personified natural forces.

      1.6.4.2. Con:
      Shinto belief supports the separation of religion and science into non-overlapping magisteria [758].

        1.6.4.2.1. Pro:
        Shinto is focused on rituals, practices, and forms of knowledge that are distinct from the scientific worldview (pp. 98, 120 [759]).

        1.6.4.2.2. Con:
        Insofar as Shinto argues in favor of a unified cosmology that encompasses both natural and supernatural causes [760], it inherently makes assertions about reality that overlap with scientific claims about the natural world.

      1.6.4.3. Pro:
      Shinto promotes belief in a number of divination [761] techniques.

        1.6.4.3.1. Pro:
        Shinto divination includes practices such as interpreting the cracks in heated animal bones and tortoise shells, crossroads divination, and oracular dreams (pp. 87–88 [762]).

        1.6.4.3.2. Con:
        Regardless of their objective truth, Shinto divination practices support the mental health of followers [763] during uncertain times and act as a source of cultural identity.

      1.6.4.4. Con:
      Shinto does not present itself as an empirical belief system, and is instead based upon human experiences of awe and the emotions that they elicit (pp. 25–26 [764]).

        1.6.4.4.1. Pro:
        Shinto is more concerned with human experiences, such as aesthetics and beauty [765], than with intellectual or rational truth.

        1.6.4.4.2. Con:
        Researchers studying the elements of human awe experiences found that the Shinto concept of such experiences does not differ notably from that of other cultures and groups (pp. 3, 11 [766]).

    1.6.5. Con:
    Shinto is a source of human conflict.

      1.6.5.1. Con:
      Shinto offers simple sets of teachings and principles that promote peaceful and ethical behaviour. [767]

        1.6.5.1.1. Con:
        Shinto has directly contributed to the legitimisation of aggression and expansionism (p. 495 [768]).

        1.6.5.1.2. Pro:
        Shinto supports peaceful coexistence [769] and the cultivation of collective solidarity [770].

      1.6.5.2. Con:
      Shinto promotes religious tolerance [771].

        1.6.5.2.1. Pro:
        Shinto is generally considered polytheistic [772], and some denominations teach inclusive monotheism [773]; thus, their followers respect the gods of others as manifestations originating from the same source.

        1.6.5.2.2. Con:
        Some branches of Shinto have been expressly anti-Buddhist [774].

      1.6.5.3. Pro:
      Shinto shrines commemorating Japanese soldiers who died during service [775] have been an ongoing source of social conflict.

        1.6.5.3.1. Con:
        Such shrines are an example of Shinto promoting reverence and respect for ancestors [776], which contributes to social cohesion (p. 10 [777]).

        1.6.5.3.2. Pro:
        In many Asian countries, Shinto remains a palpable reminder of Japanese aggression during the Second Sino-Japanese War [778] (p. 492 [779]).

      1.6.5.4. Pro:
      Shinto has suppressed Christian people and institutions (p. 2 [780]).

        1.6.5.4.1. Pro:
        In the early 17th century, Shinto-supported leaders [781] outlawed Christianity in Japan and executed Christians, and during the Japanese occupation of Korea in the 1930s, Shinto authorities actively suppressed Christian churches and schools [782].

        1.6.5.4.2. Con:
        Japanese oppression of Christianity has historically been motivated by political [783], rather than religious, reasons.

    1.6.6. Con:
    Shinto takes advantage of its followers.

      1.6.6.1. Pro:
      Shinto shrines and practices have historically been co-opted [784] as mandatory methods of political control [785].

        1.6.6.1.1. Con:
        State Shinto was officially outlawed in 1945 [786], during the US occupation of Japan.

        1.6.6.1.2. Pro:
        A number of nationalistic elements [787] have persisted in modern Shinto, including a belief in the emperor's divinity [788].

      1.6.6.2. Pro:
      Some famous Shinto shrines have been revealed as highly profitable and tax-free [789] family businesses.

        1.6.6.2.1. Con:
        Shinto shrines are forbidden from accepting tax funds [790], as this would constitute religious establishment.

        1.6.6.2.2. Pro:
        Followers donate to Shinto based on the belief that they will be rewarded by the kami [791] for their generosity.

      1.6.6.3. Con:
      Shinto humanitarian training programs [792] support the independence of farmers rather than encouraging reliance on the religion or foreign aid.

        1.6.6.3.1. Pro:
        Shinto-based farming initiatives in Myanmar have helped to establish sound ecological and social practices that encourage sustainability (p. 2 [793]).

        1.6.6.3.2. Con:
        Shinto humanitarian efforts have often reinforced hierarchical views [794] of Japanese culture as inherently superior.

      1.6.6.4. Con:
      Shinto shrines operate as a community hub and help provide followers with emotional support [795].

        1.6.6.4.1. Pro:
        Shinto festivals throughout the year [796] create continuity and offer followers essential opportunities to experience communitas [797].

        1.6.6.4.2. Con:
        The number of those who identify their religion as Shinto has continued to decrease [798], indicating that the religion is no longer playing a central role in community life.

  1.7. Thesis:
  Sikhism [799]

    1.7.1. Pro:
    Following Sikhism is beneficial to society.

      1.7.1.1. Con:
      Sikhism is opposed to homosexuality [800].

        1.7.1.1.1. Con:
        The Guru Granth Sahib does not mention homosexuality [801], which implies that the religion does not consider it problematic.

        1.7.1.1.2. Pro:
        Sikh authorities have opposed same-sex marriage [802] laws.

      1.7.1.2. Con:
      Some Sikhs are opposed to marriage outside the faith, and have interfered with such marriages [803] as a sign of protest.

        1.7.1.2.1. Con:
        Sikhism does not oppose interfaith marriage, but the traditional marriage ritual [804] is reserved for those who have adopted the faith.

        1.7.1.2.2. Pro:
        Some Sikhs believe that it is impossible to fully practise one's faith [805] in an interfaith marriage.

      1.7.1.3. Pro:
      Sikh scripture embraces gender equity; God is seen as gender-neutral [806], and the religious obligations of women and men do not differ [807].

        1.7.1.3.1. Pro:
        Treating all people as equal [808] within their religion encourages Sikhs to practise this in their daily lives, which benefits society [809].

        1.7.1.3.2. Con:
        Despite a belief in equality, in practice, Sikh women have often been excluded from equal participation [810] in the religion.

        1.7.1.3.3. Con:
        The Guru Granth Sahib refers to reincarnation as a woman as a punishment for idolatry (p. 874 [811]).

      1.7.1.4. Pro:
      Sikhism teaches its followers to fight not only for their own rights, but also for the rights of others [812] outside of their faith.

        1.7.1.4.1. Pro:
        Social justice [813] is a key concept in Sikhism.

        1.7.1.4.2. Con:
        Many Sikh communities have strayed from the core of the teachings, perpetrating social injustice via caste distinctions [814].

    1.7.2. Pro:
    Following Sikhism has positive benefits for the individual.

      1.7.2.1. Pro:
      Sikhism teaches a strong work ethic [815] that helps adherents to avoid both poverty and idle wealth.

        1.7.2.1.1. Pro:
        The Guru Granth Sahib expressly recommends hard work and forbids followers from begging (p. 40 [816]).

        1.7.2.1.2. Con:
        Many Sikhs come from the Jatt caste [817], who own most of the land in Punjabi; hence, their wealth may be intergenerational rather than the result of hard work.

      1.7.2.2. Con:
      The Sikh religion is overwhelmingly associated with the people of the Punjab region [818]; it is not easily accessible to other ethnicities.

        1.7.2.2.1. Con:
        An increasing number of Western people have converted to Sikhism [819], and there are schools devoted to teaching them.

        1.7.2.2.2. Pro:
        Almost 90% of all Sikhs reside in India [820]; in other countries they constitute a tiny minority.

      1.7.2.3. Con:
      Sikhs are often subject to discrimination and harassment [821] in many parts of the world.

        1.7.2.3.1. Pro:
        Discrimination and hate crimes [822] against Sikhs have become increasingly common in the US.

        1.7.2.3.2. Con:
        Sikh communities have a positive image in many countries and are often well integrated (p. 149 [823]).

      1.7.2.4. Pro:
      Sikhism does not place many restrictions on its adherents' lifestyles, such as dress [824] or diet (p. 20 [825])

        1.7.2.4.1. Pro:
        Restrictions on recreational substances are often interpreted leniently [826] by Sikhs.

        1.7.2.4.2. Con:
        The 'Five K's' of Sikhism [827] impose unnecessary restrictions on followers' appearance.

    1.7.3. Pro:
    Sikhism is a complete and well-established system of belief.

      1.7.3.1. Con:
      Sikhism is a fairly new religion.

        1.7.3.1.1. Pro:
        The practice of Sikhism wasn't formalised [828] until the late seventeenth century.

        1.7.3.1.2. Con:
        Like other young religions [829], Sikhism was created to respond to the needs [830] of the world at the time.

      1.7.3.2. Con:
      Some scholars have argued that Sikhism is a branch of Hinduism [831] rather than a distinct religion.

        1.7.3.2.1. Con:
        While it may have grown out of Hindu roots and borrows heavily from the faith, Sikhism teaches distinctly different beliefs [832] from Hinduism in many areas.

        1.7.3.2.2. Pro:
        Sikhism was founded by a Hindu [833] and continues to borrow [834] substantially from the faith.

          1.7.3.2.2.1. Pro:
          Sikhism retains the Hindu doctrines [835] of karma and rebirth [836].

          1.7.3.2.2.2. Con:
          Guru Nanak was born to a Hindu family, but he chose to reject the faith [837] over doctrinal differences.

      1.7.3.3. Pro:
      Sikhism relies on one primary text, the Guru Granth Sahib [838], for spiritual and doctrinal authority.

        1.7.3.3.1. Con:
        The Guru Granth Sahib is a compilation [839] of devotional writings, poetry, and hymns rather than a document that establishes the authority of the Sikh faith.

        1.7.3.3.2. Pro:
        The Guru Granth Sahib is considered the central authority [840] for all Sikhs.

      1.7.3.4. Pro:
      Sikhism has numerous temples, known as gurdwaras [841], which serve as places of prayer and inclusive community centres.

        1.7.3.4.1. Pro:
        Sikh gurdwaras usually have four entrance doors as a symbolic reminder that they are open to all [842] in the community.

        1.7.3.4.2. Con:
        Those belonging to the Dalit caste have often been excluded from entering Sikh gurdwaras [843] and participating equally in the faith.

    1.7.4. Con:
    Sikhism takes advantage of its followers.

      1.7.4.1. Con:
      Sikhism promotes compassion and selfless behaviour [844], and places a high value on serving those in need.

        1.7.4.1.1. Con:
        The Sikh emphasis on giving without thought for personal gain [845] is unrealistic; self-interest drives a great deal of charity (p. 13 [846]).

        1.7.4.1.2. Pro:
        Sikh organizations provide a wide range of services and support [847] to community members in need.

      1.7.4.2. Pro:
      Sikhism practises tithing [848] and claims that it will ensure the prosperity of followers.

        1.7.4.2.1. Pro:
        Some Sikh charities have been accused of misappropriating funds [849].

        1.7.4.2.2. Con:
        Tithing, or Dasvandh, is not a mandatory financial obligation in Sikhism, and followers can contribute to their communities [850] in a number of different (non-monetary) ways.

      1.7.4.3. Pro:
      Victims of sexual abuse [851] have often been silenced in Sikh communities.

        1.7.4.3.1. Pro:
        The high value placed on virginity [852] before marriage within the Sikh faith has led to many underage – particularly female – victims of sexual abuse being discouraged from speaking up about their experiences.

        1.7.4.3.2. Con:
        A number of Sikh organisations are working to support [853] victims of abuse and helping them to speak up, as well as encouraging further research into how Sikh culture has enabled abuse (p. 42 [854]).

      1.7.4.4. Con:
      Sikh community meals, known as langar, are open to all and demonstrate Sikhism's rejection of caste restrictions (pp. 1–2 [855]).

        1.7.4.4.1. Pro:
        Sikh gurdwaras were instrumental in providing free meals to the needy [856] in their communities during the coronavirus pandemic, regardless of affiliation or social class.

        1.7.4.4.2. Con:
        Despite the religion formally rejecting caste, many Sikhs have yielded to social pressure and continue the practice in their personal lives [857].

    1.7.5. Con:
    Sikhism is a source of human conflict.

      1.7.5.1. Pro:
      Sikhism does not oppose the use of violence, which has led to both religious [858] and political [859] conflicts (p. 6 [860]).

        1.7.5.1.1. Pro:
        Sikhism has often been associated with martial culture [861].

        1.7.5.1.2. Con:
        Sikhism discourages aggression and only supports the use of violence in cases of self-defense or defense of others [862].

      1.7.5.2. Pro:
      Some branches of Sikhism have committed human rights abuses [863] against civilians and minority groups.

        1.7.5.2.1. Pro:
        Fundamentalist Sikh groups have often aligned with nationalistic political factions [864] responsible for civilian attacks massacres, bombings, and assassinations [865].

        1.7.5.2.2. Con:
        The radicalisation of some branches of Sikhism is a result of the extensive human rights abuses committed against them by secular authorities [866].

      1.7.5.3. Con:
      Sikhism is strongly associated with political liberalism and cultural pluralism (p. 191 [867]).

        1.7.5.3.1. Pro:
        The central principles of Sikhism are consistent with humanism [868].

        1.7.5.3.2. Con:
        Sikhism is not inherently liberal; there are many politically conservative Sikhs who support right-wing ideologies [869].

      1.7.5.4. Con:
      Sikhism strongly supports religious freedom [870], and opposes the use of coercive religious practices.

        1.7.5.4.1. Pro:
        Sikhism does not actively seek converts and forbids proselytising [871].

        1.7.5.4.2. Con:
        Many gurdwaras refuse to hold interfaith weddings [872], which can place undue pressure on those in such relationships to convert.

    1.7.6. Con:
    There is no evidence to support the assertions of Sikhism.

      1.7.6.1. Con:
      Sikhism directly opposes superstitious [873] beliefs and ritual practices.

        1.7.6.1.1. Pro:
        Sikhism views ritual and superstition as spiritually useless (p. 1 [874]), and opposes the use of such practices as a method of control and oppression. [875]

        1.7.6.1.2. Con:
        Rituals can offer people a sense of regularity and stability in uncertain times and improve mental health [876] by decreasing stress.

      1.7.6.2. Pro:
      Sikhism promotes belief in a range of supernatural powers [877].

        1.7.6.2.1. Con:
        Sikhism teaches that a focus on supernatural powers is an obstacle to spiritual development [878].

        1.7.6.2.2. Pro:
        Sikhism teaches that a number of psychic and metaphysical powers are attainable through devotion and meditation [879].

      1.7.6.3. Con:
      The Sikh creation account is consistent with scientific opinion, including the Big Bang [880].

        1.7.6.3.1. Pro:
        The creation account in the Guru Granth Sahib is concerned with the nature of creation [881] rather than factual descriptions, so Sikhs find no conflict between their religion and scientific evidence.

        1.7.6.3.2. Con:
        The Sikh account of creation relies upon the existence of God [882], for which there is insufficient evidence to support scientific belief.

      1.7.6.4. Pro:
      There is insufficient evidence to believe that Guru Nanak's claim of divine revelation [883] is true.

        1.7.6.4.1. Pro:
        The fact that there appear to be no witnesses to the experience other than Guru Nanak himself [884] make it difficult to believe this encounter was genuine.

        1.7.6.4.2. Con:
        There are many accounts of people who claim to have witnessed Guru Nanak perform miracles (p. 20 [885]).

  1.8. Thesis:
  Satanism [886]

    1.8.1. Pro:
    Following Satanism is beneficial to society.

      1.8.1.1. Pro:
      Satanism supports the equality of all genders and ethnicities.

        1.8.1.1.1. Con:
        Satanism is expressly opposed to egalitarianism [887].

        1.8.1.1.2. Pro:
        LGBTQ+ people are a majority [888] in some Satanic churches.

      1.8.1.2. Con:
      Satan represents rebellion and lawlessness [889]; following Satanism can encourage anti-social or illegal behaviour.

        1.8.1.2.1. Con:
        Organised, religious Satanism [890] is not associated with increased criminality.

        1.8.1.2.2. Pro:
        Some researchers have identified correlations between Satanic spirituality and psychopathy (p. 101 [891]).

      1.8.1.3. Con:
      Satanism promotes greed and selfishness [892].

        1.8.1.3.1. Con:
        A great deal of what is commonly considered selfish is actually just healthy self-interest [893], which is beneficial to society.

          1.8.1.3.1.1. Pro:
          A great deal of philanthropy [894] is motivated by self-interest.

        1.8.1.3.2. Con:
        Sacrificing oneself for the benefit of others is not inherently good, and is often a sign of manipulation or exploitation [895].

        1.8.1.3.3. Pro:
        Satanism promotes a self-centered view that encourages followers to prioritise their desires [896] over those of others.

      1.8.1.4. Pro:
      Satanism advocates the pursuit of justice [897].

        1.8.1.4.1. Con:
        Some branches of Satanism have been co-opted [898] in support of liberal politics and social justice activism, which stand in contrast to the individualistic nature of Satanism.

          1.8.1.4.1.1. Pro:
          Some Satanic organisations expressly promote social justice causes [899] and social equality.

        1.8.1.4.2. Pro:
        Satan has long been associated with the imposition of judgment and punishment [900].

    1.8.2. Pro:
    Satanism is a complete and well-established system of belief.

      1.8.2.1. Con:
      Satan is traditionally considered an evil figure, so any church or religion that worships him is willingly associating with evil.

        1.8.2.1.1. Con:
        The beliefs of other religions have no bearing on the morality of Satanism.

          1.8.2.1.1.1. Pro:
          The concept of Satan espoused by many branches of Satanism [901] is not the same as the Satan represented in other religions.

        1.8.2.1.2. Con:
        God is equally considered an evil figure [902] in some forms of Satanism, and his worship is also considered immoral.

        1.8.2.1.3. Pro:
        Satanism reveres a character who is rebellious and evil, which encourages followers to do the same.

          1.8.2.1.3.1. Con:
          Religious concepts of good and evil are highly variable, and what is seen as positive in one religion may be negative in another.

      1.8.2.2. Con:
      Modern concepts of Satan are not credible, as they do not rest on the foundational sources of knowledge in the Bible [903].

        1.8.2.2.1. Pro:
        The primary written sources of knowledge concerning Satan come from the Christian Bible, wherein Satan works as God's subordinate [904].

          1.8.2.2.1.1. Con:
          Modern concepts of Satan have been extricated from biblical tradition [905] and expounded at length in a variety of sources, including the Satanic Bible [906], the Satanic Scriptures [907], and many others [908]

        1.8.2.2.2. Con:
        The traditional, biblical concept of Satan is based on myth and superstition [909].

      1.8.2.3. Pro:
      Records dating to at least the 17th century [910] have documented the existence of Satanic practices.

        1.8.2.3.1. Pro:
        The veneration of Satan has been heavily suppressed by mainstream religious authorities [911], so it is likely that a great deal of historical sources on its practices have been destroyed as heretical.

        1.8.2.3.2. Con:
        Satanism was not established as an official, distinct religion [912] until 1966.

      1.8.2.4. Pro:
      Satanism is predicated upon Judeo-Christian beliefs and scriptural sources [913], so its origins are equally well established.

        1.8.2.4.1. Pro:
        The Judeo-Christian concept of Satan as God's adversary was well established by the 7th century during the Second Temple period (pp. 9–10 [914]).

        1.8.2.4.2. Con:
        Satanism is a mockery [915] of Judeo-Christian beliefs [916], not an evolution of them.

    1.8.3. Pro:
    Following Satanism has positive benefits for the individual.

      1.8.3.1. Con:
      Satanism encourages its followers to indulge [917] in their desires rather than abstain from them.

        1.8.3.1.1. Pro:
        Indulging all one's desires can lead to harmful behaviours, such as drug abuse or sexual addiction.

          1.8.3.1.1.1. Con:
          Since Satanism enshrines the individual above all else, it strongly discourages compulsive or addictive behaviours [918].

        1.8.3.1.2. Con:
        Indulging one's desires supports self-actualisation and the fulfillment of human potential [919].

        1.8.3.1.3. Con:
        Religiously motivated abstinence can be a source of damaging repression [920].

      1.8.3.2. Con:
      Satanism promotes hubris, pride, and arrogance (p. 8 [921]).

        1.8.3.2.1. Pro:
        Satanism teaches its followers that man is above God [922].

          1.8.3.2.1.1. Con:
          Satanism teaches that God is a human creation [923] and therefore considers the worship of God to be a proxy for the worship of man.

        1.8.3.2.2. Con:
        Satanism teaches that pride can be either beneficial or harmful, depending on whether or not it is productive. Counterproductive pride [924] is a sin in Satanism.

      1.8.3.3. Pro:
      Satanism stands for individual freedom and liberty [925].

        1.8.3.3.1. Pro:
        Satanism supports the bodily autonomy [926] of individuals, consent [927] in sexual relationships, and women's [928] reproductive rights [929].

        1.8.3.3.2. Con:
        Widespread perceptions of Satanism as a source of deviance, immorality, and criminality often result in the demonisation and marginalisation of Satanists (p. 28 [930]).

      1.8.3.4. Pro:
      Satanism advocates for rationality [931] and common sense [932].

        1.8.3.4.1. Pro:
        Satanism challenges adherents to critically consider its own tenets and adapt only the practices that make sense to them (pp. 4–5 [933]).

        1.8.3.4.2. Con:
        Satanic self-worship does not support the formation of rational, supportive relationships [934].

    1.8.4. Con:
    Satanism takes advantage of its followers.

      1.8.4.1. Pro:
      There have been widespread claims of ritual abuse of children [935] by Satanists.

        1.8.4.1.1. Con:
        Satanism expressly commands its adherents to not harm children [936].

        1.8.4.1.2. Con:
        Many such allegations occurred during the Satanic panic [937] that swept the US during the early 1980s; the allegations were overwhelmingly found to be baseless upon investigation by the FBI (pp. 39–40 [938]).

        1.8.4.1.3. Pro:
        Abusers have used Satanism to justify [939] the sexual abuse of children.

      1.8.4.2. Con:
      Satanism actively fights [940] against the type of theocracy that seeks to control and take advantage of people.

        1.8.4.2.1. Pro:
        Satanism advocates for religious freedom [941] for all and actively promotes the separation [942] of church and state.

        1.8.4.2.2. Con:
        Some branches of Satanism have sold initiatory degrees [943] rather than promoting spiritual or personal development.

        1.8.4.2.3. Pro:
        Satanism challenges its adherents to revolt against cruel and unjust [944] internalised god-images.

      1.8.4.3. Pro:
      Involvement with Satanism is correlated with poor mental health in adolescents (p. 56 [945]).

        1.8.4.3.1. Con:
        Some Satanists have credited their practices with improving their mental health [946] in times of crisis.

        1.8.4.3.2. Pro:
        The stigmatisation and marginalisation associated with Satanic identity can contribute to poor mental health in adolescents (p. 6 [947]).

          1.8.4.3.2.1. Con:
          Studies on the relationship between poor mental health and Satanism in adolescents have found that the subjects were likely to have been exposed to to detrimental environmental factors [948] prior to – rather than as a result of – their involvement with Satanism.

      1.8.4.4. Con:
      Satanism places a distinct emphasis on the development of self-reliance [949].

        1.8.4.4.1. Pro:
        Satanism encourages adherents to eschew belief in an external savior and to develop, and rely on, their own strength [950].

        1.8.4.4.2. Con:
        Some Satanic churches offer an array of social support programs [951], which can lead to unhealthy reliance and over-involvement.

    1.8.5. Con:
    Satanism is a source of human conflict.

      1.8.5.1. Pro:
      Satanism promotes intolerance [952] by encouraging its followers to destroy bothersome people and to respond to disrespect with cruelty.

        1.8.5.1.1. Pro:
        Satanism discourages belief in human benevolence [953], and encourages its followers to treat disrespectful and inconsiderate people with an equal lack of courtesy.

        1.8.5.1.2. Con:
        Due to the Paradox of Tolerance [954], tolerant behaviour inevitably results in the tolerance of intolerance; rational intolerance may be more effective at promoting reasonable behavior.

          1.8.5.1.2.1. Pro:
          Despite being frequently misrepresented as a source of social conflict, Satanism often promotes peaceful coexistence [955].

      1.8.5.2. Pro:
      A number of murders [956] have been inspired by Satanism.

        1.8.5.2.1. Pro:
        Serial killer Richard Ramirez [957] was inspired by Satanism.

        1.8.5.2.2. Con:
        While the murders cited above were done largely in the name of Satan [958], this is contrary to the beliefs of Satanism, which does not believe in any deity, including Satan.

      1.8.5.3. Con:
      Satanism encourages compassion and empathy [959].

        1.8.5.3.1. Pro:
        Satanism promotes the ethical treatment of animals [960].

        1.8.5.3.2. Con:
        Satanism is philosophically opposed to such values as compassion and empathy, as they detract from the goal of self-deification (pp. 90, 222 [961]).

      1.8.5.4. Con:
      Satanism advocates forgiveness for mistakes and openness to changing one's beliefs [962].

        1.8.5.4.1. Con:
        Some Satanic churches encourage vengeance [963] rather than forgiveness.

        1.8.5.4.2. Pro:
        Satanic forgiveness is predicated on the benefits it offers oneself [964] rather than on its effects on the offending party.

    1.8.6. Con:
    There is no evidence to support the assertions of Satanism.

      1.8.6.1. Con:
      Satanic beliefs [965] are largely based around the acceptance of scientific fact [966] and philosophical thinking. Such assertations are difficult to refute.

        1.8.6.1.1. Pro:
        Scientific evidence and theories [967] have long been associated with Satanism by religious leaders, who often have a vested interest in maintaining fundamentalist worldviews.

        1.8.6.1.2. Con:
        Science and religion inherently address different aspects of human existence (pp. 3–4 [968]), so the Satanic reliance on science reduces its capacity to produce meaning and value.

      1.8.6.2. Pro:
      Some branches of Satanism promote belief in magic [969].

        1.8.6.2.1. Con:
        Magic as defined by Satanism, while relying on non-empirical or supraempirical methods, can be empirically validated by its effects (p. 3 [970]).

        1.8.6.2.2. Pro:
        The principles underlying magic are contrary to scientific thinking, testing, and rationality [971].

      1.8.6.3. Pro:
      Some branches of Satanism are theistic [972] and worship Satan as a real rather than symbolic entity despite the lack of evidence for such a being.

        1.8.6.3.1. Pro:
        Earlier forms of theistic Satanism considered Satan, in the form of the Biblical serpent, to be the hero and redeemer of mankind [973].

        1.8.6.3.2. Con:
        Most Satanic churches only use the image of Satan as a metaphor [974].

      1.8.6.4. Con:
      Many forms of Satanism are philosophically rooted in materialism [975] (p. 21 [976]).

        1.8.6.4.1. Pro:
        A great deal of Satanic literature considers any proposed existence beyond the material world to be illusory or imaginary (p. 19 [977]).

        1.8.6.4.2. Con:
        The consciousness-raising focus [978] of some Satanic groups is logically inconsistent with a materialistic worldview [979].

  1.9. Thesis:
  The Bahá'í Faith [980]

    1.9.1. Pro:
    The Baháʼí Faith is a complete and well-established system of belief.

      1.9.1.1. Con:
      The Bahá'í Faith is less than two centuries [981] old.

        1.9.1.1.1. Pro:
        Some Muslim authorities consider Baháʼí to be a heretical sect of Islam rather than an independent religion (p. 449 [982]).

        1.9.1.1.2. Con:
        Bahá'ís believe in progressive revelation [983], so their teachings are consistent and have been progressively revealed [984] by God via world religions throughout history.

      1.9.1.2. Pro:
      The Bahá'í Faith has an established organisational structure [985] and numerous institutions [986].

        1.9.1.2.1. Con:
        The Bahá'í Faith lacks an organised priesthood and ritual practices [987].

        1.9.1.2.2. Pro:
        The Universal House of Justice is the international governing body of the Bahá’í Faith, created in line with the instructions of its founder, Bahá’u’lláh (p. 1 [988]).

      1.9.1.3. Pro:
      The Bahá'í Faith has extensive, authoritative scriptures [989], which promotes doctrinal unity.

        1.9.1.3.1. Pro:
        Baháʼí scriptures are based on the original copies of Baha’u’llah’s writings, which were authoritatively translated and interpreted by his great-grandson (p. 54 [990]).

        1.9.1.3.2. Con:
        The power to interpret Baháʼí scripture was vested in the descendants of Baháʼu'lláh; since there have been disputes over succession and childless descendants [991], there is no one today with an authentic claim to official interpretation.

      1.9.1.4. Con:
      The Baháʼí teaching that all religions are manifestations of the same truth leads to irreconcilable contradictions [992] about the nature of God and reality.

        1.9.1.4.1. Con:
        The Bahá’í Faith distinguishes between temporary teachings, which were established for a given time and group, and eternal spiritual truths [993], which are shared by all religions.

        1.9.1.4.2. Pro:
        Since some religions blatantly contradict each other, it cannot be the case that both are true.

    1.9.2. Pro:
    Following the Baháʼí Faith has positive benefits for the individual.

      1.9.2.1. Pro:
      The Bahá’í period of fasting has been shown to bring many physical and mental benefits (p. 1 [994]).

        1.9.2.1.1. Pro:
        Baháʼís are not obligated to fast when sick or otherwise enfeebled [995].

        1.9.2.1.2. Con:
        There is no need to follow a religion in order to gain the benefits of fasting. For example, intermittent fasting [996] has become increasingly common.

      1.9.2.2. Con:
      In many places, Bahá'ís remain subject to severe persecution [997].

        1.9.2.2.1. Pro:
        Followers of the Bahá'í Faith are being deliberately forced [998] to flee Iran by negative propaganda and violent raids.

        1.9.2.2.2. Con:
        Religious persecution [999] remains common across the globe for followers of various faiths. Bahá'ís are not unique in this regard.

      1.9.2.3. Pro:
      The Bahá'í Faith forbids its adherents to use alcohol, opium, or other addictive drugs [1000], which promotes their good health.

        1.9.2.3.1. Con:
        The Bahá’í Faith makes no distinction between the use and abuse of drugs and alcohol [1001], and forbids even low-risk social drinking [1002].

        1.9.2.3.2. Pro:
        Drugs and alcohol undermine one's capability of pursuing the virtues and goals [1003] espoused by the Baháʼí Faith.

      1.9.2.4. Con:
      Bahá'í writings are heavily censored, and there have been accusations that the faith seeks to control the speech and behaviour of followers [1004] through propaganda.

        1.9.2.4.1. Pro:
        The requirement that Baháʼí writers submit their works for review by officials prior to publication [1005] has resulted in a lack of critical academic writing about the faith.

        1.9.2.4.2. Con:
        The Baháʼí review process is intended to prevent the misrepresentation of the faith or its teachings [1006], as the general population remains unaware of many Baháʼí principles (pp. 20–21 [1007]).

    1.9.3. Pro:
    Following the Baháʼí Faith is beneficial to society.

      1.9.3.1. Pro:
      The Bahá'í Faith emphasises the importance of care and development of children and young people [1008].

        1.9.3.1.1. Pro:
        The education of children and young people within Bahá'í is focused on self-improvement and social change [1009].

        1.9.3.1.2. Con:
        Despite claims that Bahá’í education classes do not constitute religious indoctrination, [1010] such lessons often promote religious values [1011] and have, at times, been forced on students [1012].

      1.9.3.2. Con:
      Bahá'í writings display racial prejudice [1013] against African people.

        1.9.3.2.1. Con:
        The Bahá'í Faith preaches against all forms of prejudice [1014].

        1.9.3.2.2. Pro:
        Abdu’l-Bahá, who was head of the Baháʼí Faith between 1892 and 1921, is presented by the faith as a champion of social justice and exemplary Bahá’í [1015]; however, his writings reveal deep-seated prejudice [1016] against African peoples.

      1.9.3.3. Con:
      The Bahá'í Faith has become increasingly fundamentalist [1017]; many Bahá'ís support the long-term goal of establishing theocracy.

        1.9.3.3.1. Pro:
        The Bahá’í Faith does not support the separation of church and state [1018].

        1.9.3.3.2. Con:
        The literature discussing the theocratic goals of the Baha'i Faith has been written by non-Baha'is and suffers from an incomplete understanding of the faith's principles (p. 1 [1019]).

      1.9.3.4. Pro:
      The Bahá'í Faith values the equality of the sexes [1020].

        1.9.3.4.1. Con:
        Women are forbidden [1021] from joining the Baháʼí Faith's governing council, the Universal House of Justice [1022].

        1.9.3.4.2. Pro:
        The Bahá’í Faith supports the right of women to equal education, recognition, and opportunity [1023].

    1.9.4. Con:
    There is no evidence to support the assertions of the Baháʼí Faith.

      1.9.4.1. Pro:
      The Bahá'í Faith teaches its adherents that angels [1024] exist.

        1.9.4.1.1. Con:
        Abdu'l-Bahá, the son of Baháʼu'lláh and second head of the Baháʼí Faith, taught that the term "angels" refers to prophets and divine messengers [1025] rather than supernatural beings.

        1.9.4.1.2. Pro:
        The Baháʼí Faith has asserted multiple, contradictory explanations [1026] of angels, which lack empirical evidence.

      1.9.4.2. Con:
      The Bahá’í Faith teaches that religion should conform with scientific evidence [1027].

        1.9.4.2.1. Pro:
        Bahá'ís believe in the essential harmony [1028] of science and religion and teach that religion and science complement one another in the search for truth.

        1.9.4.2.2. Con:
        Some [1029] Bahá'í teachings [1030] contradict science [1031].

      1.9.4.3. Con:
      The Bahá’í teaching that humanity is characterized by unity in diversity [1032] is supported by a modern understanding of human genetics (p. 1 [1033]).

        1.9.4.3.1. Pro:
        Secular organisations, such as the UN, have also adopted the human genome [1034] as a symbol of human unity through diversity.

        1.9.4.3.2. Con:
        The Bahá’í focus on unity can overlook social inequalities and discourage challenges to the status quo (p. 20 [1035]).

      1.9.4.4. Pro:
      There is no evidence that humans have an eternal soul [1036] as taught by the Bahá'í Faith.

        1.9.4.4.1. Con:
        Bahá'ís believe that dreams [1037] are evidence of the soul's existence.

        1.9.4.4.2. Pro:
        The Bahá’í explanation of the soul [1038] relies upon an appeal to mystery [1039].

    1.9.5. Con:
    The Baháʼí Faith is a source of human conflict.

      1.9.5.1. Con:
      The Baháʼí Faith promotes democracy [1040] and the decentralisation of state power, which are opposed to harmful nationalism.

        1.9.5.1.1. Pro:
        The Bahá’í system of democracy avoids power-seeking behavior [1041] and promotes responsible public service.

        1.9.5.1.2. Con:
        Nationalism and democracy are in no way inherently opposed; one has often been instrumental in the development of the other (p. 153 [1042]).

      1.9.5.2. Con:
      The Bahá'í Faith preaches peace [1043] and opposes militarism.

        1.9.5.2.1. Pro:
        The Baháʼí Faith teaches the unity of humanity [1044] and promotes cooperation, interfaith dialogue, and the elimination of prejudice as means for achieving peace.

        1.9.5.2.2. Con:
        The Baháʼí opposition to armed conflict [1045] ignores the causes of many wars, such as historical inequity and oppression, and only serves to reinforce the status quo.

      1.9.5.3. Pro:
      Baháʼís have often been arrested on charges of foreign espionage [1046].

        1.9.5.3.1. Con:
        Accusations of Baháʼí espionage have been part of the systematic persecution of the faith [1047] by authoritarian, theocratic governments.

        1.9.5.3.2. Pro:
        The Baháʼí Faith is headquartered in Israel [1048] and is thus heavily influenced by Zionism [1049], leading to suspicions of espionage.

      1.9.5.4. Pro:
      The Bahá’í Faith places inordinate social pressure on those who question or withdraw from the faith [1050].

        1.9.5.4.1. Pro:
        The Universal House of Justice, central authority for the Bahá'í Faith, has issued statements supporting the shunning of those who oppose their interpretation [1051] of the faith's teachings.

        1.9.5.4.2. Con:
        The Baháʼí Faith considers the independent investigation of truth [1052] a moral obligation.

    1.9.6. Con:
    The Baháʼí Faith takes advantage of its followers.

      1.9.6.1. Pro:
      Bahá'ís are expected to tithe [1053], and the requisite amount increases with their surplus income.

        1.9.6.1.1. Pro:
        Tithing in Bahá’í, known as Huququ’llah the or Right of God [1054], is considered a debt and is expected even after a follower's death.

        1.9.6.1.2. Con:
        Huququ'llah is entirely voluntary [1055], and Bahá'ís are expressly prohibited from soliciting such funds.

      1.9.6.2. Pro:
      There have been allegations of sexual impropriety [1056] against Bahá'í officials and cover-ups [1057] by the faith.

        1.9.6.2.1. Con:
        The accusations leveled against the Baháʼí Faith are characteristic of demonization and unsupported by evidence (pp. 197–198 [1058]).

        1.9.6.2.2. Pro:
        In 2022, Ardeshir Sorianosis Zehtab-Jadid confessed to grooming and sexual assault of a minor [1059], who he was mentoring during Bahá'í volunteer activities.

      1.9.6.3. Con:
      The Baháʼí Faith organizes youth empowerment programs [1060] that help adolescents engage with issues in their communities.

        1.9.6.3.1. Pro:
        Baháʼí youth empowerment programs [1061] increase adolescent engagement, set positive expectations, reduce risk, and positively impact community health.

        1.9.6.3.2. Con:
        There have been reports of significant religious peer pressure and manipulation [1062] within Baháʼí youth groups.

      1.9.6.4. Con:
      The Bahá’í Faith supports a wide range of social action initiatives, such as refugee assistance programs [1063], that help followers improve their communities.

        1.9.6.4.1. Pro:
        Baháʼí organisations actively support people seeking asylum from trafficking and other forms of gender-based violence [1064].

        1.9.6.4.2. Con:
        Opportunities for enacting social change from within the Baháʼí Faith are limited, as political activism is largely forbidden [1065].

  1.10. Thesis:
  Taoism [1066]

    1.10.1. Pro:
    Following Taoism is beneficial to society.

      1.10.1.1. Pro:
      Taoism teaches beneficial moral and ethical principles [1067].

        1.10.1.1.1. Con:
        Taoism teaches that people should be ruthlessly discarded [1068] when they are no longer useful.

        1.10.1.1.2. Con:
        Taoism does not always promote moral good. Instead, it seeks to establish a balance between good and evil [1069], which are considered to have equal moral value.

        1.10.1.1.3. Pro:
        Later Taoist scriptures, such as the Lingbao, present a far more developed and practical moral code [1070] than that of earlier writings.

      1.10.1.2. Con:
      The lack of emphasis on self-determination in Taoism can be seen as ethical justification for denying others the right to make informed decisions, which can support totalitarian behaviour (p. 29 [1071]).

        1.10.1.2.1. Con:
        Taoism promotes a minimalist approach to governance (p. 5 [1072]).

        1.10.1.2.2. Pro:
        The Taoist belief in the lack of distinction between individuals undermines important social concepts, such as privacy and individual choice (pp. 97–98 [1073]).

      1.10.1.3. Pro:
      The Taoist religion is closely associated with ecological consciousness [1074].

        1.10.1.3.1. Pro:
        A number of Taoist teachings are directly related to humanity's relationship with nature [1075].

        1.10.1.3.2. Con:
        Taoist contributions to ecological awareness have often been overstated and romanticized; there is no evidence that the practise of Taoism has led to better environmental policies (p. 5 [1076]).

      1.10.1.4. Pro:
      Taoism supports equality.

        1.10.1.4.1. Pro:
        Taoism allows women to become priests [1077].

        1.10.1.4.2. Con:
        Taoism has traditionally supported sex work for women, and Taoist manuals have been used to train sex workers (p. 7 [1078]).

      1.10.1.5. Con:
      The Taoist principle of wu wei [1079] encourages people to be inactive and not participate in world affairs.

        1.10.1.5.1. Con:
        Many problems arise from political engagement, as it leads to the polarisation [1080] of society and causes harm.

        1.10.1.5.2. Pro:
        Some followers of Taoism interpret the principle of wu wei as justification to leave society and live as hermits [1081].

        1.10.1.5.3. Con:
        Taoists have a long history of active political participation, such as the Yellow Turban Rebellion [1082].

        1.10.1.5.4. Pro:
        Taoist beliefs assert that the return to the Tao is imminent [1083] and requires no special action. Regardless of what action one performs, the finality will be the Tao, so it doesn't matter if one takes action or not.

    1.10.2. Pro:
    Following Taoism has positive benefits for the individual.

      1.10.2.1. Pro:
      Taoism teaches useful meditation techniques [1084] that promote calmness, clarity, and compassion.

        1.10.2.1.1. Pro:
        T'ai chi and other forms of Taoist qigong practice can provide a number of physical and mental health benefits [1085] to practitioners.

        1.10.2.1.2. Con:
        One need not follow Taoism or embrace its principles in order to gain the benefits of meditation.

      1.10.2.2. Con:
      Taoism can discourage followers from seeking support for mental health conditions, since doing so undermines the notion that one should not try to alter nature (p. 36 [1086]).

        1.10.2.2.1. Con:
        There is evidence to suggest that Chinese Taoist cognitive therapy (CTCT) may be useful in the treatment of clinical depression (p. 9 [1087]).

        1.10.2.2.2. Pro:
        Some mental health conditions require professional treatment [1088] in order to improve; doing nothing in accordance with wu wei [1089] would prevent any improvement.

      1.10.2.3. Con:
      The Taoist concept of decentralised selfhood is contradictory and does not support normal human ambition [1090] (p. 20 [1091]).

        1.10.2.3.1. Con:
        What some consider normal ambition [1092] can often lead to a great deal of stress, anxiety, and depression.

        1.10.2.3.2. Pro:
        Taoism is often considered to be opposed to education, as ignorance [1093] is believed to be more favourable for creating contentment.

      1.10.2.4. Pro:
      Taoism teaches its adherents to accept the nature of things [1094] as they are, rather than as we wish them to be.

        1.10.2.4.1. Con:
        Individuals and society should not accept things that are corrupt or morally wrong, such as slavery.

        1.10.2.4.2. Pro:
        Taoist beliefs on acceptance have proven effective when integrated into modern psychotherapy (p. 4 [1095]).

    1.10.3. Pro:
    Taoism is a complete and well-established system of belief.

      1.10.3.1. Con:
      Tao is difficult to define [1096], as it is inherently contradictory.

        1.10.3.1.1. Con:
        A number of observable physical [1097] and psychological [1098] phenomena involve inherent paradoxes, so the contradictory nature of Tao is not especially problematic and may offer an explanation for such things.

        1.10.3.1.2. Con:
        As a principle encompassing and underlying [1099] all existence, Tao need not be clearly defined or understood; Taoism teaches that the unknowable nature of existence should be embraced (pp. 3, 17 [1100]).

        1.10.3.1.3. Pro:
        Taoism asserts that Tao is non-existence (pp. 5, 14 [1101]); however, if Tao exists, then Tao cannot be non-existence.

          1.10.3.1.3.1. Con:
          Taoism asserts that existence necessitates the reality of non-existence [1102] in the same way that concepts like long and short imply the existence of the other.

      1.10.3.2. Con:
      Many laypersons and scholars disagree on whether Taoism [1103] is a philosophy, a religion, a science [1104], or a combination of these.

        1.10.3.2.1. Pro:
        Taoism lacks [1105] a belief in God or gods, a centralised dogma, and an established institutional structure.

        1.10.3.2.2. Con:
        Taoism is often practised as a religion [1106], and often includes rituals and devotion to supernatural entities.

      1.10.3.3. Pro:
      Taosim has a long history [1107].

        1.10.3.3.1. Con:
        Taoist beliefs and practices have become integrated with those of Buddhism, Confucianism, and Chinese folk religion [1108] in such a way that makes Taoism difficult to specifically address.

        1.10.3.3.2. Pro:
        Taoism has played an important role [1109] in the development of art, culture, science, and medicine.

      1.10.3.4. Pro:
      There is a large body of canonical Taoist literature [1110].

        1.10.3.4.1. Pro:
