        The stated goal [1710] of Scientology is to help people identify their mental aberrations [1711] and offer techniques for overcoming them.

        1.14.6.1.3. Pro:
        The requirements [1712] to be a member of the Church of Scientology realistically mean that only those who are financially well-off [1713] are able to join.

      1.14.6.2. Pro:
      The current leader of the Church of Scientology has been accused of child trafficking [1714] and abuse [1715].

        1.14.6.2.1. Pro:
        Scientology has used signed arbitration contracts [1716] to prevent former adherents from pursuing claims of harassment and sexual assault.

        1.14.6.2.2. Con:
        As of 2023, David Miscavige has not been convicted [1717] of any crimes involving trafficking or abuse.

      1.14.6.3. Con:
      Scientology supports and promotes the United Nations Universal Declaration of Human Rights (UDHR [1718]).

        1.14.6.3.1. Pro:
        The Church of Scientology has worked to spread awareness of human rights [1719] in Mexico and help promote policy changes.

        1.14.6.3.2. Con:
        Scientology is well know for carrying out some practices that actively contravene [1720] human rights.

      1.14.6.4. Con:
      The Church of Scientology operates a wide range of humanitarian programs [1721].

        1.14.6.4.1. Pro:
        Scientology operates numerous Narconon [1722] drug rehabilitation centres and outreach programs.

        1.14.6.4.2. Con:
        Scientology humanitarian aid efforts, such as those to the survivors of the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami, often involve practices best described as faith healing [1723].

  1.15. Thesis:
  Pagansim [1724]

    1.15.1. Pro:
    Following Paganism is beneficial to society.

      1.15.1.1. Pro:
      Many Pagan traditions have only one distinct tenet – harm none and do as you will [1725] – which allows great levels of autonomy whilst still respecting others.

        1.15.1.1.1. Pro:
        Some Pagan rituals, such as tarot [1726], are associated with increased interiority and critical reflection. This can make people more aware of their role in the world and improve their interactions.

        1.15.1.1.2. Con:
        The tenet 'harm none' isn't very useful because it fails to define what 'harm' is. As such, Paganism could excuse a number of negative acts.

      1.15.1.2. Pro:
      Some forms of Paganism are useful vehicles for exploring women's role in society [1727]; by liberating people from the patriarchy, Paganism facilitates a better world.

        1.15.1.2.1. Con:
        Historically, many pagan societies have been patriarchal [1728].

        1.15.1.2.2. Pro:
        Paganism is an attractive option for those who are dissatisfied with traditional gender roles, as it allows for more flexible interpretation of such norms (p. 47 [1729]).

      1.15.1.3. Con:
      Modern forms of Paganism can be exclusionary [1730].

        1.15.1.3.1. Pro:
        Some branches of Paganism have become a draw for racism [1731] and far-right idealogies.

        1.15.1.3.2. Con:
        Most Pagan communities are inclusive and welcome members from diverse backgrounds [1732].

      1.15.1.4. Con:
      Paganism lacks a developed notion of good and evil [1733], encouraging harmful moral relativism [1734].

        1.15.1.4.1. Con:
        Paganism recognises that the terms 'good' and 'evil' are associated with articles of faith [1735] and, as such, can be divisive and used to malign those of other faiths.

        1.15.1.4.2. Con:
        Paganism is aligned with modern psychology in accepting that absolute [1736] good and evil are socially created concepts [1737], which depend on individual context and lived experience.

        1.15.1.4.3. Pro:
        A clear concept of evil is necessary for society to identify, and prevent, morally significant [1738] detrimental events.

      1.15.1.5. Pro:
      Paganism is traditionally Earth-centred, placing a high value on the sort of environmentally aware activities needed to fight climate change [1739] and other pollution problems (p. 1 [1740]).

        1.15.1.5.1. Pro:
        Pagan holidays are tied to the seasons and promote awareness of both vegetation and solar cycles [1741].

        1.15.1.5.2. Con:
        The increased popularity and resulting commercialisation of Paganism [1742] has eroded the connection between practitioners and their natural surroundings.

    1.15.2. Pro:
    Following Paganism has positive benefits for the individual.

      1.15.2.1. Pro:
      Paganism promotes the development of individual responsibility [1743].

        1.15.2.1.1. Pro:
        Paganism encourages adherents to take ownership of their actions and personal development [1744], which encourages self-actualisation.

        1.15.2.1.2. Con:
        Paganism's focus on the individual and the rise of solo practitioners has undermined the ability of the faith to enact widespread social change [1745].

      1.15.2.2. Con:
      Many Pagans experience substantial conflict and stigma over following a different belief [1746] than their family or community.

        1.15.2.2.1. Pro:
        Pagans are often perceived as cult members [1747] or Satanists [1748] by those outside the movement.

        1.15.2.2.2. Con:
        Such stigmatisation is likely to subside with the rapidly increasing popularity of Paganism [1749] in Western countries.

      1.15.2.3. Pro:
      Pagan rituals promote the personal development of practitioners and can improve their psychological well-being (p. 250 [1750]).

        1.15.2.3.1. Pro:
        Pagan rituals empower adherents by bypassing their rational minds and reconnecting them with their subconscious (pp. 69–70 [1751]).

        1.15.2.3.2. Con:
        Few Pagans are well-versed in the principles of ritual design and structure, so the rituals of many practitioners can be ineffective or even harmful.

      1.15.2.4. Con:
      Pagans are a small religious minority [1752] regardless of where they live, so followers often have little opportunity [1753] to participate in a community.

        1.15.2.4.1. Pro:
        Many Pagans choose to practise their religion alone [1754], as the few existing communities are often divided by doctrinal and political differences [1755].

        1.15.2.4.2. Con:
        Pagans without a local community often participate in one of the many virtual Pagan communities or advocacy groups (p. 11 [1756]).

    1.15.3. Pro:
    Paganism is a complete and well-established system of belief.

      1.15.3.1. Pro:
      Many Pagan traditions have long, rich histories [1757] that predate today's major world religions.

        1.15.3.1.1. Con:
        Some Pagan traditions are modern in origin; for example, Wicca was created by Gerald Gardner [1758] in the early 20th century.

        1.15.3.1.2. Pro:
        Many modern practitioners of Paganism base [1759] their conventions on pre-Christian cultures.

      1.15.3.2. Con:
      Paganism largely consists of reinterpretations and revivals of ancient practices and traditions borrowed from other religions rather than distinct religious traditions (p. 1 [1760]).

        1.15.3.2.1. Pro:
        Paganism has often appropriated the beliefs and practices of Indigenous peoples (p. 11 [1761]).

        1.15.3.2.2. Con:
        Many Pagan practices have historically been suppressed [1762] and appropriated [1763], so their revival is a form of reappropriation (p. 9 [1764]).

      1.15.3.3. Con:
      The many branches and sects [1765] of Paganism are too diverse [1766] in their beliefs and practices to constitute a coherent religion.

        1.15.3.3.1. Con:
        Diversity of belief does not show that Paganism is invalid or incoherent, but instead demonstrates that it has been personalised by different adherents and communities.

        1.15.3.3.2. Pro:
        Due to the great number of sects and few followers affiliated with each, Pagan traditions often lack formal places of worship [1767] and institutional structures.

          1.15.3.3.2.1. Con:
          The lack of a hierarchical organisational structure [1768] in many Pagan traditions brings a number of benefits to practitioners.

      1.15.3.4. Pro:
      Pagan traditions have extensively developed and well-established rituals, holidays, and mythologies [1769].

        1.15.3.4.1. Pro:
        Many Pagan traditions draw upon well-established mythologies [1770] as a primary source.

        1.15.3.4.2. Con:
        Many Pagan holidays today are reconstructions of older rites that bear little resemblance to their original form. For example, the modern celebration of Beltane and Walpurgisnacht largely omits the fertility aspect [1771] of older Pagan May Day celebrations.

    1.15.4. Con:
    There is no evidence to support the assertions of Paganism.

      1.15.4.1. Pro:
      Many Pagan traditions promote belief in animism [1772], including the existence of spirits associated with particular places and inanimate objects.

        1.15.4.1.1. Con:
        Animism is concerned with the context in which things exist and the relationships between them; animistic beliefs are based on a different form of observation than science (p. 8 [1773]).

        1.15.4.1.2. Pro:
        Some Pagan traditions believe that crystals have metaphysical properties [1774], despite there being no scientific evidence [1775] for this.

      1.15.4.2. Pro:
      Paganism promotes belief in magic [1776].

        1.15.4.2.1. Con:
        Magic relies on the subjective state of the practitioner [1777] to such an extent that objective proof of it is not possible.

        1.15.4.2.2. Pro:
        Pagan magic presupposes pathways of causality that cannot be empirically demonstrated to exist (p. 3 [1778]).

      1.15.4.3. Con:
      Not all Pagan beliefs are meant to be taken literally. Many Pagan practices make extensive [1779] use of psychodrama [1780] and symbolism [1781].

        1.15.4.3.1. Pro:
        Pagans do not treat mythology as factually true; instead, it is used as a source in the construction of identity and a vehicle for spiritual truths (p. 9 [1782]).

        1.15.4.3.2. Con:
        Some branches of Paganism exhibit aspects of fundamentalism [1783], particularly in regard to historicity, the existence of gods, and gender roles.

      1.15.4.4. Con:
      Paganism relies heavily on empirical evidence and is compatible with a great deal of scientific knowledge (p. 15 [1784]).

        1.15.4.4.1. Pro:
        The rediscovery of early Pagan philosophy was a major contributing factor to the Renaissance and Scientific Revolution (p. 290 [1785]).

        1.15.4.4.2. Con:
        Most forms of Paganism also rely on belief in supernatural energies and entities [1786], which is inherently at odds with the methodology of science.

    1.15.5. Con:
    Paganism is a source of human conflict.

      1.15.5.1. Pro:
      Paganism is historically associated with anti-Semitism [1787].

        1.15.5.1.1. Pro:
        Many high-ranking Nazis [1788] followed Pagan beliefs.

        1.15.5.1.2. Con:
        There are many parallels between Jewish and Pagan beliefs, as embodied in contemporary forms of Jewish Paganism [1789].

      1.15.5.2. Pro:
      The early Christian church was widely opposed [1790] and persecuted [1791] by Pagans.

        1.15.5.2.1. Pro:
        The rise of Christianity disrupted the Roman Pagan temple economy, providing an incentive for widespread persecution (p. 118 [1792]).

        1.15.5.2.2. Con:
        Many Christian beliefs were directly opposed to the established Pagan social order and were considered politically subversive (pp. 11–12 [1793]).

      1.15.5.3. Con:
      Many modern branches of Paganism are closely identified with peace activism (pp. 30–31 [1794]).

        1.15.5.3.1. Pro:
        Many Pagan goddess traditions espouse pacifism [1795] and support of progressive social causes [1796].

        1.15.5.3.2. Con:
        This depends entirely on the branch and individual; many Pagans continue to venerate war gods, such as Ares [1797] and Athena [1798].

      1.15.5.4. Con:
      Paganism is traditionally open-minded to other gods and beliefs [1799] and does not seek to convert [1800] followers through force.

        1.15.5.4.1. Pro:
        The Pagan belief [1801] in many different deities – and the diverse ways that individuals may be drawn to them – is opposed to forcing anyone to follow a specific god or practice.

        1.15.5.4.2. Con:
        There are a number of examples of religious persecution [1802] and forced conversion [1803] by Pagans.

    1.15.6. Con:
    Paganism takes advantage of its followers.

      1.15.6.1. Pro:
      There have been a number of incidents of sexual abuse [1804] occurring as part of Pagan rituals.

        1.15.6.1.1. Con:
        While the perpetrators of these acts may have used Paganism as the reason for the abuse, proponents of Pagan pathways say there is nothing sexual [1805] about their practices.

        1.15.6.1.2. Con:
        Pagan communities have adopted resolutions [1806] to ensure that allegations of abuse are duly investigated and that victims are fully supported.

        1.15.6.1.3. Pro:
        Many of the myths upon which Pagan traditions are founded describe the gods raping mortals [1807].

      1.15.6.2. Con:
      Pagan organisations have supported humanitarian efforts to benefit both Pagans [1808] and society at large [1809].

        1.15.6.2.1. Pro:
        Pagan and Wiccan organisations contribute to a number of social causes [1810], including assistance to victims of domestic violence, abused children, and those affected by HIV/AIDS.

        1.15.6.2.2. Con:
        Charity is not a Pagan virtue [1811] and has generally been treated as a means for enhancing the giver's reputation.

      1.15.6.3. Con:
      Pagans have opened a Pagan credit union to support the community and address the discrimination [1812] they often face in the financial sector.

        1.15.6.3.1. Pro:
        Research has demonstrated hiring discrimination against Pagans (p. 119 [1813]).

        1.15.6.3.2. Con:
        The alleged financial discrimination against Pagans is based on factors that affect everyone equally [1814], so it does not constitute discrimination.

      1.15.6.4. Pro:
      Many purported Pagan authorities take advantage of followers by trivialising their faith as a product rather than a valid spiritual path (p. 3 [1815]).

        1.15.6.4.1. Pro:
        Many Pagan practices and beliefs have been appropriated and commercialised [1816] as products [1817] devoid of religious meaning.

        1.15.6.4.2. Con:
        Many Pagans openly oppose the commercialisation of their beliefs and designate such practices and products as inauthentic (p. 1 [1818]).

  1.16. Thesis:
  Islam [1819]

    1.16.1. Con:
    Islam takes advantage of its followers.

      1.16.1.1. Pro:
      There have been instances of serious abuse [1820] by Muslim authorities.

        1.16.1.1.1. Pro:
        Prompted by the #MeToo movement, a number of victims have come forward alleging sexual and spiritual abuse [1821] at the hands of well-known Muslim leaders.

        1.16.1.1.2. Pro:
        Illegal corporal punishment and sexual abuse [1822] of children in UK Muslim schools is widespread.

        1.16.1.1.3. Con:
        Muslim leaders have issued coordinated responses [1823] to such cases, condemning abuse in unequivocal terms, calling for support for victims, and promoting wider awareness of the issue.

      1.16.1.2. Con:
      Charity and service to others [1824] are important in Islam.

        1.16.1.2.1. Pro:
        The Islamic practice of zakat [1825] transfers an immense amount of wealth to Muslims in need.

        1.16.1.2.2. Con:
        Many Muslim charitable funds remain idle and underutilised due to poor management and bookkeeping [1826].

      1.16.1.3. Con:
      Mosques and imams do not rely on the congregation to support them financially (p. 52 [1827]).

        1.16.1.3.1. Pro:
        A majority of the mosques outside the Islamic world are supported by Islamic associations [1828].

          1.16.1.3.1.1. Con:
          Regardless of the source of funding, the internal management of mosque funds remains largely unregulated in many places (p. 193 [1829]), so funding is not always used to the benefit of the congregation [1830].

        1.16.1.3.2. Con:
        Government-funded mosques are subject to undue control by the state [1831].

          1.16.1.3.2.1. Pro:
          The Saudi government has mandated the installation of surveillance cameras in mosques [1832] so the content of sermons can be reviewed by a state ministry.

      1.16.1.4. Pro:
      Muslim leaders have often encouraged martyrdom [1833].

        1.16.1.4.1. Pro:
        Some Muslim leaders have encouraged adherents to participate in suicide attacks with promises of rewards in the afterlife (p. 75 [1834]).

        1.16.1.4.2. Pro:
        Iranian authorities have martyred [1835] individuals who died in the opposition with Syria.

        1.16.1.4.3. Con:
        The idea of religious martrydom is not present in the Qur'an, and early Islamic descriptions of martyrdom lack any militant or political association (pp. 6–7 [1836]).

    1.16.2. Con:
    Islam is a source of human conflict.

      1.16.2.1. Con:
      Islam promotes reconciliation between opposing parties and offers many practical examples of conflict resolution [1837].

        1.16.2.1.1. Pro:
        The Qur'an opposes holding grudges [1838] against another person whilst emphasising reconciliation on the grounds that both promote peace as well as personal growth.

        1.16.2.1.2. Con:
        The schism between Shia and Sunni Muslims has been a recurring source of conflict [1839] for centuries.

      1.16.2.2. Pro:
      Islam is intolerant of other faiths.

        1.16.2.2.1. Con:
        The Qur'an forbids compulsion [1840] in religious matters.

        1.16.2.2.2. Pro:
        Interfaith marriage is prosecuted in many Muslim countries, at times enforced via vigilante 'honor killings [1841]'.

      1.16.2.3. Pro:
      The Qur'an advocates [1842] the use of violence [1843] against non-believers [1844].

        1.16.2.3.1. Con:
        Islam often advocates benevolence and mercy.

          1.16.2.3.1.1. Con:
          The Qur'an only advocates mercy amongst Muslims, and promotes severity against disbelievers [1845].

        1.16.2.3.2. Con:
        The Qur'an only advocates the use of violence in self-defence [1846] or for retribution against those who have persecuted others [1847].

        1.16.2.3.3. Pro:
        The Prophet Muhammad preached peace in Mecca, but converted few. His later Medina period produced exhortations to violence against non-believers in the Qur'an and hadith, and these are difficult to reconcile with the earlier teachings [1848].

      1.16.2.4. Con:
      Islam is a religion of peace.

        1.16.2.4.1. Con:
        Different Muslim groups hold divergent beliefs about violence; while traditional groups do not accept religious justifications for violence, fundamentalist factions [1849] can find ample scriptural support for violence in the Qur'an.

          1.16.2.4.1.1. Con:
          Muslim extremists are not representative of the entire Islamic faith.

        1.16.2.4.2. Pro:
        Islam wholly rejects [1850] all forms of terrorism.

          1.16.2.4.2.1. Pro:
          The opening sections of the Qur'an specifically condemn [1851] any actions which deliberately cause fear.

          1.16.2.4.2.2. Con:
          ISIS [1852] consider themselves strict adherents of Islam, yet their belief seems to lead them to great violence.

    1.16.3. Pro:
    Following Islam is beneficial to society.

      1.16.3.1. Con:
      Islam incentives problematic behaviour towards LGBTQ+ people and apostates.

        1.16.3.1.1. Pro:
        Muslims who leave Islam are scrutinised for blasphemy and, in some places, are subject to the death penalty [1853].

        1.16.3.1.2. Con:
        Islam is egalitarian [1854] and teaches that righteousness is the only basis for distinguishing between individuals.

        1.16.3.1.3. Pro:
        Homosexuality carries the death penalty [1855] or prison sentences in a number of Muslim countries.

      1.16.3.2. Con:
      A number of Islamic practices are harmful to women and girls.

        1.16.3.2.1. Pro:
        Domestic violence against women is supported by certain Qur'an passages [1856] and is widespread [1857] in Muslim communities.

        1.16.3.2.2. Con:
        Although Muslim women are often represented as victims without agency [1858] by both outsiders and other Muslims, some Muslim women freely choose to live in accordance with traditional customs.

        1.16.3.2.3. Pro:
        Islam supports child marriage [1859], as practised by the Prophet Muhammad (p. 2 [1860]).

      1.16.3.3. Pro:
      Islam promotes active participation and involvement [1861] in one's community.

        1.16.3.3.1. Con:
        Islam undermines the separation of church and state by supporting the role of religious leaders in politics [1862].

        1.16.3.3.2. Pro:
        Islam supports civil engagement [1863], integration with society at large, and respect for local law.

      1.16.3.4. Pro:
      Islam teaches a valuable moral code; the Qur'an forms the basis of an entire legislative system (p. 10 [1864]).

        1.16.3.4.1. Con:
        Sharia law [1865] is often criticised for being incompatible with modern ideas of human rights.

          1.16.3.4.1.1. Pro:
          Islamic Sharia law recommends harsh and inhumane punishments [1866] for a number of crimes; these are incompatible with modern views of punishment and torture.

          1.16.3.4.1.2. Con:
          Human rights are a Western construct [1867] and should not be applied to everyone.

          1.16.3.4.1.3. Con:
          Sharia law is not used [1868] in all Muslim countries.

        1.16.3.4.2. Pro:
        Islam advocates service to others [1869].

    1.16.4. Pro:
    Following Islam has positive benefits for the individual.

      1.16.4.1. Con:
      Islam imposes unreasonable restrictions on its followers' freedoms.

        1.16.4.1.1. Pro:
        Islam prescribes restrictive dress codes [1870] for its adherents.

        1.16.4.1.2. Con:
        Islamic dietary rules promote good health [1871] and are not excessively restrictive.

      1.16.4.2. Pro:
      Islam promotes self-awareness and continuous self-improvement [1872].

        1.16.4.2.1. Con:
        Muslim psychologists often reject findings and practices that contradict religious teachings (p. 182 [1873]).

        1.16.4.2.2. Pro:
        Practices taken from Sufi Islam [1874] have influenced many areas of psychology both within and outside of Islam.

      1.16.4.3. Pro:
      Islam provides practical guidance [1875] for a wide variety of circumstances, fostering a stable life.

        1.16.4.3.1. Pro:
        The collected sayings and actions of the Prophet Muhammad, known as hadith, offer practical solutions to many common situations [1876].

        1.16.4.3.2. Con:
        The traditional values espoused by many branches of Islam are often impractical in modern contexts [1877].

      1.16.4.4. Con:
      Islam requires adherents to fast during Ramadan [1878], which can have negative repercussions on their physical and mental health [1879].

        1.16.4.4.1. Con:
        Islamic practices, such as fasting [1880], teach Muslims self-control and self-discipline [1881].

        1.16.4.4.2. Pro:
        Muslims may feel obliged to fast [1882] during Ramadan despite it not being safe or healthy for them to do so due to uncertainty over whether taking medications is acceptable during fasting (p. 82 [1883]).

        1.16.4.4.3. Con:
        This indicates a need for better understanding of fasting within the medical field, in order that it may better support those who choose to do so (p. 86 [1884]).

    1.16.5. Pro:
    Islam is a complete and well-established system of belief.

      1.16.5.1. Pro:
      The Qur'an is an authentic religious text, and its text has not been changed [1885] for secular or political purposes.

        1.16.5.1.1. Pro:
        Since the Prophet Muhammad's recitations of the Qur'an, there has been a documented chain of transmission [1886] that ensures the preservation and authenticity of the text across generations.

          1.16.5.1.1.1. Pro:
          The entire Qur'an was transcribed directly from the words of the Prophet Muhammad [1887] by followers during his lifetime.

          1.16.5.1.1.2. Con:
          Early copies of the Qur'an discovered in Yemen contain a number of deviations from the accepted text [1888], which indicates that the accepted transmission record of the Qur'an may be inaccurate.

        1.16.5.1.2. Con:
        There is evidence that some sections of the Qur'an were written long before the Prophet Muhammad [1889].

          1.16.5.1.2.1. Con:
          The Qur'anic fragments that supposedly predate the Prophet Muhammad [1890] have not been adequately tested to support such a claim, and they mention him by name.

      1.16.5.2. Con:
      Islamism [1891] has become so enmeshed in the politics of many countries that religious repression [1892] has become commonplace.

        1.16.5.2.1. Con:
        This is an example of leaders scapegoating Islam in order to oppress other groups. The Qur'an itself preaches tolerance [1893] towards those of other faiths.

        1.16.5.2.2. Pro:
        In some countries [1894], criticising or refusing to follow [1895] Islam is punishable [1896] by lengthy prison sentences or, in some instances, death.

      1.16.5.3. Con:
      Islam's holy book, the Qur'an, contains contradictions.

        1.16.5.3.1. Con:
        Islamic epistemology is logically consistent [1897] and marries different sources of knowledge.

        1.16.5.3.2. Pro:
        Islam considers Jesus a prophet [1898], yet early [1899] Christian sources [1900] from well before the Council of Nicaea support the idea that Jesus claimed to be God [1901], which contradicts Islamic doctrine [1902].

      1.16.5.4. Pro:
      The structure and teachings of the Qur'an are completely coherent [1903].

        1.16.5.4.1. Con:
        There are numerous contradictory verses [1904] in the Qur'an, which call its coherence into question.

        1.16.5.4.2. Pro:
        The Qur'an is structured in such a way that many apparent contradictions and debated passages [1905] are made clear through the coherence of its structure.

    1.16.6. Con:
    There is no evidence to support the assertions of Islam.

      1.16.6.1. Pro:
      Islam promotes superstitious beliefs.

        1.16.6.1.1. Pro:
        Islam promotes belief in supernatural beings, known as djinn (p. 351 [1906]).

        1.16.6.1.2. Pro:
        Islam supports the belief that holy men can possess karamat [1907] (magical or miraculous powers).

        1.16.6.1.3. Con:
        Islam has made miraculous predictions [1908].

      1.16.6.2. Con:
      While a few subjects remain contentious, Muslims generally consider their religion to be compatible with science [1909].

        1.16.6.2.1. Pro:
        The Qur'an can be interpreted as specifically instructing the pursuit [1910] of science.

        1.16.6.2.2. Con:
        While Islam remains, in theory, supportive of science, many Muslim nations oppose [1911] scientific principles and advancement.

      1.16.6.3. Pro:
      Islam makes unfounded claims with only the Prophet Muhammad as their witness.

        1.16.6.3.1. Con:
        There were witnesses to the Prophet Muhammad's teachings and practices: those among whom he lived.

        1.16.6.3.2. Con:
        The Prophet Muhammad's credibility is verified by the miracles [1912] granted to him by Allah.

        1.16.6.3.3. Pro:
        The Prophet Muhammad claimed that the entire Qur'an was dictated to him by the angel Gabriel, yet no one else saw or heard the angel [1913].

      1.16.6.4. Con:
      The Qur'an contained many accurate [1914] descriptions of the natural world centuries before they were discovered to be true. This supports the credibility of the Qur'an (pp. 2–4 [1915]).

        1.16.6.4.1. Con:
        The Qur'an was never intended to be a scientific document, and treating it as such abuses its purpose [1916].

        1.16.6.4.2. Pro:
        The Qur'an described how water is an essential component of life [1917] before this was known to science.

          1.16.6.4.2.1. Con:
          It is self evident [1918] that life depends on water, particularly for desert-dwelling people.

  1.17. Thesis:
  Cao Dai [1919] (Đại Đạo Tam Kỳ Phổ Đội)

    1.17.1. Pro:
    Following Caodaism is beneficial to society.

      1.17.1.1. Pro:
      Cao Dai promotes respect and equality for women.

        1.17.1.1.1. Pro:
        Cao Dai teaches that femininity is an essential aspect of divinity (pp. 6–7 [1920]).

        1.17.1.1.2. Con:
        Although Cao Dai allows women to join the priesthood [1921], they remain forbidden from holding the highest offices [1922].

      1.17.1.2. Pro:
      Cao Dai promotes Confucian morality [1923].

        1.17.1.2.1. Pro:
        Confucian moral values [1924], including benevolence, righteousness, propriety, wisdom, and fidelity, promote social order and cohesion [1925].

        1.17.1.2.2. Con:
        Confucian morality is anthropocentric and largely unconcerned with responsible environmental practices (p. 62 [1926]).

      1.17.1.3. Con:
      Devoted followers of Cao Dai are expected to eschew materialism [1927]. However, materialism is often necessary for societies to function successfully.

        1.17.1.3.1. Pro:
        Materialism contributes to a sense of collective culture [1928] and can fuel economic progress (p. 0 [1929]).

        1.17.1.3.2. Con:
        Materialism exacerbates [1930] poverty.

      1.17.1.4. Con:
      Cao Dai's focus on the unification of all religions [1931] is reductive and ignores the diversity of religious belief and culture.

        1.17.1.4.1. Con:
        Western criticism of Cao Dai's hybrid nature ignores the religion's unique history and reflects the dismissive and superior attitude associated with colonialism (pp. 137–138 [1932]), to which Cao Dai, as a new religious movement [1933], offers an alternative.

        1.17.1.4.2. Pro:
        Cao Dai's placement of religious icons from other faiths alongside popular culture icons and political figures can be perceived as blasphemy [1934] by many, and works contrary to interfaith dialogue and understanding.

    1.17.2. Pro:
    Cao Dai is a complete and well-established system of belief.

      1.17.2.1. Con:
      Cao Dai is a relatively new religion.

        1.17.2.1.1. Con:
        While the formalisation of Cao Dai is relatively recent, many of the various teachings and practices it encompasses date back thousands of years [1935].

        1.17.2.1.2. Pro:
        The Cao Dai religion was only established [1936] in the early twentieth century.

      1.17.2.2. Con:
      Cao Dai incorporates teaching and beliefs from a wide range of other religions [1937], which undermines its authenticity as a distinct religion.

        1.17.2.2.1. Pro:
        Some scholars have derided Cao Dai efforts to assimilate the teachings of multiple faiths into a coherent whole (p. 7 [1938]).

        1.17.2.2.2. Con:
        Cao Dai teaches that all religions derive from spiritual truth but have been misinterpreted by humanity [1939]; it seeks to identify the underlying truth behind other traditions.

      1.17.2.3. Pro:
      Cao Dai has established temples [1940], a priesthood [1941], and an official organisational structure [1942].

        1.17.2.3.1. Con:
        Although Cao Dai was originally governed by a three-branch organisational structure, since 1975, the religion has been controlled by the Vietnamese government [1943].

        1.17.2.3.2. Pro:
        Despite having only been created in the 1920s [1944], Cao Dai has established a large number of temples in Vietnam [1945] and across the globe [1946].

      1.17.2.4. Pro:
      Cao Dai is now practised in numerous countries [1947] apart from Vietnam.

        1.17.2.4.1. Con:
        While Cao Dai has spread beyond the borders of the country, opportunities to practise in other countries remain quite limited. For example, France, Germany, and the UK each have only one official Cao Dai temple [1948].

        1.17.2.4.2. Pro:
        Many followers of Cao Dai left Vietnam [1949] after the fall of Saigon [1950], allowing the religion to expand overseas.

    1.17.3. Pro:
    Following Cao Dai has positive benefits for the individual.

      1.17.3.1. Con:
      The idea of family [1951] is central to the Cao Dai philosophy. This is exclusionary to many people.

        1.17.3.1.1. Pro:
        While there is no Cao Dai scripture that refers to it, non-traditional family units, such as those in the LGBTQ+ [1952] community, do not align with its philosophy [1953] of yin and yang.

        1.17.3.1.2. Con:
        Family relationships have a profound influence on both mental and physical well-being (p. 1 [1954]).

      1.17.3.2. Pro:
      The diverse origins of Cao Dai teachings and beliefs encourage adherents to seek inspiration and truth regardless of the source.

        1.17.3.2.1. Pro:
        Cao Dai encourages adherents to pull inspiration from various [1955] religions and scriptures.

        1.17.3.2.2. Con:
        Cao Dai places an emphasis on the truth of particular, sanctioned experiences in a way that promotes emotional thinking over critical thought [1956].

      1.17.3.3. Pro:
      Adherents claim that Cao Dai promotes health [1957] in both body and mind.

        1.17.3.3.1. Pro:
        Cao Dai promotes a vegetarian diet [1958], which is beneficial to both individual health and the environment.

        1.17.3.3.2. Con:
        Any increase in mental and physical health indicators associated with practising Cao Dai may be the result of religious practice [1959] in general, rather than specifically related to Cao Dai or its constituent parts.

      1.17.3.4. Con:
      Cao Dai forbids divorce in all cases other than adultery or disrespect of in-laws (p. 132 [1960]).

        1.17.3.4.1. Con:
        Cao Dai's stance against divorce is intended to liberate [1961] women from male polygamy and protect their children's future.

        1.17.3.4.2. Pro:
        Being forced to stay in an unhappy marriage can have detrimental [1962] effects on an individual and their family.

    1.17.4. Con:
    Cao Dai takes advantage of its followers.

      1.17.4.1. Con:
      The Vietnamese government monitors Cao Dai to prevent exploitation and abuse [1963].

        1.17.4.1.1. Con:
        Cao Dai congregations exist in other countries [1964], who may not have such policies in place.

        1.17.4.1.2. Pro:
        Cao Dai seances have been banned [1965] in Vietnam since 1975.

      1.17.4.2. Con:
      Cao Dai preaches the spiritual equality of people [1966], and discourages the use of religion to take advantage of others.

        1.17.4.2.1. Pro:
        Cao Dai recognises that, while different people may possess different skill sets [1967], equality is universal.

        1.17.4.2.2. Con:
        Cao Dai's attitude towards equality has not prevented unequal representation [1968] in leadership roles within the religion.

      1.17.4.3. Pro:
      Cao Dai has unethically drawn members and donations by promising people access to messages from deceased relatives [1969] via seance.

        1.17.4.3.1. Pro:
        Despite promoting the efficacy of seances, Cao Dai has proclaimed that only those held by the Holy See [1970] have spiritual authority.

        1.17.4.3.2. Con:
        Most Cao Dai seances are focussed on communication with beneficial divine beings, and do not involve expensive offerings (pp. 36–37 [1971]).

      1.17.4.4. Pro:
      There have been allegations of child sexual abuse and institutional cover-ups committed by Cao Dai priests (pp. 14–15 [1972]).

        1.17.4.4.1. Pro:
        Victims of abuse by Cao Dai officials have been threatened, harassed, and forced into hiding in remote areas due to police complicity in protecting the perpetrators (p. 15 [1973]).

        1.17.4.4.2. Con:
        Sexual abuse of children is pervasive in Vietnam [1974]; it is impossible to attribute sexual abuse in Cao Dai independent of the larger context in which it occurs.

    1.17.5. Con:
    Cao Dai is a source of human conflict.

      1.17.5.1. Con:
      Cao Dai is actively critical of colonialism and helps to counteract the harmful effects of Western hegemony (pp. 120–121 [1975]).

        1.17.5.1.1. Pro:
        Cao Dai has been instrumental in providing community and identity to Vietnamese refugees around the world (pp. 114, 128 [1976]).

        1.17.5.1.2. Con:
        Cao Dai's amalgamation of native and foreign influences [1977] and acceptance by the colonial administration [1978] argue against it as an anti-colonial institution.

      1.17.5.2. Pro:
      Cao Dai had its own dedicated army, which at times supported the French against Hồ Chí Minh (p. 124 [1979]).

        1.17.5.2.1. Pro:
        Cao Dai forces under Trình Minh Thế carried out bombings in Saigon [1980] during the early 1950s.

        1.17.5.2.2. Con:
        The Cao Dai army was disbanded [1981] in 1956.

      1.17.5.3. Pro:
      The Tây Ninh Holy See has often imposed an unreasonable amount of control over local Cao Dai temples [1982] both within Vietnam and in other countries, contributing to ongoing conflict.

        1.17.5.3.1. Pro:
        The Holy See has worked with the Vietnamese government to seize control of independent Cao Dai temples [1983].

        1.17.5.3.2. Con:
        Unregistered temples are not allowed in Vietnam, so Cao Dai temples that choose not to belong to any of the 13 accepted branches place themselves in danger of being closed by the government [1984] (p. 231 [1985]).

      1.17.5.4. Con:
      Cao Dai teaches that all religions are one [1986].

        1.17.5.4.1. Pro:
        Since Cao Dai believes that, ultimately, all religions are one and the same, it promotes the idea that all religious teachings are valid [1987].

        1.17.5.4.2. Con:
        Religions cannot all be one because many have core beliefs that are logically incompatible. For example, Hinduism [1988] believes in multiple gods, while the Abrahamic religions [1989] believe in one.

    1.17.6. Con:
    There is no evidence to support the assertions of Cao Dai.

      1.17.6.1. Pro:
      Cao Dai has been heavily influenced by spiritism [1990], including practices, such as the use of Ouija boards, for communicating with God and the deceased.

        1.17.6.1.1. Pro:
        Cao Dai claims to receive divine messages [1991] directly from God via seance [1992].

        1.17.6.1.2. Pro:
        Cao Dai claims to have received divine messages [1993] from the spirit of French writer Victor Hugo [1994].

        1.17.6.1.3. Con:
        The informational veracity and mental health benefits of mediumship have been demonstrated by a number of studies (p. 1 [1995]).

      1.17.6.2. Pro:
      There is no reason to believe that the wide variety of world religions will become unified [1996] as foretold by Cao Dai divination.

        1.17.6.2.1. Pro:
        Global religious diversity has continued to increase since WWII (p. 7 [1997]).

        1.17.6.2.2. Con:
        As a synthesis of all previous religions, the Cao Dai religion itself represents this unification [1998]; there is no expectation that other traditions will convert to Cao Dai.

      1.17.6.3. Con:
      The Cao Dai creation narrative is consistent with the Big Bang theory [1999].

        1.17.6.3.1. Con:
        The Big Bang theory supports the existence of four fundamental forces [2000] at work in the early universe rather than a paired male and female force.

        1.17.6.3.2. Pro:
        Some theories on the Big Bang support the idea that the universal forces may have been unified [2001] at a sufficiently high temperature, only resolving into different forces as the universe cooled.

      1.17.6.4. Con:
      Due to its diverse origins and focus on the limited awareness of humanity, Cao Dai remains open to revising its views based on new scientific evidence (pp. 347–348 [2002]).

        1.17.6.4.1. Pro:
        Cao Dai is not opposed to science, but rather to its misuse and application towards harmful purposes (pp. 46–47 [2003]).

        1.17.6.4.2. Con:
        Cao Dai continues to posit the existence of numerous types of discarnate spirits [2004] despite a lack of evidence, indicating a limited interest in the pursuit of scientific truth.

"The term religion denotes a set of common beliefs and practices pertaining to the supernatural (and its relationship to humanity and the cosmos), which are often codified into prayer, ritual, scriptures, and religious law. These beliefs and practices are typically defined in light of a shared canonical vocabulary of venerable traditions, writings, history, and mythology. As religious traditions are often deeply embedded into specific cultural contexts, these traditions often contain moral codes that outline the relationships that a believer is expected to cultivate with respect to themselves, other believers, outsiders, and the supernatural world. Finally, a common element of many religious traditions is the division of the world in two comprehensive domains, one sacred, the other profane. In this context, religious thought and practice are aimed at delineating and reifying these two disparate realms through personal effort and/or communal ritual."

"In the period following the recording of the niddâ laws in Leviticus, the term
evolved from a narrow definition of the menstrual discharge to include the menstruant herself. This term was also used by Ezekiel (36:17) and Ezra (9:10-11) as a metaphor for moral impurity and degradation. [...] This greatly impacted the woman’s daily life and her status in society. She regularly became the “discharged,” the one that should be avoided during her menstrual period. This led many sects of the Second Temple period to quarantine the woman during her period in separate quarters to protect the larger community from the impurity."

"One particularly striking aspect of Jewish law [...] is the very noticeable and deliberate absence of a specific role definition for women. Had the Law intended to preclude from women all roles but that of mother, it could easily have done so. The Law clearly prescribes the obligations of a husband to his wife and vice-versa, and the obligations of parents to children and vice-versa. It could have made mandatory for women not only marriage and procreation but also the entire range of household duties which would have defined an exclusive role for them.
[...]
Recognizing that women could easily be disadvantaged by that position, the Law attempts to even the playing field somewhat and encourage the exercise of that choice. It does so by religiously incentivizing motherhood, making sure that women who choose to enter motherhood are societally appreciated and socially compensated to the greatest extent possible, just like Article 5(b) would have it."

[23] https://www.bbc.co.uk/bitesize/guides/zv626yc/revision/8
"Judaism’s food laws are known as 
kashrut. These rules are contained within the mitzvot mainly in the Books of Deuteronomy and Leviticus. Following them shows obedience and self-control.

Food that is allowed is called 
kosher. Food that is not allowed is called treif or trefah.

Land animals must have cloven (split) hooves and must chew the cud, meaning that they must eat grass.

Seafood must have fins and scales. Eating shellfish is not allowed.

It is forbidden to eat birds of prey. Only clean birds, meaning birds that do not eat other animals, can be eaten. Poultry is allowed.

Meat and dairy cannot be eaten together, as it says in the Torah: do not boil a kid in its mother’s milk (Exodus 23:19). So Jews who follow these dietary rules cannot eat cheeseburgers for example. Often this rule is extended further, so that people wait up to six hours after eating meat before they eat dairy."

"When discussing the broader Jewish community, there are some divisions that can be made between different types of Jewish people. The largest Jewish ethnic groups are the Ashkenazi, Sephardic, and Mizrahi Jewish communities. There are other smaller Jewish groups, but these are the largest divisions because they each represent a group of Jewish people who migrated during the Diaspora in the 1st and 2nd century CE.

The largest Jewish group in the world, the Ashkenazi people, represent all Jewish communities that settled in northern Europe, especially in Germany. Sephardic Jews are the descendants of those who fled to Iberia and North Africa. Not all Jewish communities fled Roman persecution though; many stayed behind in the Levant and the Middle East and over time would become known as the Mizrahi Jewish people."

"Jewish spirituality has some distinctive characteristics. Unlike some popular forms of meditation, for example, it tends to affirm and incorporate a wide range of emotional experience. The Buddha sits in equanimity; the Hasid dances with the ups and downs of life. And unlike monastic asceticism, which has only rarely occurred in Jewish communities, most Jewish spirituality embraces the sensual world of eating, dancing, having sex, and so on.

For traditionalists, that embrace may still be constrained by law. But even in such cases, one rarely (though not never) finds in Jewish contexts a total sublimation of the material into the spiritual. Embodiment remains in all but the most abstruse of Jewish mystical practices, as does the embrace of joy, sadness, ecstasy, thinking, feeling – the entire range of human psychological and somatic experience."

[45] https://www.myjewishlearning.com/article/the-formation-of-the-oral-torah/
"The Oral Torah refers to the later works of the rabbinic period — most prominently the Mishnah and the Gemara, jointly known as the Talmud — that explain and expound upon the statutes recorded in the Written Torah. The traditional Jewish view is that both these Torahs were revealed at Mount Sinai, but the Oral Torah was passed down as oral tradition (hence the name) until the destruction of the Second Temple in the early part of the Common Era, when fear of it being lost forever led to it being committed to writing for the first time. 

The classic statement of the authority of the Oral Torah is found in the first mishnah in Avot 1:1: “Moses received the Torah at Sinai and transmitted it to Joshua, Joshua to the elders, and the elders to the prophets, and the prophets to the Men of the Great Assembly.” This statement was meant to establish that the traditions practiced during the time of the Mishnah were not human creations, but traced their authority back to Sinai."

[62] www.myjewishlearning.com/article/pacifism-in-jewish-law/
"There is one element of pacifism that is clearly found in the Jewish tradition: the minimization of violence. In nearly all situations where Jewish law allows violence to prevent an evil from occurring, it mandates that the minimal amount of violence be used to accomplish one’s goal. Thus, if one can stop a murderer from committing the crime without the use of deadly force, deadly force is prohibited (Tur, Hoshen Mishpat 425. Maimonides, Murder 1:13). If one can separate combatants without using physical force, non-violent means are certainly preferred (Shulkhan Arukh, Hoshen Mishpat 421:11).

Judaism accepted that it is best not to use violence and violence was the last resort, but when no other action would suffice, violence was morally acceptable and typically mandatory."

[78] https://www.myjewishlearning.com/article/the-death-penalty-in-jewish-tradition/
"The Torah prescribes death as punishment for a number of serious sins — among them murder, idol worship and desecrating the Sabbath — as well as several seemingly less serious ones, like serially disobeying one’s parents. In practice, however, death sentences were rarely carried out by Jewish courts.

A famous Mishnah passage states that a religious court that executed someone once in 70 years was considered destructive. That gap between principle and practice is often cited as evidence that Judaism is deeply uncomfortable with capital punishment, so much so that the rabbis of the Talmud erected significant legal bulwarks to make it exceedingly rare."

The courts may impose another penalty in these cases under certain circumstances. In practice, capital punishment has been carried out only once since the advent of the State of Israel in 1948."

"Judaism includes an ideology and a code of law and ethics affirming that it is an obligation of both the individual and the community to care for the poor and, if possible, to help them earn a living, which we describe as tzedakah.

The tradition does not view the poor as mere passive recipients of others’ largesse: they too have duties incumbent upon them. Additionally, Jewish law requires that Jews provide for communal needs by building and maintaining synagogues, schools, and healthcare institutions of various sorts.

One concept fundamental to the matrix of laws and traditions relating to tzedakah concerns the nature of the relationship between the community and the individual.

Although Judaism affirms that we are all unique individuals created in the image of God, it also asserts that we are fundamentally and inextricably part of a community."

"Vodou is also known as Vodoun, Voodoo, and by several other variants. It is a syncretic religion that combines Roman Catholicism and native African religion, particularly from the religion of the Dahomey region of West Africa (the modern day nation of Benin).
[...]
Vodou began when African slaves brought their native traditions with them as they were forcefully transported to the new world. However, they were generally forbidden from practicing their religion. To get around these restrictions, the slaves started to equate their gods with Catholic saints. They also performed their rituals using the items and imagery of the Catholic Church.
[...]
Vodou is a monotheistic religion. Followers of Vodou -- known as Vodouisants -- believe in a single, supreme godhead that can be equated with the Catholic God. This deity is known as Bondye, "the good god".

Vodouisants also accept the existence of lesser beings, which they call loa or lwa."

It is an organized form of communal support that provides meaning to the human experience in relation to the natural and supernatural forces of the universe."

"Syncretism is the formation of new religious ideas from multiple distinct sources, often contradictory sources. All religions (as well as philosophies, systems of ethics, cultural norms, etc.) possess some level of syncretism because ideas do not exist in a vacuum. People who believe in these religions will also be influenced by other familiar ideas, including their previous religion or another religion with which they are familiar.

Islam, for example, was originally influenced by 7th-century Arab culture, but not by African culture, with which it has no initial contact. Christianity draws heavily from Jewish culture (since Jesus was a Jew), but also bears the influence of the Roman Empire, in which the religion developed for its first several hundred years."

Vodou is a complex system of rites and beliefs that has been shrouded in mystery for centuries, often mistakenly labeled as witchcraft or black magic. Unlike other spiritual practices, there is no central sacred text in Vodou, and its secrets are passed down through oral tradition and guarded by initiated practitioners. Despite this, there is a rich body of literature available, including works on Vodou cosmogony, personal accounts of initiates, and anthropological studies."

[181] https://zenstudiespodcast.com/lineage-in-buddhism/
"In many forms of Buddhism, particularly in Zen, we have a concept called “lineage.” The idea is that the essential aspects of our collective religious tradition have been passed down through the generations from one real, live person to another – from a teacher to a student, who then becomes a teacher and passes the tradition on to their students.

At least in Zen, we keep careful track of these face-to-face relationships, tracing our Buddhist lineages back through time all the way to Shakyamuni Buddha. I mean this quite literally: In Zen chanting services, done daily or at least weekly, we recite the lineage from the Buddha all the way through the last teacher in our particular lineage . . . through a list of over 80 names. In doing so, we not only honor those who have made it possible for us to encounter Buddhism, but also establish the legitimacy of our practice."

"In Buddhism, the word Tripitaka (Sanskrit for "three baskets"; "Tipitaka" in Pali) is the earliest collection of Buddhist scriptures. It contains the texts with the strongest claim to being the words of the historical Buddha.
[...]
At first, these texts were preserved by being memorized and chanted, and as Buddhism spread through Asia there came to be chanting lineages in several languages. However, we have only two reasonably complete versions of the Tripitaka today.

What came to be called the Pali Canon is the Pali Tipitaka, preserved in the Pali language. This canon was committed to writing in the 1st century BCE, in Sri Lanka. Today, the Pali Canon is the scriptural canon for Theravada Buddhism."

"The Pali Canon is the collection of Buddhist teachings as it was recited during the first council meeting of 500 Arahants (enlightened disciples of the Buddha) immediately after the Parinibbāna of the Buddha, i.e. the final complete liberation after the death of his body, around 500 BC.

The teachings or discourses in the Pali Canon are called sutta, which means ‘thread’ or ‘yarn’ and may indicate the interconnection between subjects and explanations.

The suttas were learned by heart during the first centuries and passed on orally from generation to generation.

During two subsequent council meetings, it was checked whether the various monks were still reciting the same version and differences were corrected."

[...]

The goal was to open up the possibility of buddhahood (becoming a Buddha) to all sentient beings. The Buddha ceased to be simply a historical figure, but rather was interpreted as a transcendent figure who all could aspire to become."

"In the beginning the bhikshus lived an itinerant lifestyle, staying at the foot of trees and going to villages and towns to gather their daily meal in an alms bowl and to give Dharma teachings. Although they were dependent upon the lay followers for alms, the optimal condition for achieving liberation was said to be staying in seclusion in the forest, aloof from society. As the sangha grew, the Buddha sent the bhikshus out to disseminate the teachings far and wide saying, “Let not two go in the same direction.” This instruction helped prevent the formation of strong bonds of attachment to places or people. Gradually the bhikshus and bhikshunis began to assemble in seasonal settlements (vihara) for three months during the rainy season to avoid stepping on the insects that abounded during that time. Eventually these viharas became more or less fixed residences, developing into separate communities for the bhikshus and bhikshunis."

There is no question the Dalai Lama is the most famous Buddhist teacher in the world and one of humanity’s moral and spiritual leaders. That’s the result of many factors—his deep realization, his engaging personality, his courageous leadership of an oppressed people, and a message the world needs and wants to hear—but not because he has any formal position or title in world Buddhism."

Let us now investigate the term “absolute truth.” Absolute truth is called paramartha-satya in Sanskrit. Lily the cat has fur and limbs and whiskers and organs. These parts can be further reduced to atoms. I understand that atoms can be further reduced somehow, but I'll let the physicists sort that out.
[...]

[...]

"The two truths doctrine in Buddhism differentiates between two levels of truth in Buddhist discourse, a low, or commonsense truth, and a high, or “ultimate” truth or between a relative and an absolute truth. It is used to avoid confusion between doctrinally accurate statements about the true nature of reality (e.g., there is no “self”) and practical statements that make reference to things that, while not expressing the true nature of reality, are necessary in order to communicate easily and help people achieve enlightenment (e.g., talking to a student about “himself” or “herself”)."

"The Buddha taught there are three main categories of dukkha. These are:

-Suffering or Pain (Dukkha-dukkha). 
Ordinary suffering, as defined by the English word, is one form of dukkha. This includes physical, emotional and mental pain.

-Impermanence or Change (Viparinama-dukkha). 

Anything that is not permanent, that is subject to change, is dukkha. Thus, happiness is dukkha, because it is not permanent. Great success, which fades with the passing of time, is dukkha. 

-Conditioned States (Samkhara-dukkha). 

To be conditioned is to be dependent on or affected by something else. According to the teaching of dependent origination, all phenomena are conditioned. Everything affects everything else. This is the most difficult part of the teachings on dukkha to understand, but it is critical to understanding Buddhism."

[243] https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3807561/pdf/fpsyg-04-00784.pdf
"The 63 meditators in their first experiment had completed 6 months to 5 years of prior Zen practice. In the evening, between 6 and 9pm, one group (led by a Zen master) then meditated for 20 min. The second Zen group served as controls. They relaxed at the same time, without meditating, also for 20 min. Both groups then went to individual cubicles. There they performed three sets of five Remote Associates Tests using a computer screen. (For example, given three words, search your associations for that one fourth word which they all share in common.) The subjects who had just meditated solved more test items (7.00) than did those who had merely relaxed (5.94), p = 0.02.

In the second experiment, the response times of 32 Zen meditators were measured during similar word association tests. Again, the subjects who had just meditated solved more Remote Associates Test items than did their controls (6.82 vs. 4.87), p < 0.01. They also solved them faster."

"Some Buddhists are strictly vegetarian, and others eat meat. Both justify their positions on the basis of Buddhist texts and teachings.

[...]
In one of the key Buddhist texts, The Connected Discourses of the Buddha (Saṃyutta Nikāya), Buddha presents the case against meat-eating within the context of a broader rejection of violence – which causes suffering to both victim and perpetrator. Connected with this is a rejection of working in the meat trades.

But this is challenged by the fact that under the Buddhist Vinaya (moral codes) meat-eating is permissible for monks. A great irony is that the Buddha himself died eating contaminated pork.

As a monk he was obliged to eat whatever was offered, and so it is said that he ate the contaminated pork – some suggest knowingly."

[...]
Kamma, or karma in Sanskrit, is the law of moral causation. All of our volitional thoughts, words, and deeds create an energy that brings about effects and that process is called karma.

The important point here is that Kamma Niyama is a kind of natural law like gravity that operates without having to be directed by a divine intelligence. In Buddhism, karma is not a cosmic criminal justice system, and no supernatural force or God is directing it to reward the good and punish the wicked.

Karma is, rather, a natural tendency for skillful (kushala) actions to create beneficial effects, and unskillful (akushala) actions to create harmful or painful effects."

[286] https://www.britannica.com/topic/Bon-Tibetan-religion
"Bon, indigenous religion of Tibet that, when absorbed by the Buddhist traditions introduced from India in the 8th century, gave Tibetan Buddhism much of its distinctive character.

The original features of Bon seem to have been largely magic-related; they concerned the propitiation of demonic forces and included the practice of blood sacrifices. Later, there is evidence of a cult of divine kingship, the kings being regarded as manifestations of the sky divinity (reformulated in Buddhism as the reincarnation of lamas); an order of oracular priests (their counterpart, the Buddhist soothsayers); and a cult of the gods of the atmosphere, the earth, and subterranean regions (now lesser deities in the Buddhist pantheon)."

"Cognitive dissonance occurs when a person holds two related but contradictory cognitions, or thoughts. The psychologist Leon Festinger came up with the concept in 1957.

In his book A Theory of Cognitive Dissonance, Festinger proposed that two ideas can be consonant or dissonant. Consonant ideas logically flow from one another, while dissonant ideas oppose one another.
[...]
Cognitive dissonance can affect people in a wide range of ways. The effects may relate to the discomfort of the dissonance itself or the defense mechanisms a person adopts to deal with it.

The internal discomfort and tension of cognitive dissonance could contribute to stress or unhappiness. People who experience dissonance but have no way to resolve it may also feel powerless or guilty."

Some of these would not find any commonality with Buddhist philosophy. "It seems that reality is not static, solid or independent and does not consist of singular, isolated material or immaterial factors, but of systems of dependent bodies. Most systems consist of more than two bodies, but there is no system that consists of less than two bodies. In quantum physics we call such fundamental two-body systems: earth/moon, electron/positron, quark/antiquark, particle/field, etcetera. Nagarjuna calls his systems or dependent pairs: mover/distance to move within, fire/fuel, agent/action, viewer/view, etcetera.

Both quantum physicists and Nagarjuna deal with two-body systems or two entities which have bodies that are neither properly separate, nor properly joined together. They do not unite into one, nor do they fall apart. These bodies are not independent and cannot be observed singly because in their very existence and constitution they are dependent on each other and cannot exist or function independently."

[311] https://www.learnreligions.com/buddhism-and-karma-449992
"Karma is a Sanskrit word that means "action." Sometimes you might see the Pali spelling, kamma, which means the same thing. In Buddhism, karma has a more specific meaning, which is volitional or willful action. Things we choose to do or say or think set karma into motion. The law of karma is therefore a law of cause and effect as defined in Buddhism. 

Sometimes Westerners use the word karma to mean the result of karma. For example, someone might say John lost his job because "that's his karma." However, as Buddhists use the word, karma is the action, not the result. The effects of karma are spoken of as the "fruits" or the "result" of karma."

[358] https://www.artsmia.org/art-of-asia/buddhism/buddhism-origins.cfm
"A new Buddhist sect, called Mahayana, emerged in the first century A.D. It elevated the Buddha Shakyamuni to the status of a deity and expanded the pantheon with past and future Buddhas and attendant bodhisattvas. Bodhisattvas were enlightened beings who postponed their own nirvana to assist humankind on the path to salvation, which now became available to laymen as well as to monks. Mahayana Buddhism spread from India along the trade routes to Central Asia and was especially popular in the Far East, including China, Korea, and Japan.

Major theological ferment in India during the seventh century A.D. resulted in a system of esoteric dogma far removed from the original teachings of Buddha. The new complex of doctrines combined elements of Buddhism and Hindu belief with necromancy—that is, sorcery involving spirits of the dead—mystical symbolism, and magical rites. This third form, called Tantrism or Vajrayana Buddhism, was universally popular among the Himalayan cultures."

"Buddhist monks have been leaders in developing various forms of martial arts. The Shaolin Order is perhaps the best known of these, famed for their fighting prowess.

Martial arts would seem to be about as far from non-violence as you can get, but Buddhist forms of martial arts have very strict rules about how violence can be used.

The Shaolin teaching forbids the monk from ever being the aggressor, and instructs him to use only the minimum necessary defensive force. By becoming skilled in physical conflict the monk has a better understanding of violence and is able to use sophisticated techniques to avoid harm, ranging from simple parrying of clumsy blows to paralysing grips and knockout blows in the face of extreme violence - but always using only the amount of force needed to refuse the violence that is being offered to them."

"Science doesn’t have the processes to prove or disprove the existence of God. Science studies and attempts to explain only the natural world while God, in most religions, is supernatural.

Science and religion draw on different aspects of human experience. In science, explanations are based on evidence drawn from observing the natural world and conducting experiments. Because these explanations are based on evidence, they can be checked independently by others.

Scientific questions (aka hypotheses) are framed in ways so that they can be confirmed or disproved by evidence. If the evidence shows that the hypothesis is wrong, the hypothesis must be reframed and tested again or rejected.

Religious beliefs don’t depend only on empirical evidence. They can also be based on faith and typically involve supernatural forces or entities."
[399] https://withalliamgod.wordpress.com/2013/01/01/kierkegaard-the-folly-of-proving-gods-existence/
"Let us call the unknown God. It is only a name we give to it. Now it hardly occurs to the understanding to want to demonstrate that this unknown exists. If, namely, God does not exist, then of course it is impossible to demonstrate it. But if he does exist, then it is also foolishness to want to demonstrate it, for in the very moment the demonstration commences, you would presuppose his existence. Otherwise you would not be­ gin, easily perceiving that the whole thing would be impossible if he did not exist.

One never reasons in conclusion to existence, but reasons in conclusion from existence. For example, I do not demonstrate that a stone exists but that something, which exists, is a stone. The court of law does not demonstrate that a criminal exists but that the accused, who does indeed exist, is a criminal. Whether you want to call existence an addition or the eternal presupposition, it can never be demonstrated."

"By subjective truth I mean that the belief or claim is made true by the subject’s personal preference. So if I said, “The best flavor of ice cream is Butterscotch Ripple,” and you said, “The best flavor of ice cream is Chocolate Peanut Butter,” both claims about the best flavor of ice cream would be true. 
[...]
Objective truth is very different. Objective truth is about the way the world really is. It’s when a belief or claim corresponds with reality. If I say, “Insulin regulates diabetes,” then I am making an objective truth claim about the real world. 
[...]
Every world religion makes claims about the real world. Just take the central claim of Christianity that Jesus physically rose from the dead. This is a historical claim. It’s about an event that took place in time and space. It either happened or it didn’t. He either rose or He didn’t. But, make no mistake, it’s not the kind of thing that can be true for me but not for you."
[423] https://www.formpl.us/blog/observer-bias
"1. Observer-expectancy effect: The observer-expectancy effect can occur in several different ways such as when the researcher unconsciously treats participants in different groups differently, leading to unequal results between groups (for instance, if they are more likely to ask questions or give directions to one group).
[...]
2. Actor–observer bias: The Actor–observer bias refers to the phenomenon in which we attribute our actions to external factors (e.g., “I failed the test because it was too hard”), but attribute other people’s actions to their internal traits (e.g., “She failed the test because she is dumb”).
[...]
3. Hawthorne effect: The Hawthorne effect is a type of observer bias that can occur in research studies in which the behavior of one or more people being observed changes simply because they are being observed. 
[...]
4. Experimenter bias: The experimenter bias of the observer bias is that the researcher believes what they are looking for, and therefore will find it."

"Almost by definition, all religions make unfalsifiable claims. This presents two problems for religion: 

First, by definition, there is simply no way of vetting or validating any unfalsifiable claim or of qualitatively differentiating one from another. This means that, as a matter of pure logic, all unfalsifiable claims are equally (in)valid. 

Second, because unfalsifiable claims are unconstrained by any requirement that they can be falsifiable, the potential number of such claims is literally limited only by imagination. Consequently, we see an explosion of contradictory claims among, and even within, various religions. 

Put one and two above together and you come to an inescapable conclusion: There's no principled way to choosing between a nearly endless number of unfalsifiable religious claims, or of persuading others to your way of thinking. Any decision to accept any particular unfalsifiable religious claim is therefore one made purely from blind faith."

"The argument proposes, in place of an explanation, the assertion that there can be no explanation, i.e. that the fact to be explained is unexplainable.
[...]
 Appeal to Mystery is one form of what is often called an "untestable hypothesis." There are various ways in which a hypothesis might be untestable. Some hypotheses are untestable for merely practical reasons, often involving technological limits or budgetary constraints. (For example, the hypothesis that mass is caused by the Higgs Boson was untestable when the theory was first proposed because a particle accelerator large enough to test the hypothesis had not yet been built.) Appeal to Mystery is untestable for a more fundamental reason. It offers as an explanation something that is mysterious, i.e. untestable by definition."

[538] https://rationalwiki.org/wiki/Pascal%27s_wager
"Blaise Pascal's original wager was as a fairly short paragraph in Pensées amongst several other notes that could be considered "wagers". Its argument is rooted in what has subsequently become known as game theory. The wager argues that the best course of action is to believe in God regardless of any lack of evidence, because that option gives the biggest potential gains. Pascal's original text is long-winded and written in somewhat convoluted philosophy-speak, but it can be distilled more simply:

1. If you believe in God and God does exist, you will be rewarded with eternal life in heaven: thus an infinite gain.
2. If you do not believe in God and God does exist, you will be condemned to remain in hell forever: thus an infinite loss.
3. If you believe in God and God does not exist, you will not be rewarded: thus a finite loss.
4. If you do not believe in God and God does not exist, you will not be rewarded, but you have lived your own life: thus a finite gain."
[539] https://iep.utm.edu/pasc-wag/

If God does not exist then theists will enjoy finite happiness before they die (say 250 units worth), and atheists will enjoy finite happiness too, though not so much because they will experience angst rather than the comforts of religion. Regardless of whether God exists, then, theists have it better than atheists; hence belief in God is the most rational belief to have."

"The Atheist’s Wager, popularised by the philosopher Michael Martin and published in his 1990 book Atheism: A Philosophical Justification, is an atheistic response to Pascal’s Wager regarding the existence of God.

One version of the Atheist’s Wager suggests that since a kind and loving god would reward good deeds – and that if no gods exist, good deeds would still leave a positive legacy – one should live a good life without religion. Another formulation suggests that a god may reward honest disbelief and punish a dishonest belief in the divine."

If we do not believe in the Christian God, the argument continues, then if he exists then we will receive an infinitely great punishment in hell while if he does not then we will have gained little or nothing. The possible outcomes of belief in the Christian God, then, are on balance better than the possible outcomes of disbelief in the Christian God. It is better to either receive an infinitely great reward in heaven or lose little or nothing than it is to either receive an infinitely great punishment in hell or gain little or nothing."

"The truth or falsity of moral judgments, or their justification, is not absolute or universal, but is relative to the traditions, convictions, or practices of a group of persons.

With respect to truth-value, this means that a moral judgment such as ‘Polygamy is morally wrong’ may be true relative to one society, but false relative to another. It is not true, or false, simply speaking. Likewise, with respect to justification, this judgment may be justified in one society, but not another. Taken in one way, this last point is uncontroversial: The people in one society may have different evidence available to them than the people in the other society. But proponents of MMR usually have something stronger and more provocative in mind: That the standards of justification in the two societies may differ from one another and that there is no rational basis for resolving these differences. This is why the justification of moral judgments is relative rather than absolute."

"Moral relativism is the idea that there are no absolute rules to determine whether something is right or wrong. Unlike moral absolutists, moral relativists argue that good and bad are relative concepts – whether something is considered right or wrong can change depending on opinion, social context, culture or a number of other factors.

Moral relativists argue that there is more than one valid system of morality. A quick glance around the world or through history will reveal that no matter what we happen to believe is morally right and wrong, there is at least one person or culture that believes differently, and holds their belief with as much conviction as we do."

[...]

""Moral truths are truths of reason; that is, a moral judgment is true if it is backed by better reasons than the alternatives."

A truth of ethics is a conclusion that is backed by reasons: The correct answer to a moral question is simply the answer that has the weight of reason on its side. Such truths are objective in the sense that they are true independently of what we might want or think. We cannot make something good or bad just by wishing it to be so, because we cannot merely will that the weight of reason be on its side or against it. And this also explains our fallibility: We can be wrong about what is good or bad because we can be wrong about what reason commends. Reason says what it says, regardless of our opinions or desires."

"We also situate our research within the intergenerational solidarity framework, which identifies the dimensions of connection that link family members across generations. Key among these dimensions are affectual solidarity (emotional closeness), structural solidarity (geographic distance), normative solidarity (filial obligation), functional solidarity (help and support), and consensual solidarity (agreement in opinions and beliefs). Affectual, structural, and normative solidarities, to the extent that they are strengthened by religiosity and parental vulnerability, serve as potential mediating factors in the relationship between religious exposure and the provision of help and support.

We conceive of joint religious participation as a form of consensual solidarity or agreement in values, opinions, and beliefs—is linked to better quality and more actively supportive relationships between adult children and their middle-aged and older parents."

"Jainism (pronounced jayn-izm), traditionally known as Jain Dharma, is a dharmic religion with its origins in the prehistory of India, still practiced today by several million people. Jainism has as its religious ideal the perfection of man’s nature. The universe is seen as being eternal—having no beginning and no end—precluding God from being a creator. Perfection of the individual is achieved through the practice of an ascetic life, without any divine assistance. Jain monastics and lay people follow the same fivefold path of nonviolence (ahinsa, or ahimsa); truth (satya); non-stealing (asteya); chastity (brahmacharya); and non-possession or non-possessiveness (aparigraha), but to different degrees."

[642] https://www.researchgate.net/publication/369639711_Navigating_the_Excluded_Middle_The_Jaina_Logic_of_Relativity
"In the field of philosophy, however, the Jaina tradition is known for its distinctive approach to prima facie incompatible claims about the nature of reality. In some ways analogous and in some ways directly contrary to the famous negative dialectic practiced by the Buddhist philosopher Nāgārjuna, the Jaina approach to conflicting views is to seek an integration or synthesis, in which apparently contrary views are resolved into a vantage point from which each view can be seen as expressing part of a larger, more complex truth. Viewed by some contemporary Jaina thinkers as an extension of the principle of ahiṃsā into the realm of intellectual discourse, Jaina logic marks quite a distinctive stance toward the concept of logical consistency."

[...]

[...]

[651] https://www.britannica.com/topic/Jaina-canon
"Jaina canon, the sacred texts of Jainism, a religion of India, whose authenticity is disputed between sects. The Svetambara canon consists principally of 45 works divided as follows: 
(1) 11 Aṅgas, the main texts—a 12th has been lost for at least 14 centuries; 
(2) 12 Upāṅgas, or subsidiary texts; 
(3) 10 Prakīrṇakas, or assorted texts; 
(4) 6 Cheda-sutras on the rules of ascetic life; 
(5) 2 Cūlikā-sutras on cognition and epistemology; and 
(6) 4 Mūla-sutras on miscellaneous topics. 
[...]
The Digambara sect disputes the authenticity of the entire Svetambara canon. The Digambara believe that the original is lost but that the substance of Jaina doctrine has been preserved in a variety of religious and philosophic texts written by various leaders and scholars of the Jaina community over the centuries."
